nytimes.com.title: In Praise of My Typewriter
nytimes.com.text:
I first met my colleague Dylan Freedman at a conference this spring. I already knew about him. He’s kind of a legend at the paper for the investigative work that he has enabled. A software-engineer-turned-journalist, he puts A.I. agents to work to sift through vast data sets and help break stories.
But he’s also a purist when it comes to A.I.-proofing the more creative parts of our work. And what Dylan told me in March was that he writes on a typewriter. I was amazed — and I had so many questions. Today, he writes on what it is about this old-school tech that so effectively keeps him in touch with his humanity (an essay first drafted, of course, on his vintage Olivetti Lettera 22).
An A.I. editor’s ode to his typewriter
By Dylan Freedman
I use artificial intelligence in my work every day.
As the A.I. projects editor for The New York Times, my job is twofold: I enlist A.I. to help reporters find needles in vast haystacks of documents and multimedia data — like the Jeffrey Epstein files or President Trump’s speeches — and I report on developments in A.I. technology. But I also draw a thick line: I never, ever, use A.I. for writing.
Which is why I often write with a typewriter.
I compose most of my first drafts, including for this article, on an Olivetti Lettera 22 from the 1950s. The typewriter provides me with an essential dose of minimalism, a break from the crowded browser tabs and blinking terminal windows on my computer screen.

nytimes.com.title: Can Roof Tiles Reduce Indoor Heat? India Is Finding Out.
nytimes.com.text:
In India, the rising frequency of heat waves and brutal summers is drawing attention to the toll on the human body of repeated exposure to extreme heat — both during the day and night, indoors and out.
There is growing evidence that heat stress affects people’s health and productivity.
The government has largely focused on creating awareness about dehydration and heatstroke, and making action plans aimed at providing relief during periods of extreme heat. Increasingly, researchers and nonprofit groups are experimenting with ways to make indoor living more comfortable for the most vulnerable.
In many parts of the country, indoor temperatures can reach 45 degrees Celsius (113 degrees Fahrenheit) during heat waves, according to India’s National Disaster Management Authority. Roofs contribute as much as 70 percent of the heat in a building when temperatures are high, according to SEEDS, a New Delhi-based nonprofit that works with communities on climate resilience and conducted a study for the disaster authority.
Materials typically used to build homes include cement and brick, which absorb heat during the day and release it slowly at night. Without proper ventilation, these essentially create indoor heat traps.
The SEEDS study proposed multiple ways that roofs could be cooled down, including straightforward solutions like painting them white, which reflects, rather than absorbs, solar heat. Reflective tiles also help because they insulate a home from absorbing too much heat, as do more traditional materials like bamboo and thatch that can be overlaid on top of concrete roofs to provide a layer of insulation and reduce heat absorption. Growing creepers on house walls can reduce heat absorption — although in some cases, domesticated animals render them less effective by chewing on them.

nytimes.com.title: The Threat to a Sanctuary for Children of North Korean Defectors
nytimes.com.text:
Kang Il-kwon, 17, barely remembers North Korea. He was a toddler when his parents fled their totalitarian homeland with him, defecting to South Korea.
But at school, classmates singled him out for his North Korean roots, daring him to insult the North’s leader, Kim Jong-un, as if to test his loyalties.
He thought he had escaped that stigma when he enrolled at a school dedicated to the children of North Korean defectors. After risking their lives to escape the North, defectors arrive in the South to face indifference, prejudice and often a life near the bottom of the social ladder. For many of their children, Yeomyung School in western Seoul is a sanctuary.
Now, this refuge is under pressure.
Neighborhood residents have put up posters at bus stops around the school, demanding that it move elsewhere and calling for the site to host “facilities for us.” In an aging country where communities compete to attract schools, they are campaigning to drive one away because of its students’ backgrounds, although the pupils are South Korean citizens with a constitutional right to education.

nytimes.com.title: A Japanese Volleyball Player Breaks a Taboo
nytimes.com.text:
Rui Takahashi was nervous.
For years the professional volleyball player had lived with a secret: He is gay. In Japan, where gay men and lesbians often struggle to be accepted, he worried that coming out could end his career.
But now, after months of conversations with his family, friends and managers, Mr. Takahashi, 26, had resolved to speak up. On a quiet September night, he broadcast a message for his fans on a radio program.
“I would like to share something with you all today,” he said. “I want to let you know that I am a sexual minority — specifically I am gay. Ever since I was a teenager, I have struggled with this. I am 26 years old now, and for a long time — since I was young — I viewed this part of myself in a very negative light.”
The next morning, Mr. Takahashi avoided looking at his phone, worried he might be criticized for opening up about his sexual orientation. But when he did look, he was surprised to see a flood of rainbow and heart emojis and comments like “Proud of you” and “Cheering you on!”
“I didn’t know how things would turn out, and I thought about the worst-case scenario — that I might even have to quit playing volleyball,” he said in a recent courtside interview after practice with his team, the Suntory Sunbirds, at their training center in Osaka.
Mr. Takahashi is one of only a few professional athletes in Japan who have come out in recent years; the news media has described him as the first male athlete to do so. In Japan, volleyball has a wide following, particularly among women, and some games receive heavy television coverage. Star athletes like Mr. Takahashi are often treated as pop idols, garnering millions of fans online and endorsement deals.

nytimes.com.title: U.K. Releases Files on Peter Mandelson, Ambassador Tied to Jeffrey Epstein
nytimes.com.text:
When Peter Mandelson, Britain’s ambassador to the United States, was fired last year over his friendship with the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, one question came to dominate British political debate:
How had he ever been appointed in the first place?
Twice before he had resigned from government over other scandals. And information about his ties to Mr. Epstein was already in the public domain.
On Thursday, the British government released new documents relating to Mr. Mandelson’s ambassadorial appointment. They followed the release earlier this year by the U.S. Justice Department of files making clear the ties between him and Mr. Epstein.
Other documents remain unpublished while the police investigate accusations that he passed confidential information to Mr. Epstein in the late 2000s. Mr. Mandelson has not been charged with a crime and has denied any criminal wrongdoing.
Here are three things we learned from the new documents.
1. The vetting process seemed like an afterthought.
It emerged earlier this year that Jonathan Powell, Britain’s national security adviser, had described Mr. Mandelson’s appointment as “weirdly rushed.” The documents published Thursday underscored that.
After the prime minister then, Keir Starmer, announced that Mr. Mandelson had gotten the job on Dec. 20, 2024, the vetting process unfolded in fits and starts over the winter holiday and involved several civil servants.
One message, dated Dec. 23, asked, “I wanted to check if Lord Mandelson had returned his completed Conflict of Interest forms and if so if you could send them on to me for processing please?”

nytimes.com.title: Ontario Premier Says He’d Use a Gun to Protect His Family
nytimes.com.text:
Doug Ford, the premier of Ontario, Canada’s most populous province, said he would not hesitate to shoot at violent home intruders to protect his family, responding to growing fears after two high-profile attacks in affluent Toronto neighborhoods.
“I’m a legal gun owner, and I would use it in a heartbeat if someone came in with a gun ready to shoot up my house, my family,” Mr. Ford, characteristically blunt, told reporters at the province’s legislative building in Toronto on Thursday. “Like I said, I’ll blow the guy right through the front door.”
He said his gun and ammunition are kept in separate containers, per Canada’s firearm license holder requirements.
Unlike Toronto’s wave of automobile thefts two years ago, which affected drivers of everyday vehicles as well as owners of high-end S.U.V.s and sports cars, the two recent home intrusions have happened in wealthier areas.
In one of those neighborhoods on Wednesday, intruders broke into a home and fatally shot Michael Eckert, 39, in what police said was a robbery gone wrong.
About a month earlier, a family of four was attacked at their home in the Bridle Path, a prominent affluent neighborhood that is home to many of Canada’s wealthiest people, including the rapper Drake. David Morton, the chief executive of a real estate and corporate housing company, was shot and injured, along with his two daughters, according to investigators, who said that the attackers also struck Mr. Morton’s wife with a hammer. The police arrested a 24-year-old man in connection with the case and are still searching for two others they believe participated.
Overall, home invasions in Toronto, Canada’s largest city, peaked at about 150 in 2024, and are now at 111 for this year, according to police data.
Canada regulates guns at the federal level as a licensed privilege, unlike the United States, where the Second Amendment treats firearm ownership as a constitutional right with laws varying by state.
Canadians have a right to self-defense, within certain limitations, under the country’s criminal code, distinct from “stand your ground” laws in the United States that protect the right to use force against an attacker.

nytimes.com.title: Judges in Israel Suggest Dropping Key Corruption Case Against Netanyahu
nytimes.com.text:
The judges presiding over the long-running corruption trial of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel said on Wednesday that the attorney general should consider dropping one of three cases against him, in which he was charged with bribery.
The judges, who will ultimately decide Mr. Netanyahu’s fate, also questioned whether any offense had been committed in another of the cases. The move dealt a blow to state prosecutors and bolstered Mr. Netanyahu’s position in a trial that has dragged on for six years and divided the country.
The country’s attorney general, Gali Baharav-Miara, was summoned to attend the hearing at the Jerusalem District court on Wednesday and is the only one with the authority to make decisions on whether or not cases should proceed.
Ms. Baharav-Miara told the court that she and her team would take the judges’ suggestions under consideration and were open to all options, based on the evidence, according to a transcript provided by a Justice Ministry spokeswoman.
Mr. Netanyahu was indicted in 2019 on charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust in three separate but interlocking cases. They center on claims that he granted regulatory favors and diplomatic support to business tycoons in exchange for gifts and sympathetic media coverage for him and his family.
Israel’s longest serving prime minister, Mr. Netanyahu, a conservative, has denied any wrongdoing, claiming to be the victim of a witch hunt by a liberal deep state. He and his supporters have long insisted that the cases would collapse in court.

nytimes.com.title: Two Italians Killed in Iranian Drone Attack on Kuwait, Officials Say
nytimes.com.text:
An Iranian drone attack killed two Italians in Kuwait on Thursday, Kuwait’s defense ministry said, in the latest deadly strike on a Gulf Arab state since the United States and Israel started the war against Iran in February.
The unnamed individuals, who worked for the Italian subsidiary of Rheinmetall, the German military group, were working on an air-defense system used by the Kuwaiti Armed Forces, the Italian foreign ministry said in a statement.
The Kuwait defense ministry said the Iranian attack was targeting a “vital site” and the individuals were hit by shrapnel.
Antonio Tajani, Italy’s foreign minister, told lawmakers the attack also injured a Kuwaiti army captain and a Pakistani civilian.
A spokesman for the Iranian armed forces denied that it had attacked Kuwait, in a statement carried by state media.
The episode follows a series of Iranian attacks over recent weeks targeting Gulf Arab states, which host vast American military installations and thousands of U.S. troops. Kuwait and Bahrain said that they had intercepted Iranian attacks this month. In previous attacks, Iran said it had targeted U.S. air-defense systems and launch platforms in Kuwait, and a radar system at a Bahraini air base.
The Middle East has been in limbo for months as talks between the United States and Iran have failed to reach a resolution. Iran has repeatedly targeted Gulf Arab countries since the United States and Israel began the war.
The United States sent more military assets to the Middle East earlier this month, and it struck Qeshm Island in Iran in what American officials said was a defensive measure. Several Gulf countries have lobbied against another round of fighting and pushed for a comprehensive deal to end the war.
In a separate episode on Thursday, the Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen struck a refinery in the Saudi city of Jazan, according to Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki, a spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis.
That attack, which occurred a day after the Houthis said they had struck Ras Tanura, Saudi Arabia’s largest refinery, killed a worker from Nepal, injured others and halted operations while emergency responders brought a fire under control, the Saudi energy ministry said in a statement.
The Houthis have said that they were retaliating for deadly Saudi airstrikes in Yemen.
Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni of Italy expressed her “deepest sorrow” and condolences to the families of the victims of the drone attack, in a statement on social media.
Rheinmetall did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Elisabetta Povoledo contributed reporting from Rome and James Paton from London.

nytimes.com.title: Net Migration to U.K. Falls to Lowest Level Since 1997, Excluding Pandemic
nytimes.com.text:
Net migration to the United Kingdom has fallen to 77,000, its lowest level in almost three decades, excluding the Covid pandemic, according to official figures released on Thursday.
The latest statistics, which are provisional estimates for a 12-month period ending in June, underscore a huge drop in recent years as successive British governments have worked aggressively to cut both legal and illegal immigration following a public backlash.
Leaders around the world have seized on migration as a major political issue, with populist parties making gains in several countries and pushing the political center toward stricter rules on immigration. As migration crackdowns have played out across the United States and Europe, the flow of newcomers has slowed in many places.
“This is something which we are also seeing in other high-income countries,” said Ben Brindle, a senior researcher at the Migration Observatory, a research group based at the University of Oxford. In places like Britain, “it’s mostly the result of policy changes.”
Meghan Benton, director of the global program at the Migration Policy Institute, said that she thinks of some national policies, like Canada’s, as “topiary” — trying to trim migration around the edges in response to political pressure and practical needs — and others, like that of the United States, as “chain saw.”
Britain, she said, falls somewhere in the middle.
“Generally, the overall trend is to respond to this public trust crisis by reducing numbers overall,” Ms. Benton said, explaining that the public are worried about high-profile instances of uncontrolled migration.

nytimes.com.title: After Cyberattacks and Bomb Threats Hit Europe, Survivalism Goes Mainstream
nytimes.com.text:
Sales of canned goods, shelf-stable milk and paper maps are up in Europe. Grocers on the continent are selling emergency preparedness packages. Survivalists have broadened their marketing to target demographics like women and older people, and influencers are offering prepping tips.
Unsettling recent events including cyberattacks and extreme weather have persuaded more Europeans to pack emergency kits and go bags, according to interviews, experts and government officials. The episodes fueled concerns about the vulnerability of everyday life.
In stockpiling essentials like windup radios, pocketknives and cash in different currencies, Europeans are embracing the kind of disaster preparedness that was once the domain of survivalists and conspiratorial corners of the internet.
“It does just feel like we’re entering a phase of uncertainty where you don’t properly know what’s going to happen,” Daniel Monger, who lives in a village in the English Midlands, said. He packed his first emergency kit a few weeks ago and quickly began selling assembled kits after struggling to find some of the products himself.
When the British government unveiled a national disaster preparedness campaign in late October, Mr. Monger, 24, said it “was a bit of a wake-up call” to a changing world.
The British announcement came around the time of a cyberattack that targeted supermarket refrigeration systems in eight European countries, and hoax bomb threats grounded flights and forced thousands of schools to evacuate in Italy, Ireland, Poland and elsewhere. A global Microsoft outage also left government agencies and hospitals nearly everywhere without email access, and measures elsewhere like the nationwide ground stop in the United States added to a global sense of precariousness.

cnn.com.title: ‘Could you send me some nude photos?’: Soccer players accuse coach of abuse, urge FIFA to act in lightning rod case
cnn.com.text: As far back as she can remember, soccer player Florencia Mercau has supported one of Argentina’s best-known teams – River Plate. So when in 2014 the call came telling her she would be moving to Buenos Aires to join the club of her childhood heroes, Mercau was over the moon. For a young girl who grew up in a poor neighbourhood of Marquesado, in San Juan province, “it was the best thing I’ve ever been told,” Mercau said. “I’m a River fan. The chance to be at (Argentina’s) biggest club, and to know that, after the tough childhood I had, that I was able to reach River… It was my dream and I’ll give it my all.” But that dream quickly began to unravel, she said, when a week after she joined, age 20, she met the club’s recently hired new coach, Diego Guacci. “Not even a day had gone by and he sent me a text, addressing me as ‘Flor’ and saying, ‘Could you send me some nude photos,’” Mercau told CNN in an exclusive interview, the first time she has publicly discussed the abuse she says she endured. She says she deleted the texts and fought off Guacci’s advances, but that only provoked what she felt was a more dangerous version of him. “He’d come to me in practice and grab me from behind… he’d tell me, ‘delete the conversation, delete it because if you don’t, I will kill you and all your family,’” she said. “I didn’t even want to tell my mom because I thought it was wrong – I thought I was the one who was wrong.” Traumatized by the abuse, she said, but still wanting to play for the team she loved, Mercau found herself in an impossible position. One day, she said, she felt she could no longer continue. “In that moment I made the worst decision, I said I don’t want to live anymore, I don’t want to endure it anymore,” she said. “I don’t want to suffer anymore; I don’t deserve it because I always gave my best.” Mercau, now 32, survived the suicide attempt and is one of five Argentinian footballers to recently file a complaint with FIFA, soccer’s international governing body, against Diego Guacci. They accuse the former River Plate and Argentinian women’s national youth team coach of inappropriate conduct, including sexual harassment, threats and psychological abuse. But this isn’t the first time FIFA has been alerted to his alleged abuse. In 2020 and 2021, five other women filed a complaint alleging sexual harassment and psychological abuse, and even testified in an official FIFA investigation into Guacci. An investigatory committee recommended sanctioning him in 2021, but Guacci – who has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing – emerged from the ordeal mostly unscathed. “The Chamber believes that the evidence on file is insufficient to corroborate, to its comfortable satisfaction, the Players’ account of the events,” the adjudicatory chamber of FIFA’s Ethics Committee said in its findings. “Notwithstanding the above, the Chamber wished to stress that such conclusion shall not be considered as a recognition that the reported facts did not occur.” The decision left Guacci, who had moved on from River Plate to coach U15 and U17 women at the Argentinian national team, free to continue coaching, and the players in shock. It was “an absolute blow,” one of the players who filed the initial complaint, Gabriela Garton, told CNN. “If five players’ testimony is not enough, what do you need?” The new complaint has now fed into a political firestorm in Argentina, after Guacci’s wife, Andrea Guacci, brought further attention to the case by helping draft legislation that would increase jail time for those convicted of falsely accusing someone of a crime involving gender violence, sexual abuse, or crimes against minors. Critics say the legislation, which is expected to be voted on soon in the senate, is an alarming attempt to erode hard-won protections for women under a right-wing government which critics say has shown little concern for gender-based violence. Diego Guacci declined CNN’s request for an interview and did not respond to questions regarding the allegations against him, which he denies. The first investigation Garton, a former Argentinian national team player, was one of the first to file a complaint about Guacci’s behaviour, six years ago. Garton was 23 when she began playing for River Plate and had been at the club for a year when Guacci joined in 2014. Initially she had been excited to work with him, saying he seemed “really enthusiastic about women’s football” and appeared to want to “push the game forward.” But then Garton says the red flags started appearing. First, three or four players who’d worked with him before left the club, saying they “didn’t want to work with him,” she said. Months later she found out why. One of her teammates told her that Guacci had exposed himself to her, sending nude photos – and asking for nudes in return – and that player’s testimony was also part of the original FIFA investigation against Guacci. After that, Garton says she began to notice Guacci’s coercive behavior. One instance, after a difficult loss to rivals Boca Juniors, was so vile she still remembers it vividly, she said. “After the game, he said something along the lines of like, ‘if you girls play like that again, I’m going to put you all in the showers and… f**k you in the ass,’” Garton recalled. She too began thinking about leaving the club, while at the same time focusing on her call-up to the Argentinian women’s national team. That didn’t sit well with Guacci, she said. “He was saying that my behaviour was quite despicable, and that at the end of the day, I was like everyone else on the national team, willing to pull down my pants and be raped to be on the national team,” Garton said. Garton’s testimony became part of a FIFA investigation process that lasted roughly two years after soccer’s ruling body was first made aware of the allegations against Guacci in January 2020 and began a preliminary probe. FIFPRO, a global organization that represents professional soccer players, became involved the following month. By November 2020, FIFPRO had provided FIFA with a full report on behalf of four players, acting as legal representative for them. A fifth player came forward in 2021. “The investigation was almost non-existent. The procedure was extremely slow and sloppy,” FIFPRO’s senior legal counsel Alexandra Gómez Bruinewoud told CNN. FIFA launched formal investigation proceedings in April 2021 and invited Guacci to respond. In September of that year, he submitted a nine-page statement rejecting the accusations. Despite his rebuttal, the investigatory chamber found him to have breached several articles of FIFA’s Code of Ethics. It concluded that he sexually harassed one of the players and psychologically abused the others, recommending to the adjudicatory chamber that he be sanctioned. But that never happened. Soon afterwards, the three-man adjudicatory panel concluded there wasn’t enough evidence to impose any sort of sanction. “How many players need to present their testimony for a panel – a panel composed only of men – to decide that there was abuse?” Gómez Bruinewoud said. Guacci and his supporters, chief among them his wife Andrea, have publicly spun the outcome as an acquittal and launched a PR and legal campaign against the accusers, filing lawsuits against the five players and one journalist that became involved in the story. The same players and said journalist have also filed counter defamation claims against Guacci and those cases are still ongoing in Argentina. “It’s all lies, all lies,” Guacci repeatedly alleged in interviews on Argentinian television and social media segments, claiming the five players didn’t have the courage to show up for his hearing. “We were never invited to the hearing with the adjudicatory chamber,” Gómez Bruinewoud countered. “We found out there was a hearing with Guacci after it happened.” Adding to the players’ distress, Guacci also publicly named four of the women he believed were accusing him during the investigation. The players’ lawyers say FIFA then compounded the violation by publishing their initials in its final report, making their identification much easier. The outed players felt they had little choice but to publicly defend themselves in the face of a brutal smear campaign, which saw them attacked on social media by the Guaccis and their allies. The players and those who spoke out on their behalf say they were pressured and even threatened by Guacci’s supporters in a bid to make them walk back their accusations. Despite the pressure, Gabriela Garton, Luana Muñoz, Aldana Cometti and Camila Gómez Ares have maintained their version of events – the fifth player, known only as player E, has too, but decided to remain anonymous. CNN asked FIFA about the initial accusations against Guacci, and the fresh allegations put forward this year. Soccer’s governing body did not respond to questions sent by CNN, but defended its ruling and the procedures it has in place, saying it takes “any allegation of misconduct reported to it, including sexual abuse and harassment, extremely seriously and has a clear process in place.” It added that investigations follow the principle of due process, in accordance with its own code of ethics, guided by the law in Switzerland – where it is based – the European Court of Human Rights and the Court of Arbitration for Sport. FIFA also did not confirm or deny it was looking into fresh allegations against Guacci, though insiders have told CNN it is normal for the organization not to disclose whether or not it has opened an investigation. Law on false accusations Although FIFA didn’t sanction Guacci, the Argentine Football Association (AFA) decided not to renew his contract. Guacci and his wife say the accusations against him destroyed his career and he has since moved to Italy. CNN was able to trace Guacci to a small town in central Italy. Two social media announcements from FC Fossacesia indicate he has been working with a youth team since July. The club confirmed Guacci had been volunteering with the team but provided no additional details. CNN reached out to Guacci and exchanged several emails with the former River Plate and Argentina manager over more than a month, submitting multiple requests for an interview. In his responses, Guacci repeatedly denied the allegations but declined to sit down for an interview or to answer any questions. Guacci claimed ongoing defamation lawsuits in Argentina prevented him from speaking publicly. Guacci has said in media appearances that he would like to resume his coaching career in Argentina, where the political climate has shifted under the right-wing government of President Javier Milei. Andrea Guacci has been a vocal advocate of the draft bill that would increase penalties for making false accusations of violence, proposed in 2024. She has presented her husband’s case as an example of a life forever damaged by what the couple say were false allegations against him. In Argentina, false accusations of gender-based violence account for a tiny fraction of complaints, according to a 2026 study by Argentina’s public prosecutor’s office. Andrea Guacci did not respond to CNN’s requests for comment. For Luana Muñoz, one of the five athletes who first filed the complaint against Guacci, the fact FIFA’s controversial decision is now being used by Andrea Guacci to promote this agenda is particularly worrying. “We started this to protect women, to protect kids, and it’s concerning because it will mean that they will take rights away from women,” Muñoz told CNN of the proposed bill, adding that it could make it even more difficult for victims of abuse to come forward. Both Muñoz and Garton said they were hopeful that with five more women coming forward in the new complaint against Guacci, soccer’s governing body would reopen the case. “You see women’s football and women’s rights in the world, how far we’ve come, but when things like this happen they kind of make you put your feet on the ground and understand there’s so much more that we have to fight for,” Muñoz said. Mercau has stayed out of the spotlight since her suicide attempt. But she told CNN that she too was committed to pursuing the case despite fears of retribution. “I’m scared to walk, I’m even scared to breathe,” she said. “But it’s that fear that won’t let me rest; that’s why I’m here today – so that all this can come to an end and I can get on with my life in peace.”

cnn.com.title: American farmers are paying the price for US aid cuts halfway across the world
cnn.com.text: Jim Darnell’s family has been farming beans in Nebraska for three generations, but he says the past few years have been some of the more difficult for his crops and his sales. And the future, the 77-year-old said, also looks tough. “It’ll be a difficult time in farming for the next year,” Darnell told CNN. Farmers like Darnell in western Nebraska have suffered blow after blow in recent years. Extreme drought, cripplingly high prices for fuel and fertilizer, and the disruption of a market for surplus crops – America’s foreign food aid – have weakened the bottom line for his business, JD Farms. Washington’s funding cuts to food assistance programs and the abrupt dismantling of the US Agency for International Development early last year meant that farmers and crop elevators weren’t able to sell as much to aid programs like Food for Peace or the McGovern-Dole Food for Education Program, which feed millions globally. “Anytime we lose an end user, it eventually affects our prices… So, it did disrupt it for the price of beans,” Darnell said, adding that he is proud to contribute to any program that reduces global hunger. “That’s a great thing – any program that helps. And beans are a great thing to put in a program like that, because they’re great in protein and they store so well.” The United States has a long, bipartisan history of backing food assistance programs aimed both at helping domestic farmers and tackling global hunger. Food for Peace, which purchases agricultural products from American farmers each year to send to food-insecure populations overseas, has fed more than 4 billion people since it was created in the 1950s, according to the US State Department. “That’s a win-win for everybody,” said Cathy Kaufman, whose husband Mike runs a family farm that has been growing beans and corn for five generations. “It’s kind of amazing when you think that Nebraska farmers can help to achieve world security, as an end product, and feed the hungry.” But Congress recently cut government funding for Food for Peace by about 25%, from about $1.62 billion annually to $1.2 billion for FY2026. And the Trump administration has sent even less of that money out the door. The amount spent by the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) on food aid commodities in 2025 and 2026 has fallen by about 55% compared to the spending levels in 2024 under the Biden administration, according to an analysis of USDA data conducted by the Center for Global Development (CGD). “The impact of this is playing out in human lives in the most catastrophic way imaginable,” said Sam Vigersky, an international affairs fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, a New York-based think tank. “These are some of the most… impactful programs that the US government has anywhere in the world,” said Vigersky, who previously served as a senior humanitarian adviser to the US ambassador to the UN. “When you take money out of a program like Food for Peace, you’re taking food out of the mouth of starving children.” The White House originally proposed cutting the entire budget for Food for Peace and the McGovern-Dole International Food for Education program. But “Congress has really signaled continued support for food commodity programs,” according to Jocilyn Estes, a senior policy analyst at CGD. Food assistance programs have historically been protected by a bipartisan coalition of agricultural interests, shipping companies and humanitarian organizations. Experts have long noted that shipping bulk purchases of agricultural commodities overseas isn’t the most efficient way to administer humanitarian assistance, and in many cases, food could be purchased closer to crisis areas. “But right now, given the myriad of challenges and crises that the world’s most vulnerable populations are facing, I think any amount of bipartisan support for human care and assistance is good, and we should be really focusing in on how to improve that,” Estes told CNN. A spokesperson for the White House Office of Management and Budget told CNN that Food for Peace and McGovern-Dole are “inefficient, wasteful, and do not align with President Trump’s America First agenda,” and that they create “permanent dependency on the American taxpayer.” The budget preserves “far more efficient food aid programs,” the spokesperson added. The White House has called for cutting the funding, however, rather than redirecting it to other programs. Kaufman, who volunteers as an advocate for food assistance through the Christian nonprofit World Vision, said she believes cutting food aid programs not only threatens food security but also diminishes the United States’ global leadership. “Foreign assistance is less than 1% of our budget. I’m sorry, but that’s not going to balance our budget or even close,” Kaufman told CNN. “What it will do, though, is put our country in jeopardy of not being a world leader.” Revamped program drops countries at famine risk During the Trump administration’s dismantling of USAID, the Food for Peace program was transferred to the USDA. Some humanitarian experts have criticized that shift, arguing that the USDA lacks the same expertise in emergency management. The list of countries that the program supports has been heavily reworked under the USDA. Food for Peace provided American-grown food aid to seven non-emergency countries this year, while dropping several nations experiencing famine risk, like Somalia and South Sudan. “The administration has been clear that need is only one of the criteria, and that political objectives of the administration and the relationship with those governments is an important factor for them,” a senior official from a nonprofit told CNN, speaking anonymously because it still has US government contracts. “There are a lot of countries that are in need that, really, we’d like to see on that list.” In Yemen, which faces emergency levels of food insecurity after years of conflict, the Trump administration cut all foreign aid, including food assistance. Even still, farmers and agriculture industry workers told CNN that they applaud the USDA for its work picking up Food for Peace. Meanwhile, the senior nonprofit official told CNN that almost all its McGovern-Dole projects, which feed hungry schoolchildren overseas, were terminated in 2025, but “now some are coming back.” The official described the last two years as “unbelievably disruptive and confusing,” but added that the USDA has a “good team” working to resuscitate the work. The USDA declined to answer questions from CNN about Food for Peace but said in a recent statement that since the program was transferred “there has been over $1 billion invested in awards and agreements in principle for international emergency food assistance which utilizes approximately 467,000 metric tons of U.S. commodities.” Vigersky also noted that many countries are not only dealing with the end of Food for Peace deliveries but also facing cuts to other US aid programs plus cuts by other international donors. Grace Mavhezha, World Vision’s communications manager in Sudan, said “the funding uncertainty makes it increasingly difficult to maintain the planned scale of assistance.” The organization had to alter its food distribution plans and ration sizes this year due to funding reductions. She told CNN that “foreign food assistance is not simply about sending food overseas; it is about saving lives, protecting children, supporting families and giving vulnerable communities an opportunity to survive and recover from crises.” ‘Unbelievable need, globally’ American food companies and grain elevators up and down the country also play a role in food aid programs and are feeling the impacts of the aid cuts and last year’s sudden disruptions. Didion Inc., a family-run agricultural processing company in Wisconsin, told CNN that last year the supply chain was severely disrupted for its cereal product that’s used to treat acute malnutrition in young children overseas. The company had to suspend production, according to chief executive Riley Didion, but things have started moving again this year. “When that program stops, we also buy less corn from the farmers that are in our area,” Didion told CNN. “But the biggest impact by far will be people who don’t get fed.” Didion traveled to Kenya last October for meetings about improving the aid supply chain and the delivery of products to a refugee camp in Kakuma. “When I was there, there was a recent cut, and most of the folks were living off 30% or 40% of what they would normally get. That was really difficult to see,” he said. “There is an unbelievable need, globally.” He added that his firm is proud that its acute malnutrition products don’t bear the company’s own logo, but rather the American flag. “There’s an unbelievable gratitude that our team has the ability – and that our community has the ability – to play a part in feeding people all over the world.” CNN’s Becky Pinnington contributed to this report.

cnn.com.title: European Central Bank set to appoint its first Spanish leader
cnn.com.text: The European Central Bank is set to name Pablo Hernández de Cos as its next president, marking the first time that Spain will helm one of the world’s most influential central banks. De Cos, whose appointment must still be formally approved, will succeed Christine Lagarde when she steps down in February after euro area member states endorsed his appointment, according to President of the European Council, António Costa. His appointment and that of two new ECB board members is expected to be finalized in December, Costa said on X, at a meeting of the European Council, a body comprised of European Union leaders that sets the bloc’s political agenda. This would be the first time that someone from Spain holds the top job at the ECB, which is tasked with keeping inflation in check across the 21 countries that use the euro currency. The institution has had four presidents since it was founded in 1998. Lagarde, who was appointed in October 2019, announced last month that she would step down eight months before her term ends in order to speak more freely on issues beyond monetary policy. De Cos formerly served as governor of Spain’s central bank and is now general manager at the Bank for International Settlements, an international institution that is commonly referred to as the “central bank for central banks.” He will have to contend with inflation currently running at 4%, twice the ECB’s target. He will also take over at a time of heightened bond market turmoil, particularly in France, where high debt levels threaten a fiscal crisis in the European Union’s second-biggest economy. While the ECB has so far left it up to the French government to fix its budgetary woes, it could be forced to intervene if a sharp rise in bond yields destabilizes other European economies and financial markets. French president Emmanuel Macron said on X that “a consensus emerged” among eurozone member states on the ECB nominations. Macron added that he welcomed a “balanced trio of individuals serving the stability and prosperity of the euro area, with Pablo Hernández de Cos as President and Laurence Boone and Markus Brunnermeier on the Executive Board.” Boone is a French economist and head of corporate and investment banking at Santander in France. Markus Brunnermeier is a German economist and a Princeton University professor. He is set to replace Philip Lane as ECB chief economist, while Boone will take over from Isabel Schnabel to oversee market operations. ‘Complex backdrop’ for new leaders Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez also welcomed the selection of De Cos in a post on X in which he acknowledged two other Spaniards in governing positions within the EU: Teresa Ribera, who is an executive vice president at the European Commission, and Nadia Calviño, who is president of the European Investment Bank. “In short, a Spain that is leading in Europe as never before,” he wrote. Spain, which has transformed from a casualty of the eurozone debt crisis to the region’s fastest-growing major economy, will hold a snap general election Sunday that could see Sánchez’s Socialist party defeated by right-leaning contenders. France, Italy and Poland will all hold elections next year, which could see right-wing political parties make significant gains. The ECB’s new leadership faces a “complex backdrop” of persistent inflation, “public indebtedness,” geopolitical and technological shifts and “consequential elections across Europe over the next year,” Deutsche Bank economists Mark Wall and Michael Kirker wrote in a note Thursday. “The renewal of ECB leadership comes at a significant time,” they said.

cnn.com.title: Discovery of an Egyptian structure hidden for 2,600 years offers clues to ancient engineering
cnn.com.text: Archaeologists have rediscovered an ancient Egyptian structure that was hidden for nearly 2,600 years, with the first clues spotted from space. Using satellite radar imagery, researchers detected evidence of buried architectural features across an area larger than a football field in Egypt’s Nile Delta — a flat, low-lying region with soft, sediment-rich soil. To peer deeper beneath the surface, the team used ground instruments to send small electrical currents into the soil and measured how easily they passed through different materials, a technique known as electrical resistivity tomography, or ERT. The work allowed archaeologists to identify the ancient structure — as well as insights about its foundation that could shed new light on ancient Egyptian building practices. The researchers, who published the findings this year in the journal Acta Geophysica, conducted their investigation at the ancient city of Buto, once an important political and religious hub in northern Egypt with origins dating back to the fourth millennium BC. The city was a center of worship for Wadjet, a cobra goddess believed to protect lower Egypt. What remains of the ancient city is now a complex archaeological site, with thousands of years of history preserved beneath layers of sediment and building debris. Some of the oldest traces lie below groundwater level, which makes traditional excavations challenging because water can seep into dig sites and limit access to buried structures. By combining satellite data with ground-based surveys, researchers were able to distinguish archaeological evidence from different periods of the city’s history without the need for extensive excavation. In addition to the much older mudbrick structure from ancient Egyptian times, the team detected evidence of settlements believed to date to either the Ptolemaic period (305 to 30 BC) or the Roman period (30 BC to AD 395). The findings underscore the growing importance of pairing traditional archaeological fieldwork with advanced noninvasive technologies to uncover new details about the ancient world, said Hussein Bassir, an Egyptologist and director of the Antiquities Museum at Bibliotheca Alexandrina in Egypt, who was not involved in the study. An ancient sacred site About 10 to 20 feet (3 to 6 meters) beneath the surface, the ancient mudbrick structure measures an estimated 82 by 66 feet (25 by 20 meters) and dates to Egypt’s 26th dynasty, also known as the Saite period, which spanned the seventh and sixth centuries BC. The building’s purpose remains a mystery, but researchers suspect it served a religious function, possibly as a tomb, shrine or residence for priests, according to the study. Survey data guided the team’s excavations at the site, which uncovered several objects associated with religious practices, including amulets and an altar. “Buto was one of the most important religious and political centers of ancient Lower Egypt,” Bassir said in an email. “The identification of a substantial mudbrick structure, potentially associated with religious or administrative activities, adds another important dimension to our understanding of this historically significant site.” But what lies underneath the structure was particularly striking to the study authors. The researchers detected a layer of sand about 20 to 23 feet (6 to 7 meters) underground that they believe ancient Egyptians deliberately placed to create a level, stable foundation. The discovery could offer clues to how ancient builders adapted their construction techniques to the soft, flood-prone ground of the Nile Delta, according to the study. The Nile Delta’s clay-rich soil poses a challenge for construction because the ground expands when wet and shrinks as it dries, potentially damaging structures over time. Ancient builders may have added the sand to level out the ground, provide a sturdier foundation or spread the building’s weight more evenly across the soil beneath it, Bassir said. “This discovery reminds us that many chapters of ancient Egyptian history remain hidden beneath the ground,” Bassir said. While further archaeological investigations are needed to confirm the sand’s intended purpose, the new findings could provide valuable evidence of ancient Egyptians’ understanding of foundation engineering, he added. A new era of archaeology The study authors’ methods could offer a window into other unexplored chapters of Buto’s past. They suspect that another structure, in addition to the one recently identified at the site, may lie beneath a thick layer of clay — a possibility they plan to investigate in future research. The potential of these tools also extends far beyond ancient Egypt. Only a small fraction of Buto has been excavated, which is the reality at many archaeological sites, said Robert Littman, director of excavations at Tell Timai, another ancient settlement in Egypt’s Nile Delta. At Tell Timai, for example, archaeologists have excavated only 1% to 2% of the site despite more than a century of intermittent fieldwork, according to Littman, who was not involved in the study. “Excavation is a slow and meticulous process,” Littman said. “The use of satellite imagery and ERT combined provides a rapid and inexpensive method of seeing what is under the surface without months or years of digging.” By combining these technologies, archaeologists can identify underground structures and determine which areas are most promising to dig, saving both time and money, he added. Advancing technologies such as artificial intelligence, satellite imagery and underground mapping tools may help archaeologists piece together entire ancient landscapes, identify previously unknown settlements and better understand how past civilizations interacted with their surroundings, Bassir said. “Nevertheless, technology will never replace the archaeologist,” he said. “Ultimately, the future of archaeology lies in bringing together technological innovation, scientific investigation, and traditional archaeological expertise.”

cnn.com.title: Israel intensifies assassinations in Gaza as US urges Netanyahu to proceed with ceasefire plan
cnn.com.text: Israel has intensified its campaign of targeted assassinations in Gaza, striking and killing Hamas commanders and political leaders, as the Trump administration urges Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to proceed with the US-brokered ceasefire plan. On Thursday, the Israeli military killed Khaled Abu Nada, a senior member of Hamas’ Political Bureau and the organization’s Deputy Minister of Education, in a strike in central Gaza. According to a statement from Hamas, the strike on his residential apartment also killed his wife. The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said the killing of Abu Nada would disrupt Hamas’ “financial operations and its ability to formulate economic policy.” Hamas said the attack was the result of Israel’s “policy of systematic assassinations” and warned that “targeting civilian homes constitutes a continuous breach of the ceasefire agreement in Gaza and a flagrant violation of all international and humanitarian laws, norms, and conventions.” Since the nominal ceasefire was signed more than a year ago, Israel has carried out near-daily strikes on Gaza to target Hamas. According to the Palestinian Ministry of Health, more than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza in Israeli strikes or military operations over that period. In recent weeks, Israel has escalated those strikes. On Wednesday, Israel struck and killed Muhammad Abu al-Aouf, the head of Hamas’ internal security apparatus in northern Gaza. A day earlier, the IDF killed al-Aouf’s commander, Naeem Muhammad Abu Nahal, who led Hamas’ internal security across Gaza. In each of these cases, the IDF said the assassination was a “blow” to Hamas’ leadership capabilities, even as the militant organization has firmly entrenched its power in the half of Gaza not occupied by the Israeli military. The previous week, the IDF carried out strikes nearly every day targeting Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad, from platoon leaders to commanders of Nukhba, a special force within Hamas’ military wing. In each case, the IDF issued virtually the same justification: “Throughout the war, and particularly recently, the terrorists advanced attacks against IDF troops and Israeli civilians and operated to restore the capabilities of terrorist organizations in the Gaza Strip, in systematic violation of the ceasefire.” Hamas blamed both Israel and the US-backed Board of Peace for the ongoing attacks. The group said the board “bears political and moral responsibility for the continuation of these crimes as a result of its silence and failure to halt the aggression, and its continued provision of cover and support to the occupation.” The board was established by the Trump administration and backed by a UN Security Council resolution to advance the Gaza ceasefire plan signed in October 2025. But the plan stalled within weeks of its implementation, and much of Gaza remains in ruins. Globally isolated On Tuesday, Netanyahu spoke by phone with Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, who played a crucial role in crafting the ceasefire deal, according to an Israeli source who said they discussed Gaza. According to Axios, Kushner urged Netanyahu to carry out Israel’s obligations under the ceasefire plan, which would require Israel to stop striking Gaza and begin withdrawing forces that occupy more than half of the enclave’s territory. But Netanyahu has refused to make progress on the 20-point plan until Hamas is completely disarmed. Last week, Defense Minister Israel Katz said that Israel “will not withdraw from the current lines of the security zones” until Hamas is “dismantled.” He also warned that Israel is ready to occupy more of Gaza. Hamas has refused to unilaterally disarm, saying that it would only do so alongside a staged Israeli withdrawal from Gaza In an extensive interview with New York magazine, Kushner warned that Israel was increasingly becoming globally isolated. “I feel like the fork in the road is Israel could rise from the tragedy of October 7, (and) be much more secure and much more integrated in the world, or they can go on the current trajectory, which is to trend toward global pariah status,” he said. In another interview, with Mathias Döpfner, CEO of POLITICO’s parent company Axel Springer, Kushner called Netanyahu someone who “doesn’t always make it easy” to make progress in the Trump administration’s Gaza plan, and delivered his sharpest rebuke of Israel’s broader posture, arguing it should drop its “constant wartime mindset” and embrace economic diplomacy like Gulf Arab states do. But Netanyahu has not shown any willingness to make concessions toward Gaza to advance the ceasefire agreement, particularly as his far-right allies have advocated for more strikes in Gaza and Palestinian emigration from the shattered territory. On Wednesday, Kushner said in a podcast interview that Israel “needs to get out of the constant wartime mindset and focus on economic diplomacy.” CNN’s Tal Shalev contributed to this article.

cnn.com.title: Two Italians killed in alleged Iranian drone attack on Kuwait; Tehran denies involvement
cnn.com.text: Two Italian nationals were killed on Thursday in an Iranian drone attack on the Gulf nation of Kuwait, Italy’s Foreign Minister said. Tehran denied any involvement in the incident. Antonio Tajani said “several drones of Iranian origin targeted Kuwaiti military installations” including an “air defence detection station where two Italian technicians from (Rome-based defense company) Rheinmetall Italia were working.” “A powerful explosion occurred, and, according to reports reaching us from Kuwait, both of our fellow citizens have unfortunately died,” Tajani said in a statement. Kuwait’s defense ministry said its armed forces detected and engaged several hostile drones in Kuwaiti airspace. The ministry blamed what it called “Iranian aggression” for an attack on a “vital site,” saying falling shrapnel wounded two other people, a Kuwaiti national and a Pakistani national. Material damage also occurred as a result of the drone attack, it said. The defense ministry confirmed the two deaths and extended its “deepest condolences to the families of the deceased.” Iran denied carrying out the attack. Brig. Gen. Abolfazl Shekarchi, a senior spokesperson for Iran’s armed forces, said: “No military or offensive operations whatsoever have been conducted by the Armed Forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran in the region.” He claimed it was a “false flag” operation aimed at escalating regional insecurity. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi also denied any Iranian involvement during a phone call with his Italian counterpart, Antonio Tajani, according to Iran’s foreign ministry. Araghch also “announced Tehran’s readiness to cooperate with the governments of Kuwait and Italy to clarify the origin of the incident and examine its various aspects.” Speaking to reporters later Thursday, Tajani said the drone used in the attack was manufactured in Iran. Referring to Araghchi’s denial of Iranian responsibility, Tajani noted that “numerous pro-Iranian militias operate in the region.” The Italian technicians were in Kuwait to maintain “detection antennas” for an air defense system used by the country’s armed forces, Italy’s foreign ministry said. In response to the latest attack, Italy’s Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni expressed her “deepest sympathy” and offered her “heartfelt condolences” to the victims’ families, while Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar said the incident shows how Iran’s “unchecked aggression threatens stability and security in the Middle East and beyond.” Iran has continues to target what it says are American targets in the region in retaliation for US attacks on Iranian sites. Earlier this month, Iran targeted a Kuwaiti air base that hosts US forces after the US military hit what it said was a missile launch site in Iran. Elsewhere, Bahrain on Sunday said an Iranian attack injured at least two people. This story has been updated with additional details.

cnn.com.title: French actor Gerard Depardieu to face trial for rape, his lawyer says
cnn.com.text: Film star Gerard Depardieu, one of the leading faces of French cinema, will face trial on charges of raping actress Charlotte Arnould in 2018, his lawyer David-Olivier Kaminski said on Thursday. Arnould first accused Depardieu of rape in 2018, saying the assaults occurred in his Paris home on two separate occasions when she was in her early 20s. Depardieu, 77, has denied wrongdoing in the case, and his legal team last year appealed prosecutors’ decision for the case to be tried. Depardieu – a towering figure in French cinema, who starred in more than 200 films over five decades, including Green Card, The Last Metro and Cyrano de Bergerac – has become one of the most high-profile faces of France’s slow-burn reckoning with sexual abuse by some of its most powerful men. Earlier this month, Depardieu withdrew his appeal against a separate 2025 conviction for sexual assault, accepting his guilt and apologizing to his victims. The rape trial poses a much more serious threat to Depardieu, who could face 15-20 years in jail if he is convicted.

cnn.com.title: Alleged Russia-directed sabotage in Europe risks mass-casualty event, think tank warns
cnn.com.text: Alleged Russia-directed sabotage in Europe is intensifying, with the possibility of a mass-casualty event as Moscow reportedly targets infrastructure like rail lines, airports and energy networks, a new report from a prominent international think tank warns. While it is not directly at war with any European nation other than Ukraine, Moscow is engaged in a conflict via proxies intended to weaken the continent’s support for Kyiv, the report says. Russia has increasingly turned to sabotage over the past year, with the use of explosives and arson roughly doubling and presenting a risk of mass casualties, the report from the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), released Thursday, says. Such a disaster could bring calls for retaliation and possibly divide European governments, it says. Germany and Poland, the European countries whose logistics and industries play the largest roles in support of Ukraine, are seeing the greater percentage of reported Russian sabotage, with more than half of incidents recorded between October 2025 and September of this year in those countries, according to the report’s findings. According to an analysis by the IISS, 29 Moscow-linked incidents were recorded between October 2025 and September 2026 in Poland, including a November 2025 incident in which an explosive charge damaged a rail line linking Warsaw to the Ukraine border. Though there were no casualties, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said later the explosion was likely planned to destroy a train. “Attacks have focused on sectors critical to the Ukrainian war effort, while attacks on public infrastructure and high-profile locations also appear to be intended to undermine public confidence and support for Ukraine,” the report says. Before the report’s release, US President Donald Trump’s top envoy for Russia-Ukraine negotiations and son-in-law Jared Kushner, praised Russian leader Vladimir Putin’s “restraint” in the more than four-year-old war. “He’s agreed not to use nuclear weapons, which obviously is a big thing,” Kushner told Mathias Döpfner, CEO of POLITICO’s parent company Axel Springer, in a podcast that debuted Wednesday. But the IISS report says it’s so-called “unconventional war” – not nuclear war – that poses an immediate threat to Europe. Russian intelligence services have been able to recruit a force of proxies who are likely becoming better at sabotage, using “more complex methods, including improvised explosive devices armed with timers and detonators,” the report says. Despite the arrests of proxies in several instances – along with the expulsion of Russian intelligence officers and closure of some consulates – the Europeans have not deterred Moscow, it says. “There is no clear evidence that these measures have made sabotage a less attractive instrument of Kremlin policy,” it says. A pool of proxy recruits does not seem to be deterred either, it says, as the frequency of attacks has not changed substantially. “Arrests impose costs on proxies, but so far not on the (Russian intelligence services) that direct and enable them,” the report says. The report also says Russian-backed sabotage comes in surges across the continent, suggesting central planning in Moscow. But it also notes that there is evidence of one proxy network coordinating attacks in several countries, and that there may be competing networks so that disrupting one may not deter another. Overall, Russia’s actions are being conducted on tactical and strategic levels, according to the report, with tactical operations trying to damage or delay aid for Ukraine, while strategically trying to make support for Kyiv too economically or politically costly for European governments to bear. Meanwhile, Kushner pointed a finger at Europe for the prolonged length of the war in Ukraine, saying “provocative” statements and actions coming out of European capitals have put Putin on guard. “His view is he does not see that (the Europeans) are ready for peace. He thinks they want the strategic defeat of Russia,” Kushner told the podcast “MD Meets,” which went online Wednesday. But Kushner said Washington has put no pressure on Ukraine, despite cutting military and logistical aid during the conflict. He told the POLITICO podcast the country’s “courage and bravery and capability is one of the greatest stories we’ve seen in many, many decades.” But he was more circumspect of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who he said has wrongly “attacked” Trump. “You would think that President Zelensky would be trying to engage with (Trump) respectfully,” Kushner said.

cnn.com.title: Houthis strike Saudi oil infrastructure as Riyadh intensifies attacks on Yemen
cnn.com.text: Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis are trading increasingly intense strikes on strategic sites, including oil infrastructure and ports, marking a sharp escalation in fighting between the two sides. A projectile struck an oil refinery in Saudi Arabia’s southwestern Jazan region on Thursday, killing a Nepalese worker and injuring several others, according to the Saudi Ministry of Energy. The strike sparked a fire and temporarily suspended some operations at the facility, the ministry said. The attack came a day after the Houthis claimed to have struck Saudi Arabia’s biggest oil refinery at Ras Tanura. Satellite imagery taken Wednesday showed a huge plume of black smoke rising from the coastal peninsula following the attack. The Houthi-controlled armed forces said the attack caused a fire at Ras Tanura, part of one of the world’s largest crude oil export terminals, in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Province. A shipping source told CNN Thursday that oil loadings at the terminal were suspended after the attack, though it was unclear whether they have resumed. The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted and destroyed four drones over Ras Tanura, with falling debris but no reported injuries. Ras Tanura has a refining capacity of 550,000 barrels per day and is part of a broader complex that housed Saudi Arabia’s main crude export terminal before the US-Iran war began. Saudi state-owned oil company Aramco did not immediately respond to a request for comment from CNN. The Houthis also claimed responsibility for a strike Wednesday on Riyadh’s King Abdullah Economic City that Saudi authorities said wounded 11 people. An eyewitness told CNN that Saudi Arabia’s trillion-dollar sovereign wealth fund, the Public Investment Fund, is headquartered inside the targeted skyscraper. The Saudi-led coalition said in a later statement Wednesday that the strike was carried out by a Houthi drone and vowed a “firm response.” Strikes intensify in Yemen Saudi-led forces meanwhile have stepped up attacks across Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen. On Thursday, the coalition said it carried out a “precision military operation” against Houthi capabilities, destroying 50 targets it described as legitimate military targets across Sanaa, Hodeidah and Saada governorates. A day earlier, the coalition said it attacked “operational capabilities” at the Houthi-controlled Hodeidah port and destroyed targets in Saada and Amran governorates. The Houthi-controlled armed forces, meanwhile, said Saudi warplanes and missiles carried out 109 strikes over the previous 24 hours across Yemen including in Sanaa and Hodeidah. The Houthi-controlled health ministry in Sanaa said Thursday that at least 19 civilians had been killed and 25 others wounded in Saudi strikes over the previous 48 hours across several parts of Yemen. CNN has not been able to independently verify the claims about the strikes or casualties. Crown prince’s US visit The Houthis have repeatedly targeted infrastructure in Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, including Riyadh’s financial district. Riyadh’s international airport was also hit several times last month, killing more than a dozen people. The escalating attacks come as Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman is planning his first trip to the United States since the Iran war began, where he is expected to attend next month’s G20 summit in Miami, Florida, according to a source familiar with the plans. Saudi officials have not yet publicly confirmed his attendance. Saudi Arabia has sought US support in strengthening its defenses as it faces continued Houthi missile and drone attacks. The planned visit would set up the first in person meeting between US President Donald Trump and Prince bin Salman since the outbreak of the war. Fighting between the Houthi group and the Saudi-led coalition reignited in July after years of relative calm brought about by a 2022 UN-brokered ceasefire. Clashes intensified in recent months after the militant group made an advance toward the critical Bab el-Mandeb Strait in September, threatening a new front in the Iran war.

cnn.com.title: US authorizes SpaceX to deploy 1 million satellites for AI data centers in space
cnn.com.text: The Federal Communications Commission has authorized Elon Musk’s SpaceX to deploy 1 million satellites in space for the creation of data centers critical to powering artificial intelligence. The decision comes as the US races to lead the world in AI, a technology that promises to turbocharge innovation and economic growth. Harnessing AI is also central to SpaceX’s growth ambitions, though the company cautioned in a regulatory filing ahead of its June initial public offering that launching data centers in space relied on “unproven” technologies and “may not achieve commercial viability.” Deploying SpaceX’s “Starmind” constellation – comprised of 1 million orbital compute modules – will help meet “rapidly growing demand” for AI computing power, the FCC said in a statement Wednesday. The deployed satellites will “process massive amounts of data to be used back here on Earth,” the agency added. “This action opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth,” said FCC Chairman Brendan Carr. AI data centers require enormous amounts of energy and Musk has endorsed orbital data centers that can harness the power of the sun. “By directly harnessing near-constant solar power with little operating or maintenance costs, these satellites will achieve transformative cost ​and energy efficiency while significantly reducing the environmental impact associated with terrestrial data centers,” SpaceX ​told the FCC when it applied for permission to launch the satellites earlier this year. Musk welcomed the decision, saying on X, his social media platform, that “this will be a great asset to America and the world.” The initiative has drawn criticism from the scientific community, however, who have argued that the technology could disrupt views of the night sky and increase pollution. In a statement Wednesday, the American Astronomical Society said it was “dismayed” by the FCC’s decision, which it had opposed in earlier filings to the agency. The “proposed constellation would significantly undermine (i) decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities and (ii) the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky,” the organization said. It noted that the satellites would be visible as “extremely bright objects for longer periods in the night sky” and would generate “radio emissions” and “waste heat” that would “threaten… sensitive instruments used in regular astronomy research.” It also warned of “atmospheric pollution” from the launches and reentries so many satellites. Under the license, SpaceX must deploy at least one authorized space station by November 2033, deploy 10% of the total – or 100,000 – by November 2035 and deploy 50% by November 2038. There are currently around 16,700 operational satellites in space, according to Orbital Radar, a platform providing real-time tracking of objects in orbit. The European Space Agency puts the number of functioning satellites slightly lower, at 15,800. Earlier this month, in a historic test flight, SpaceX’s Starship spacecraft deployed Starlink internet satellites before returning to earth and pulling of an unprecedented landing.

cnn.com.title: At least 9 injured by large explosion and fire at major oil facility in Bangkok
cnn.com.text: An explosion and fire at a major oil facility in the Thai capital on Thursday injured at least nine people and forced nearby residents to briefly evacuate, authorities said. Most of the injured suffered burns and three people were in critical condition, according to Erawan Medical Center in Bangkok. Video posted on social media showed thick black smoke rising from the site in an eastern neighborhood of Bangkok. A mobile phone alert sent to residents said the incident happened around 3 p.m. and advised people to avoid the area. The city authority reported less than an hour later that the ensuing fire was put out. Officials later said nearby residents can return home, but advised those living in a 5-kilometer (3-mile) radius of the facility to be cautious of air pollution. The Pollution Control Department said it sent officials to assess air and water quality in the surrounding area. Bangchak Corp., which owns the refining and storage facility, confirmed the fire in a Facebook post and said that the cause was still being investigated. The company also said it has halted all production operations. Energy Minister Akanat Promphan said the fire appeared to start at one of the refinery units, which is about 100 meters (330 feet) away from the oil storage. He said he would inspect the site to ensure there’s no further risk. “If we’re not a hundred percent certain that the oil storage is safe, we won’t allow them to resume operations,” he said. Akanat said Thailand’s oil supply should not be affected, as there are five other refineries in the country and this facility is not among the biggest. The refinery, with a listed capacity of 120,000 barrels a day, is the fifth biggest in Thailand and the only one situated in an urban area. An explosion and fire at the refinery in July 2012 caused damage in a nearby residential neighborhood and it took two weeks to repair the facility.

cnn.com.title: Putin showed "restraint" by not using nuclear weapons, Kushner says
cnn.com.text: Russian President Vladimir Putin has “shown restraint” by not using nuclear weapons in the conflict with Ukraine, White House envoy Jared Kushner has said, while describing the Russian leader as a “grand man of politics.” In a wide-ranging interview for Axel Springer CEO Mathias Döpfner’s “MD Meets” podcast, Kushner – who is President Donald Trump’s son-in-law – said he was convinced Putin wanted peace. “My assessment is that he does not only want peace; he wants to try and change the relationship with America, and he does want to try and see if there’s maybe a way to start a new beginning.” “So far Putin has showed restraint; he’s agreed not to use nuclear weapons, which obviously is a big thing, and he’s reassured us that that’s not his intention,” he added. Kushner and his fellow US negotiator Steve Witkoff have met Putin several times, most recently this month at the Kremlin. “He’s definitely a grand man of politics, he’s a historic figure,” Kushner said. “He takes a lot of notes when we’re speaking, and he transmits very specifically. But it’s very clear he has a very deep understanding of the issues.” Kushner rejected suggestions that the US had applied pressure on Ukraine to make concessions to Russia. Ukraine has said that the US Defense Department has delayed shipments of vital air defense missiles and intelligence sharing has been disrupted. As for efforts to reach a settlement that would include issues of territorial control, Kushner said: “This isn’t about fairness or who’s right or wrong.” Kushner said border lines in Europe had changed over time. “I do believe that when people see long-term durability and a pathway to peace, I think they’ll be a little bit more flexible on where do you draw the line.” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said earlier this month that US negotiators had floated the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for membership of NATO. “The Americans raised a question: ‘What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?’ This was the first time this had been raised,” Zelensky said after meeting Kushner and Witkoff. Ukraine has long resisted the idea of ceding land to Russia, which launched an unprovoked full-scale invasion in 2022. Zelensky said if he received a “comprehensive security package” – which would include a strong Ukrainian army and guarantees from NATO and the European Union – he would put a proposal to the public. Alluding to that possibility, Kushner told Döpfner, “Without a security guarantee from America, Ukraine will not be safe in the future… President Trump has to determine that a security guarantee is in the interests of America to give.” Zelensky has previously said that Russia would not stop at taking the Donbas – whose two regions comprise nearly 10% of Ukrainian territory – but would plan further attacks. As for negotiations, Kushner said: “I wish there was a fast way to do this… There’s a lot we agree on. We all want long-term peace.” “Once we’re able to define that post-war relationship, I think the issue of territory will become much easier to resolve because right now there’s no way to bridge that last issue.” Without a settlement there was a real risk of escalation, Kushner said. “Europe is funding and arming Ukraine against Russia, and it won’t take a lot of miscalculation for this thing to escalate massively,” Kushner warned. The ultimate goal, Kushner said, was that “if you can end this war in a way where Ukraine is sovereign, secure, prosperous, and free, they could join the EU. They have a post-war economy plan. They have credible security guarantees. They have strong deterrence capabilities. That’s a huge victory for Ukraine and for Europe.”

cnn.com.title: At the gym with the CEO who made us wait 13 years for GTA VI
cnn.com.text: Strauss Zelnick strides on to the gym floor at 6:30 a.m. for a strength-training workout with the Program, the exercise group in New York City he created. He inspects each station, making sure the weights, repetitions and timing match the circuit he designed the night before. The 69-year-old CEO of Take-Two Interactive — the parent company behind Grand Theft Auto — is not a natural athlete. He was skinny well into his 30s. But Zelnick became a fitness fanatic, transformed his body and created the Program more than a decade ago. He typically exercises twice a day, using workouts as business and mentoring meetings. I have seen Zelnick’s relentless personal discipline up close. I knew him when I was a kid 25 years ago, and I’ve started working out with him and the Program over the last couple of years. Zelnick’s quest for perfection offers a window into Take-Two’s unusual strategy for Grand Theft Auto VI. The last installment of the Grand Theft Auto series came out 13 years ago. Most entertainment companies might have forced out a sequel long before, bowing to market pressure. But Zelnick doesn’t believe in doing things halfway. He was willing to endure three public delays on Grand Theft Auto VI, investor and fan angst, and sky-high expectations in pursuit of delivering something “exceptional.” “Consumers are not okay with okay,” he said in an interview with gaming site IGN last year. “Good is the new bad.” The strategy worked. Grand Theft Auto VI is poised to become the highest-earning intellectual property in entertainment history, eclipsing recent cultural phenomena like Taylor Swift’s Eras tour and The Odyssey. Getting out of the way I reach out to Zelnick for advice on health, exercise and my career every couple months. He responds almost immediately — as he does for anyone who seeks him out — even if it’s the morning of the Grand Theft Auto VI launch to decline my interview request for this article. Zelnick does not make video games or play them. It’s hard to imagine him with a controller in his hands. Instead, he is considered a master of identifying and managing highly creative people, with all their promise, brilliance and frustrations. He does this by creating corporate stability and giving them freedom to build great art. And then staying out of their way.
