Zelnick is not Jeff Bezos getting “heavily involved” in casting decisions about James Bond. “He knows what he knows, and he’s respectful of what he doesn’t,” said Jennifer Kolbe, the head of publishing at Rockstar Games, which makes Grand Theft Auto. It’s a management style Zelnick learned as a Hollywood wunderkind, the description of him that appeared in early public profiles in the 1990s. Intensely ambitious, Zelnick earned dual law and business degrees at Harvard before leaving his 20s. He became the head of Twentieth Century Fox by 32 and CEO of music recording giant BMG’s North America division by 37. Zelnick took control of Take-Two in 2007, when the company was on the brink of bankruptcy, under criminal investigation, and trading around $11 a share. (It’s at roughly $220 now.) “A lot of us at Rockstar worked within that mess at Take-Two,” said Kolbe, who has been at the company since 1996. “We stick by the premise that if (he) is going provide that stability, we’re going to provide hits.” Rockstar’s turnover is low, and roughly one in five employees has stayed with the company for more than a decade. (Rockstar has also been accused of firing dozens of employees to prevent them from unionizing. The company has said the firings were for misconduct.) Take-Two focused early under Zelnick on building out a handful of blockbuster franchises, including Red Dead Redemption, rather than churning out a constant stream of new games. “I’ve always believed the right strategy for an entertainment company is a limited number of very high-quality titles,” Zelnick told the website GamesBeat in 2008. Thousands of developers, artists, designers and other staff worked on Grand Theft Auto VI. Analysts estimated it will cost more than $1 billion — the most expensive video game ever — though Take-Two has not disclosed the figure. The mega-project stands out in an entertainment industry that has lost its appetite for expensive, time-consuming ventures. Most companies cut costs, shorten production cycles and try to pump out more with fewer resources to meet the pressures of Wall Street. Cautious corporate executives manage based on quarterly earnings targets or their own ideas about a movie script. “GTA VI is what happens when you provide the necessary financial resources to allow talented individuals to do their best work,” said Joost van Dreun, a professor at NYU Stern who studies gaming and tech. “There are few publishers that can stomach either the time horizon or the budget.” The Program Zelnick brings his obsession with structure to the gym. The Program trains in several high-end gyms around New York City a few times a week, everything paid for by Zelnick. Attending a workout requires only an invitation from one of the group’s roughly 300 members, a broad range from college students to executives in their 70s. His Program crew shows up year after year. People come to get in an hour-long workout and for the camaraderie. But they also go to develop a relationship with Zelnick, who has said he spends a quarter of his time mentoring and coaching. Zelnick is loyal, like when he recommended his shoulder surgeon to me nine minutes after I emailed him last November — “I’ve done endless research. No one else” — and reached out after the operation and during rehab. His quiet intensity can be intimidating, but I’ve found him surprisingly warm and self-deprecating. Zelnick’s motivation behind the Program is to build community, said Dan Harris, the host of the 10% Happier podcast and Zelnick’s close friend. His mother died when he was 10, his father abandoned the family and he was raised by his aunt and uncle. “What I see him doing with the Program is re-creating family,” Harris said. “The high standards and systems he puts in place are structures to create connection.” Zelnick designs most of the circuits, even when he’s on the road. After going over each station in person, he calls the group together. Everyone introduces themselves by name. Then Zelnick announces the exercises, time per station and number of reps. “Let’s go, team.” The workout begins promptly at 6:45 a.m. Like a trainer, he cheers you on and lets you know if you’re doing the wrong exercise or your form has slipped. But in a group Zelnick created and oversees, he delegates. One person leads the equipment setup. Another emails the weekly schedule out on Fridays. Someone else designs every workout playlist, with a heavy dose of Billy Joel’s “We Didn’t Start the Fire.” Zelnick seems almost incapable of small talk during the sessions, unless it’s to ask how you like the workout. He is locked in, constantly moving to achieve the next level.

cnn.com.title: SNAP’s work mandate doesn’t always require employment. There’s a lesser-known way to fulfill it
cnn.com.text: When May Rivera started receiving notices from New York City’s Human Resources Administration this spring warning that she was at risk of losing her food stamps, she was confused. The 30-year-old had heard about the work requirements in the “big beautiful bill,” but she had a job as a housekeeper for up to 12 hours a week so she thought she’d be fine. She didn’t realize that the sweeping law, passed by Republicans last year, broadened the work mandate, and she was not doing enough. Panic started to set in. Rivera, who has applied to scores of jobs over the past year with no response, thought back to when she temporarily lost her food stamps in 2024 due to a paperwork error. She had to rely on various food pantries to survive and faced having her electricity shut off because she couldn’t afford to both pay bills and buy groceries. She didn’t want to go through that experience again. Then, Rivera heard on a podcast that volunteering can count towards the work requirement. So she signed up to pack bags and boxes with fruit, vegetables, rice, peanut butter, shelf-stable milk and other goods at the West Side Campaign Against Hunger, which allows her to both maintain her $306 monthly benefit and help others in her community. “I know what it’s like to face food insecurity,” said Rivera, who loves to bake and is hoping to get a food handler certification so she can broaden her job search. “No matter what, everyone deserves to eat … it’s just a fundamental right as a human being.” Like Rivera, more low-income Americans enrolled in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program — known as SNAP, the formal name for food stamps — must now meet the work requirement. And soon, many Medicaid recipients will have to do the same to maintain their health coverage. Though many enrollees in these safety net programs have jobs, not all are working enough to meet the mandate of 80 hours a month. They can also volunteer, participate in job training programs or go to school to fulfill the requirement. Some can also qualify for exemptions. Now some cities and states, as well as nonprofit groups, are stepping up efforts to try to connect these folks with volunteer opportunities so they aren’t dropped from the programs. Sweeping new rules The work requirement in food stamps is not new. Certain food stamp enrollees have long had to have jobs or participate in other qualifying activities to receive benefits. The Republicans’ package expanded that existing mandate to parents with older teen children, people ages 55 to 64, veterans, those experiencing homelessness and former foster youth. Plus, the law made it harder for states to receive waivers during tough economic times. Some 2.4 million fewer Americans are expected to receive food stamps benefits in an average month because of the work mandate provision, according to a Congressional Budget Office analysis released in August 2025. On top of that, the first-ever federal work mandate in Medicaid will begin in January, though states can opt to delay enforcing it until July. More than 5 million more people are expected to be uninsured in 2034 due to the provision, CBO estimates. Many enrollees in these safety net programs don’t realize that volunteering allows them to satisfy the mandate. It’s an important alternative, considering many people have part-time jobs with variable hours and others can’t land employment at all. States differ widely in how well they inform food stamp recipients of the volunteer option, according to a July analysis by the Food Research & Action Center, a left-leaning advocacy group. It found that 20 states do not mention volunteering on their SNAP website, while 27 states and the District of Columbia do. Another three states just make it partially clear. Adding to the confusion, some states use an alternate calculation — a household’s monthly benefit divided by the local minimum wage — to determine how many hours an enrollee must volunteer each month. New York is one of those states, which means Rivera needs to volunteer 18 hours a month on top of her housekeeping job. Making it easier to volunteer Some government agencies and community groups are trying to raise awareness of the volunteer option and to aid enrollees in finding spots. Many of the efforts are still in the early stages and have assisted relatively few people, but the organizers hope to expand their reach over time. Pennsylvania’s Department of Human Services decided to harness its PA Navigate site — which provides residents with information about charitable food, clothing, job training and other services in their area — to point food stamp recipients to volunteer options. They just type in their zip code and search for “volunteer opportunity.” “A lot of the Pennsylvanians that we serve through both SNAP and Medicaid have hourly jobs, and they do not always have the ability to increase those hours,” the state agency’s secretary, Valerie Arkoosh, told CNN. “Our goal was to help make sure people understand that by doing some volunteer work, they could complete that 80-hour minimum commitment and be able to securely maintain their benefits.” Since the volunteer search function launched last November, it’s been used more than 4,500 times. There were 77 opportunities listed at the end of September, and the number is growing, Arkoosh said. They include working on art projects with people with intellectual disabilities in Philadelphia or stocking inventory at a civic association in Lancaster. The state is working with the Community Action Association of Pennsylvania, which supports a state-wide network of local organizations, to add more nonprofits and their volunteer opportunities to PA Navigate. The association has a team of community engagement managers, who are educating the groups on the volunteer component of the work requirement and the ability to list any spots they have on the site, said Beck Moore, the association’s CEO. Still, some people have failed to satisfy the expanded mandate. Some 123,000 Pennsylvania enrollees have lost their food stamps as of the end of September, Arkoosh said. Some volunteer opportunities can lead to paid jobs at the nonprofits or at other employers. The Houston Food Bank partners with local job training programs that refer SNAP enrollees to volunteer spots. So far this year, 12 people have fulfilled the work requirement at the food bank, said Lakesha Oludare, the nonprofit’s community service program manager. Oludare also tries to place them in positions within the food bank where they can gain employment skills. Seven of them landed jobs — including two in a warehouse and two in offices — after volunteering in similar roles at the food bank. Oludare is looking to increase the number of SNAP participants referred to the food bank by job training programs to as many as 50 people by March. “Besides assisting them in meeting the work requirements through volunteering, I want them to obtain some kind of primary employment to put them in a position so they don’t have to rely on SNAP benefits,” she said. Tracking volunteer hours In New York City, the Human Resources Administration has created several resources for SNAP participants who want to turn to volunteering to meet the work requirement. The stakes are high — some 26,500 have already been dropped from the safety net program since March, when the expanded work requirements took effect in the state. Plus, 900,000 Medicaid recipients are at risk of losing their coverage once the work requirement starts next year. The city agency set up two ways for nonprofit groups to assist food stamp recipients in logging their volunteer hours. One allows organizations to enter into an agreement with the city to host volunteers and report their hours. The other enables the nonprofit to register as a verified site where enrollees can volunteer and have their hours confirmed, though the recipient is responsible for submitting the paperwork to the agency. HRA created a map where food stamp enrollees can find dozens of volunteer opportunities across the five boroughs. And it has partnered with NYC Service, a division of the Mayor’s Office, which lists volunteer spots at 1,200 organizations around the city. In September, NYC Service added a tab on its site geared for food stamp recipients seeking to meet their work requirements, which currently has more than 200 listings. “For us it was a no brainer to just look at: How do we make our site even more accessible, make things clear for people who are seeking hours for SNAP and Medicaid, making the process as easy as possible,” said Laura Rog, NYC Service’s chief service officer. HRA said it does not yet have information on how many food stamp enrollees have been connected to volunteer opportunities, while NYC Service doesn’t track why people are signing up for listings. City Harvest, the largest food rescue organization in the Big Apple, now has 35 SNAP enrollees who volunteer to meet the work mandate. The number of shifts they’ve worked has grown from nine in August to 123 in October, said Alex Guyton, senior manager of volunteer programs. “There are a lot more folks now facing this requirement and needing to go through this process to tick that box and maintain access to these really crucial benefits,” Guyton said. The enrollees pack bags of fresh produce and build pallets in the group’s Brooklyn food rescue center for distribution to more than 400 pantries, soup kitchens and other food programs. They have also supported City Harvest’s food distribution efforts on Staten Island, where the nonprofit has had a difficult time finding enough volunteers. Tonia Lykes, who started receiving food stamps earlier this year after her unemployment benefits ran out, spends a total of 10 hours on Tuesdays and Thursdays building pallets with shelf-stable food like peanut butter, rice, pasta and cooking oil at City Harvest’s rescue center. She also volunteers twice a week at a food pantry in Brooklyn. Lykes, 56, was not aware of the work requirement until she started receiving letters from HRA earlier this year saying she was not compliant. She reached out to her job training program counselor, who suggested volunteering. She’s thankful for that option since she’s had little luck in finding a job, despite having worked in the restaurant industry for more than 20 years. Food stamps are a lifeline. “I don’t have to worry about where my next meal is coming from,” the New York City resident said. While the focus to date has largely been on food stamp recipients, it will soon broaden to include Medicaid enrollees. Some nonprofits are already preparing. Greg Silverman, CEO of the West Side Campaign Against Hunger, said he is very concerned about people losing their health coverage. So the group — which already has had 50 food stamp recipients volunteer more than 1,500 hours since March — is planning to make more slots available for those who need to fulfill the work mandate. “We’re ramping up, and we’ll continue to do more and more outreach and provide more and more opportunities for New Yorkers in need to maintain their benefits,” he said.

cnn.com.title: Trump's midterms debacle hasn't dimmed his designs on Cuba. Or those of 'President' Rubio
cnn.com.text: The historic drubbing US President Donald Trump received in the US midterm elections apparently has not dimmed the enthusiasm he feels for one of his most high-risk foreign policy goals: “Taking Cuba,” as he put it earlier this year. “I want to get Cuba done before I leave,” Trump told conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt this month. Trump said he would consider using military action to topple the island’s leadership. Even as voters in the midterms widely rejected Trump’s war in Iran, the US president suggests he still has the communist-run island just 90 miles from Florida in his crosshairs. The comments further escalated tensions with Cuba, which for months has been readying soldiers and civilian militias for a possible US invasion. “Cuba does not attack or threaten any nation,” responded Cuban President Miguel Díaz-Canel on X, “But we will reject any attempt at foreign military aggression and we are preparing for that threat.” For nearly a year, Trump has ratcheted up sanctions on the island — including an oil embargo — while alternatively portraying Cuba as both a failed state and grave threat to US national security. A US State Department report in July titled “Cuba: The Capital of 21st Century Communism” ominously accused Havana of “persuading the children of the West to turn against their own inheritance” and laid out what many observers read as the case for regime change on the island. Trump has wavered on whether the US will follow through on military action to force Cuba’s government from power, saying the country’s economy is already collapsing and that he may place a US aircraft carrier off the island’s coast before sending US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to Havana to hammer out a deal literally at gunpoint. Rubio, a Cuban-American and staunch critic of the Cuban government, has made clear that there needs to be new leadership on the island and that under US law, “regime change” is a condition for economic sanctions to be lifted. “You cannot change the economic trajectory of Cuba as long as the people who are in charge of it now are in charge of it,” Rubio told Fox News in May. “I don’t think we’re going to be able to change the trajectory of Cuba as long as these people are in charge in that regime.” In several tense meetings in 2026, US officials told Cuban counterparts they needed to liberalize the island’s economic and political models and end cooperation with US adversaries or face the consequences. The May indictment of former Cuban President Raul Castro — who is 95 but still wields enormous power on the island — just months after the US capture of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro — drove home those warnings. And while the US still technically maintains diplomatic relations with Cuba, for months the Trump administration has referred to Cuba’s government as “an illegitimate regime.” The impasse boiled over into a shouting match at the UN last month, as Cuba’s Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla tried to interrupt US Ambassador Mike Waltz from giving a speech lambasting what he called Cuban leaders’ corruption and incompetence. A Cuban diplomat was later expelled for appearing to shove a US official. Privately, Cuban officials expressed hopes that a rout for Trump in the midterm elections and US voters’ apathy toward military interventions would cool the administration’s imperial designs on the island. The electoral rout came but there appears to be little reprieve in store for the beleaguered island nation during Trump’s remaining time in office. A US official, who did not want to be named, told CNN that Washington still expects “the regime to collapse” and that the midterms fiasco will not lead to any softening of the administration’s policy towards Cuba Having resisted US pressure for nearly 70 years, Cuba does not appear to be caving now. As grim as life has become for Cubans — blackouts now can last for days, medicine and food are increasingly scarce and the value of the Cuban peso is in a seemingly perpetual death spiral — the island’s government remains firmly in control. So far, the few talks that have taken place have yielded no tangible results and there is no sign that the administration has found, as US officials put it, “their Delcy” in the Cuban government, referring to Delcy Rodríguez, Maduro’s much more pliant successor in Venezuela. Trump’s prediction that the Cuba’s leadership will offer concessions to end the pressure campaign notwithstanding, there appears to be little chance of a diplomatic breakthrough. Cuban officials view any economic benefits of a deal to be a poisoned chalice. As one Cuban diplomat told me years ago, “We know that if the Americans are for it, we should be against it.” But Havana may be missing the opportunity to make a historic and lasting deal. “It’s ‘Nixon goes to China’,” said Ricardo Herrero, the executive director of the Cuba Study Group, a non-partisan organization focused on US-Cuba relations and the Cuban private sector. “You make the deal with your staunchest adversary on the other side, because that deal becomes untouchable. It’s going to come at a higher cost. But it has much greater longevity than any deal that you strike with the Democrats,” he said. Even if Rubio — widely viewed as the architect of Trump’s Cuba crackdown — were to leave the administration to mount his own bid for the presidency in 2028, any respite for Cuba would likely be short lived. As president, Rubio would undoubtably seek to finish what Trump started with Cuba.

cnn.com.title: Artists are quitting Instagram and Facebook over fears AI will steal their work
cnn.com.text:
Matty Burnham, a watercolor artist in the United Kingdom, said he discovered a Pinterest account impersonating his illustration in 2024. The account created AI versions of his watercolors and listed them on fake profiles via Shopify, Facebook and Instagram, he told CNN.
Although Burnham tracked the Pinterest account to Ho Chi Min City, Vietnam, he does not know who was behind it.
It’s part of a wave of AI-generated artwork that’s taking business away from the creators themselves, and is especially prevalent on Meta-owned Instagram and Facebook. CNN spoke with over a dozen artists on how they are navigating the current AI landscape.
AI-generated art profiles “monetize Facebook,” Burnham said. “They have hundreds of thousands of followers who believe these fake profiles are genuine artists and direct users to various websites with shops and ads.”
The problem has pushed some independent artists to pull back from Instagram, Facebook and other Meta platforms, especially with the tech giant’s proposed updates to its terms of service. Some have considered leaving Meta-owned social media platforms entirely, pausing posting or turning to other online creator communities such as Patreon or Substack.
Meta’s updated terms would still allow automated software to scrape external websites and extract large amounts of data without permission from business account owners. This includes personal portfolios, online stores, and links to Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and Threads business accounts.
The terms were originally supposed to go into effect October 30, then got pushed back to November 20. The company announced on November 5 that the updates were delayed indefinitely.
“We’re pausing the changes as we continue to engage with stakeholders and take our time to get this right. In the meantime, our existing terms remain in effect,” a Meta spokesperson said in a statement to CNN.
Still, even with the latest delay, the proposed updates have already caused another wave of artists to leave Meta.
Samantha Waldron, co-owner of Dutcher Photography in Madison, Wisconsin, told CNN that she deleted all business and personal Facebook pages earlier this month and has since transitioned her Instagram business accounts to personal accounts, deleted a vast majority of posts, and removed all external website links from Meta account bios.
“It was the last straw that was a long time coming. I’m frankly relieved not to have to worry about keeping up on social media moving forward,” said Waldron.
Under the updated terms, independent artists’ images, style, and property could be scraped without their knowledge to train generative AI models, creators told CNN. Those AI models could then replicate or replace human-made art — and potentially impact artists’ businesses on those sites.
Megan Wimberley, founder of Cowgirl Artists of America in Tulsa, Oklahoma, is in the process of deleting all of her Meta accounts. She told CNN that she considers these new terms a major breach of trust. Wimberley believes everyone – not just artists – should be concerned about posting their personal images, video and audio due to potential AI scraping.
“I actually view Meta as a company trying to lead the way in AI and that their social media platforms are no longer really about social media but more about free licensing to train their AI,” said Wimberley. “If you’re a mother and you’re posting your children, you’re potentially licensing Meta to use your children to train their AI.”
Some even chose to “go dark” on Meta platforms from October 30 through November 6 when the updated Meta terms were initially planned to kick in, refraining from posting or sharing content in protest of the updated terms. Wimberley said she started the “Meta blackout” campaign on October 22, and it took off from there.
Nicole McKay, artists relations director at The Guild of Artists and Artisans, told CNN in a statement that many artists in the United States have begun removing their accounts from Meta platforms in response to the upcoming policy change with AI model training. Many artists have posted “goodbye” messages on Instagram and Facebook, citing Meta’s politics.
“For artists who rely on these platforms to showcase and sell their work, connect with customers, and build their businesses, leaving Meta presents a difficult choice between protecting their work and maintaining their livelihoods,” McKay said.
Artists traverse ‘AI slop’
AI-generated artwork has serious repercussions on the creator economy, artists told CNN. Online imitators are forcing artists to change their strategy on how they reach an audience.
Andrew Scott, a contemporary artist in Rochester, New York, said he directly messaged an AI art impersonator in September about copying his work.
He said the person admitted to using Scott’s original work as a starting point to build her own AI-generated art videos. The person behind the impersonating profile then shared AI clips on Instagram, giving the impression she created the actual art. Scott noted one of her posts with AI artwork received 50 million views.
Scott said he explained to the impersonator how the AI versions could potentially hurt his business. She has since unfollowed him on social media but continues to create the AI-prompted knockoffs, he said.
Nancy Chen, a ceramic artist in Canada, posts videos on social media that show how she makes sale pieces. But she understands those clips could also be vulnerable to AI model training. Chen says she’s been wary lately of posting polished images of her work on Meta platforms but hasn’t decided to leave yet.
“It makes me wonder how independent artists can present their work to the world when their transparency can be weaponized,” Chen told CNN. “AI can outpace any individual artist, so I definitely feel some pressure to compete in price, even though I feel my labor is already underpriced.”
One of the main concerns for creators is the scale and speed that AI can push content, especially compared to human-made work that can be time-consuming. That concern is compounded by questions of how generative AI is trained on artwork, usually without artists’ say, and how copyright law applies to AI.
Isaiah Steinfeld, an American Institute of Graphic Arts Board Member who builds with AI, said that protecting artists and embracing the technology don’t have to be opposing views. He noted that artists can still register work for copyright, pursue infringement claims and get unauthorized copies taken down.
For instance, Meta said creators can report instances of AI impersonators and submit takedown requests via its Intellectual Property Reporting Center.
“So, provenance has to cut both ways: protect creators from having their work appropriated and protect people using new (AI) tools from having their actual contributions erased,” Steinfeld said.
Google released an online tool, SynthID Detector, this month to the public. The free site allows anyone to upload a file to check if that image, video or audio file was made by AI from Google and partners such as OpenAI, Nvidia and Kakao.
In a press release, Google said the platform has watermarked over 180 million images and video and regularly sees over a million verification requests each day.
But this is only the beginning, and independent artists agree these changes do not go far enough. Many still grapple with whether to share content on social platforms at all, but in their line of work, it’s about brand awareness.
“Personally, I don’t trust that there will be enough done to protect artists,” Burnham said. “The UK government seems more concerned about not limiting profitable start-up tech companies than protecting artists. My hope is that the public continues to reject gen-AI in this current model.”
When CNN reached out for comment, a spokesperson for the UK Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport said: “The government has engaged extensively with creatives, industry bodies and AI firms and we are taking time to ensure we find the right approach to this issue.”
“We have been clear that we will not proceed with any course of action which does not work for our creative industries and our AI sector,” they added.

cnn.com.title: Photographer documents the 3,000-mile journey of the monarch butterfly
cnn.com.text: The arrival of monarch butterflies in the mountain forests of central Mexico each year is “pure chaos,” says photographer Jaime Rojo. Brilliant orange wings fill the sky, giant clusters of the insects hang from trees, and the sound is overwhelming. “When a million butterflies beat their wings together you can hear the murmur … Sometimes they are so abundant that when they fly over you in a clear direction, you can feel the breeze,” he says. Twenty years since Rojo first experienced the monarch butterfly migration in Mexico, he is still in awe. The creatures have been a constant in the Spaniard’s journey to becoming a world-renowned nature photographer. His book, “Monarchs,” released in October, documents the wonder and fragility of their seasonal migration. He calls it his “love letter” to the species. The odyssey Each year, millions of monarchs travel between 1,200 and 2,800 miles from northeast US and southeast Canada to the hills of Mexico, where they hibernate from November to March. While there are longer migrations in the insect world, such as the globe skimmer dragonfly and the painted lady butterfly, the monarch’s is particularly complex. The flight to Mexico is part of a yearly cycle carried out by four or five generations of butterflies. Most have a lifespan of about a month, and travel north in a relay to the US and Canada, but the so-called “super generation,” born in late summer or fall, lives up to eight months to make the epic journey south. This generation delays reproduction to conserve energy for the trip. Navigating by the sun and an internal magnetic compass, the super-generation find their way to the same forests their great-grandparents left the previous spring — a place they have never been before. The marvel captivated Rojo, who first witnessed it in 2004 when visiting the towering oyamel fir forests of Sierra Chincua, a mountain range in central Mexico. “It was a beautiful spectacle,” he says, and initially, all he was interested in was capturing that beauty — mastering the light, the composition, understanding how the monarchs behave, and “finding order in the chaos” with his lens. In 2013, his motivation changed. He was working on a project to take stills as part of a film production, but when he returned to the same forests, he couldn’t find a single butterfly. That year, WWF Mexico, which estimates the monarch’s population via the amount of forestland the butterflies occupy, found that numbers were at their lowest since 1993, when monitoring began. While populations fluctuate considerably year by year as colonies are sensitive to weather and habitat conditions, this was not a one-off. The eastern population of migratory monarchs (which overwinter in Mexico) had been declining for decades. In the 1990s, they numbered close to 400 million. According to current counts, populations have declined to around 55 million individuals. “It was my turning point,” says Rojo. “I started researching the decline, documenting the work of people, documenting the work of scientists.” Fragility The migratory species faces threats all along its route. In the US, intensive agriculture has decimated milkweed, the only plant on which monarchs lay their eggs and on which their larvae feed. Deforestation in Mexico and encroaching avocado farms are endangering the small unique ecosystem they rely on in winter. Climate change and extreme weather are also taking a toll. In Mexico, a snowstorm in 2016 killed up to 38% of the butterflies present that year. Rojo witnessed the devastating event, taking a photo of a tapestry of dead monarchs frozen across white snow. “It’s a powerful photo,” he says. “It tells a story, and it’s a photo that makes you want to know more, to think twice.” He has since followed the butterflies across the continent, documenting these threats. In his book, there are images of vast expanses of corn and soybean fields in the Midwest being sprayed with pesticide, which can kill monarchs directly and destroy their food source. But there are also images of hope: strips of prairie can be seen snaking through some crops, restored by farmers to allow milkweed to thrive. Volunteers are pictured monitoring milkweed patches in gardens or recording monarch eggs and caterpillars. In Mexico, photographs show local communities restoring forests in land once cleared for agriculture. Such conservation efforts seem to be having an effect. In 2026, according to WWF Mexico, the population of monarch butterflies at the wintering grounds increased by almost 65% compared to the previous year. It also reported a significant decrease in forest degradation in the area. Rojo is positive about the future of the species. “This is one of those rare conservation stories in which our individual actions make the difference,” he says. “Anyone that plants some milkweed in their garden is helping.” He hopes that his images will inspire people and reconnect them to the natural world. “I would like nothing more than my images to contribute to creating new habitat for the monarch.”

bbc.com.title: Major Thanksgiving storm brings flooding, flight delays across US
bbc.com.text:
- Published
A massive Thanksgiving storm hammering the Midwest and north-east with heavy rain and winds, along with high tides out west, is causing widespread disruptions across the US.
More than 80 million Americans expected to be travelling this week. On Thursday 460 flights in the US were cancelled and another 2,508 flights into, out of, or within the US were delayed, tracking site FlightAware said.
The FAA has previously warned that delays would be possible "throughout the week" as a result of the rain and wind that are forecast.
Meanwhile, almost one million households were without power on Thursday night, with Pennsylvania, Maryland and Virginia the hardest hit states.
On Thursday, a powerful storm hit the eastern US, bringing damaging winds of up to 70mph, torrential rain, and major coastal flooding.
New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill declared a state of emergency as several communities along the Jersey Shore saw widespread flooding.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul also declared a state of emergency for New York City, Long Island and Westchester County.
In New York City, organisers of the annual Macy's Thanksgiving parade have postponed the event to Saturday.
Bridges closed in Maryland due to severe winds and waves battered beaches in Delaware as water seeped onto the boardwalk.
In Maryland, almost two million customers have been asked by the water utility to use water for essential use only due to "intermittent power disruptions".
On the wettest Thanksgiving on record in Washington DC, tidal waters surged and soaked runways at Reagan Washington National Airport, according to the National Water Prediction Service.
More than 980,000 households were reporting power outages by Thursday evening, with Pennsylvania, Virginia, Maryland and New Jersey hit particularly hard.
Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro said that utility providers were working tirelessly to restore power. Meanwhile, energy companies in Virginia and New Jersey warned it may take some time, even days, for power to return, as crews had to wait until it was safe to access damaged areas.
On Thursday afternoon, President Donald Trump said he would consider releasing emergency funds for the east coast as it faces down the holiday storm.
Across the US, severe weather is also descending on the West Coast. The NWS has warned of a series of Pacific storms that are expected to bring rain, mountain snow and strong winds.
Many are bracing for potential flooding as king tides peak along the coast.
Water levels along California's vast coastline could reach over 8ft (2.4 metres) in some areas on Thursday, according to the NWS, breaking records set just last month.
Both San Diego and Los Angeles reported a high tide of over 8ft earlier in the week, and beach-goers were advised to avoid coastal areas.
Train services along the Amtrak Pacific Surfliner, which runs along the California coastline, cancelled several trains due to "washout conditions from high tides", the company shared on social media.
Storms are also forecast for the Pacific Northwest, including the Canadian province of British Columbia.
In Miami, some travel delays persisted into Thursday after a FedEx plane overshot the runway the night before, which prompted the closure of all but one runway at the airport for a brief period.
A statement FedEx provided to US media confirmed that one of its flights had "experienced an issue upon landing".
It added: "We are grateful that our crew is safe and there are no reported injuries. We are coordinating closely with investigating authorities, and any additional questions should be referred to the FAA."
An airport employee who spoke anonymously to CBS News, the BBC's US partner, raised the possibility that rainy conditions had been a factor.
"They tried as hard as they could to stop, but I don't know if it was the weather because the rain and the wind were really bad, and they just couldn't stop in time and went right off the runway and veered off into the grass," they said.
Wednesday's incident in Miami came 11 weeks after a cargo plane crashed on landing at the same airport, killing five people and injuring five others in vehicles on the ground with which it collided.
The American Automobile Association (AAA) predicted that 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles (80km) from home for the Thanksgiving holiday over a seven-day period.
Rebecka Pieder contributed reporting.

bbc.com.title: New Zealand's ruling coalition falls short of parliamentary majority by one seat
bbc.com.text:
- Published
New Zealand's ruling coalition has fallen short of a parliamentary majority by one seat, following a campaign shaped by a sluggish economy and disillusioned voters.
It now needs the support of the centrist Opportunity Party to remain in power. If they cannot reach a deal, the country may have to go back to the polls.
The incumbent National Party led by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon secured 40 out of 130 seats, while its coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First took 13 and 12 respectively.
A government led by the centre-left Labour Party is not possible, official results on Friday show, as the bloc would not have enough seats even if Opportunity threw its weight behind it.
Luxon on Friday acknowledged that negotiations "may be challenging" and will take some time.
"Kiwis won't thank us for rushing to an agreement that falls apart or for sending them back to the polls," he told reporters.
Labour leader Chris Hipkins said his party "ran an incredible campaign" but acknowledged that it doesn't have negotiating power despite winning the popular vote. "More New Zealanders voted for change at this election than for the status quo," he said.
New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions. Each person casts two votes – one for their preferred political party and another for their choice of local representative.
Labour secured 36 seats, The Greens took 17, while Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests, picked up five.
Opportunity, which has been described as this election's kingmaker, secured seven seats. Opportunity's leader Qiulae Wong told reporters her party will negotiate with National, but that all options remain on the table.
"There are seven parties in parliment and everyone is responsible for making sure we do everything we can to deliver a stable government for New Zealand. It's not just up to us," she said on Friday.
Preliminary results on 7 November, election day, had projected that National combined with its coalition partners would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc.
But today's official tally shows it had lost two seats on special votes - cast by citizens who were overseas or outside of their registered electorate on election day - which typically skew left.
Some of National's key election pledges include lower taxes, cheaper energy, more renewable generation, and a greater focus on defence.
Labour, meanwhile, had campaigned to cut healthcare, public transport and fuel costs, more government support for social housing, among other things.
In earlier interviews with the BBC, many voters had expressed frustration over spiralling costs of living and high unemployment across the country, with declining faith in their political leadership.
"There's this kind of apathy and a bit of dread," said 21-year-old Imogen Vlutger.
A 40-year-old man said he didn't vote as he could not bring himself to tick any of the boxes on the ballot paper.
More than half of the country no longer see New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to a survey by the Helen Clark Foundation, a public policy think tank.
Kiwis have been leaving the country in record numbers, with many of them, including former prime minister Jacinda Arden, moving to Australia.

bbc.com.title: Met Police ruined my life, says Kenyan man wrongly sentenced over attack on UK couple
bbc.com.text:
- Published
A Kenyan woodcutter who was wrongly sentenced to death over an attack on a British couple has told the BBC that actions by London's Metropolitan Police involved in the case destroyed his life.
Somali gunmen broke into David and Judith Tebbutt's beach bungalow on the Kenyan coast in 2011. They shot David dead and abducted Judith, holding her captive in Somalia for six months.
Met detectives flew to Kenya to assist the investigation. Their evidence helped convict Ali Kololo, who spent more than a decade in prison before his conviction was overturned.
Kololo is suing the Met, claiming a senior officer, former Detective Superintendent Neil Hibberd, gave misleading evidence at his trial and acted unlawfully to secure his conviction.
In his first media interview, he told the BBC about his 15-year ordeal and his fight for compensation, which the Met is challenging in court.
We meet on Lamu, a small island off Kenya's northern coast, once a thriving Swahili port. People and goods are still carted through its narrow stone streets by donkey rather than car.
It was here, in 2013, that Kololo was sentenced to death.
Standing at the jetty, where police once brought him ashore in handcuffs, he relishes being free. But he is struggling to rebuild his life.
"Everything was taken from me. I'm starting from zero. I don't think I'll ever go back to who I was before," he says.
Before his arrest, Kololo lived with his wife and their three young children. He had once worked as a groundskeeper at the resort where the Tebbutts were staying, but by 2011 he earned his living felling trees in a local forest and selling the wood.
"My life was very good," he says. "I was fending for myself, taking good care of my family."
Within 24 hours of the attack, Kenyan police had arrested him.
"I was beaten with clubs and thrown into a car," he says. "They beat me for days, burning me with cigarettes, forcing me to confess to things. They subjected me to torture like no other."
Kololo could not read or write. He says police made him put his thumbprint on a statement claiming he had led the attackers to the Tebbutts.
"I didn't understand anything," he says, calling the statement "a mountain of lies". "I signed it without knowing what it was because of the state they had put me in".
The Kenyan police told us it "at all times strives to work within the law". Kololo is not suing them.
Within days of the attack, a team of Met officers, led by then Detective Superintendent Neil Hibberd, arrived to support the Kenyan investigation. The UK government had instructed the officers not to accept information from the Kenyan authorities that had been obtained by interrogating detainees.
But Hibberd requested Kololo's statement and later relied on it when giving evidence for the prosecution at his trial.
In court, Hibberd also presented evidence linking Kololo to the attack. He told the Kenyan court Kololo had been wearing a type of shoe that matched footwear marks found in the sand at the resort.
The officer who had arrested Kololo said he was barefoot when he was handed to police. Hibberd did not disclose that the Met's own forensic examination could not establish whether the shoe in question had made the marks.
At the trial, Kololo did not initially have a lawyer. He had to cross-examine all the prosecution witnesses himself, including Hibberd, through an interpreter who spoke Swahili, which was not Kololo's first language.
"I believe I was framed because I am a poor man and I did not have the strength or means to fight for myself," Kololo says.
Kololo was convicted of kidnap and robbery with violence - the only person ever convicted in connection with the attack. He spent three years on death row before his sentence was commuted to life imprisonment.
He recalls seeing his prison file. In the space for the expiry date, someone had written "death".
"I was completely heartbroken. I believed I could be executed at any moment, and I would never see my family, my children, ever again."
Years later, the UK's Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) established that Hibberd had omitted significant forensic evidence at the trial. It found that he would have had a case to answer for gross misconduct, but he could not face disciplinary proceedings because he had retired from the force. At the time, his lawyer said Hibberd absolutely disagreed with the report's findings.
In April 2023, Kenya's High Court quashed Kololo's conviction, because of doubts over the prosecution's evidence. This followed years of work by the legal charity Reprieve and a Kenyan lawyer, Alfred Olaba, who represented him for free.
They were supported by Judith Tebbutt, who believed Kololo was innocent. In an interview with the BBC in 2022, she said he had been scapegoated by Scotland Yard.
"He was not there on the night. He was not part of the group that held me. They've put this man in prison without any real evidence."
More than three years after his release, Kololo says he is still living with the effects of his torture and decade in prison. As we walk the narrow streets of Lamu's old town, his thin frame moves stiffly. He is on edge. "My mind is not good," he says. "I have not recovered."
He remembers being kept in a filthy, bedbug-ridden cell with up to eight other inmates, which he thought he would never leave. Twice he contracted tuberculosis and nearly died.
Kololo is now too frail to do the woodcutting he once relied on to make a living. He tries to grow enough to eat on the land around his home, but erratic rain makes it difficult.
"I have nothing. On the days I get food, I eat, and on the days I don't, I endure."
He lives alone in a mud hut. His wife divorced him after he went to prison, and their children went to live with his mother. They dropped out of school because the family could not pay the fees. Kololo says they were not allowed to visit him in prison. When he was released, they barely remembered him, especially his youngest.
"They were too young. Only now are they starting to regain the memory that 'this is our father who disappeared'," he says. "If it weren't for my mother, my children might have died."
For much of our time together, Kololo is remarkably upbeat. He trusts that his lawyers and God will deliver him justice. But when we talk about the Met, his demeanour shifts.
"I am extremely angry with the police," he says. "I'm also angry with the Kenyan Police. They collaborated to incriminate me. What [Hibberd] said destroyed my entire life and my children's lives."
The Met has not apologised to Kololo or admitted wrongdoing. The force is contesting his compensation claim, which his lawyers say could take years to resolve.
"These people falsely accused me. Do I not deserve something?" he asks.
The Met told the BBC that neither they nor Hibberd wanted to comment on Kololo's claim, but it said: "Our thoughts are with Mr Kololo, Mrs Tebbutt, her family and all those who have been affected by this terrible crime. The Metropolitan Police remains committed to supporting the Kenyan authorities in any way that may be possible, in order to get justice for Mrs Tebbutt and her late husband."
Preetha Gopalan, Reprieve's head of UK litigation, describes the Met's behaviour in Kololo's case as "egregious".
"They've spent 10 years trying to evade accountability in every way possible, now dragging him through the courts," she says. "It's possible for them to do the right thing, but they are unwilling, and so this ordeal continues to haunt Kololo and his family."
"Even if I get a billion shillings, I will never be the same," Kololo says. "But if I get the justice I deserve, I can help my children and take care of myself when I am an old man."

bbc.com.title: Sheikh Hasina's planned return puts Bangladesh on edge - and India in a bind
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Sheikh Hasina has repeatedly vowed to return to Bangladesh.
Now the ousted prime minister has put a date on her homecoming - 16 December - and even outlined how she intends to make the journey.
The government in Dhaka, which had previously dismissed the prospect, is taking her latest declaration more seriously.
Hasina, 79, who fled to Delhi in August 2024 after a student-led uprising ended her 15-year rule, plans to go back on Victory Day, the anniversary of Bangladesh's triumph over Pakistan in the 1971 liberation war, her spokesperson said.
She was sentenced to death after being convicted of crimes against humanity for her role in the crackdown, in a trial held in her absence that raised questions about due process. Her Awami League party is banned in Bangladesh. The UN says as many as 1,400 people were killed by security forces during the uprising.
The government says she would be arrested immediately if she returned and has promised to carry out the death sentence.
Hasina now wants the Bangladesh government to arrange a flight from Delhi. If that fails, she could travel commercially or cross the land border.
"She is even prepared to walk into Bangladesh," Abu Obaidha Arin, a key aide to Hasina, told the BBC.
India and Bangladesh share a 4,096km (2,545 mile) border across five Indian states - West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. Her supporters, Arin said, had identified nine possible crossing points. "This is a carefully thought-out, precise plan. This is serious."
Dhaka has responded with defiance, insisting Hasina must be extradited.
"Reality and desire are different things," Humaiun Kobir, Bangladesh's state minister for foreign affairs, told reporters in Dhaka. "[The reality is] she's not a regular commercial passenger. She can only be brought back in handcuffs."
India's foreign ministry said on Wednesday that Hasina's extradition request was being examined through the "established process", adding that a voluntary return would be a separate matter.
Many in Dhaka believe Hasina's declaration is more than a promise of homecoming.
They believe it is an attempt to test the government's authority, force her way back into the political conversation and exploit divisions among the parties that united to oust her. It also threatens to turn India's unresolved problem of sheltering a former ally into a more immediate diplomatic crisis.
The date is significant. Hasina is invoking Victory Day to reclaim her place in Bangladesh's founding narrative. Aides say she has spent months trying to keep her party alive in exile.
Arin says Hasina has been in regular contact with party leaders and workers through interactive audio conversations on Telegram, keeping alive a network that might otherwise have been difficult to sustain from exile.
Over the past 18 months, he says, she has held more than 300 such meetings, reaching supporters across all 64 districts and the country's 300 constituencies. They are organised through the Awami League's 78 units and "can last four or five hours".
The meetings allow Hasina to listen directly to party workers, hear their grievances and understand what is happening on the ground, Arin says. He insists the response has been substantial and claims the party "could mobilise five million people to welcome her along the route from the border to Dhaka, forming a human chain".
"We have the organisational capacity to make that happen," he says.
That may be an ambitious claim. The Awami League remains a mass party with millions of supporters, but it is banned and largely shut out of mainstream politics. Much of its leadership is abroad, in jail or underground. Police have arrested supporters and filed thousands of cases against party workers.
Yet its supporters have continued to take to the streets, staging flash protests that have grown more frequent and confrontational in recent months.
Several districts have reported bomb attacks, arson and vandalism, though responsibility for some incidents remains disputed.
Gopalganj, Hasina's ancestral district, has proved particularly difficult for the authorities to control.
Awami League supporters have attacked police stations, external, torched vehicles and targeted homes and offices belonging to ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) leaders, reports say. Highways have been blocked, external with felled trees and burning tyres, bringing traffic to a standstill. In some areas, police have withdrawn, external amid fears of further attacks.
Supporters have staged 40 demonstrations and more than 140 riots up to 23 November, according to data from conflict monitoring group Acled (Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project). At least 11 people, including two civilians, have been killed in political violence this month, six directly linked to the unrest, the group says.
The party's ability to cause disruption, however, is not necessarily evidence of a broad resurgence.
Many in Dhaka remain sceptical that Hasina will actually return, viewing the announcement as a means of galvanising a demoralised party.
Yet the Awami League has achieved something politically: it is back in the conversation. Immediately after Hasina's fall, even mentioning the party was taboo. Now its future is being debated across the political spectrum.
Shafiqul Alam, editor of the English-language daily Daily Waadaa and former press secretary to the Muhammad Yunus-led interim government, believes the party is "exploiting cracks in the unity forged during the uprising".
He told the BBC that "disagreements" over the July Charter, external, proposed constitutional changes and the referendum have "widened divisions" between the elected BNP government and rivals Jamaat-e-Islami and the youth-led National Citizen Party (NCP).
"The Awami League sees an opening," Alam told the BBC. "The party believes this is an opportune moment to take to the streets, exploiting a weakened police force and divisions among the forces of the July uprising."
Analysts say if Hasina returns it could just as easily deepen hostility as revive her party's fortunes. The government has framed the sporadic recent violence as terrorism, while supporters insist their demonstrations are peaceful and accuse the authorities of repression.
The larger question is whether Bangladesh can sustain the exclusion of a political constituency as substantial as the Awami League without creating another source of instability.
For India, the dilemma is increasingly difficult to manage.
Delhi has sheltered Hasina, but her public remarks have angered Dhaka, which wants her extradited. India has sought to repair ties through diplomatic outreach and talks on trade, border security and other bilateral issues, but relations remain strained.
The chill is striking: nearly 10 months into his tenure, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has yet to visit India.
A trip was reportedly in the offing in August, but Hasina's press conference in Delhi proved a setback to efforts to reset relations.
Avinash Paliwal, who teaches politics and international studies at SOAS University of London, argues that Hasina's latest announcement has "shifted the burden of choice to Dhaka rather than Delhi".
Delhi, he says, "feels it has tried its best" to work with Rahman's government over the past 10 months - "from appointing a political heavyweight as high commissioner, external with cabinet rank to offering fresh talks on security and trade".
"The failure of this outreach has left India disillusioned with Dhaka. India seems to have decided that bilateral relations will likely remain tense whatever it does, so there is little reason to stop Hasina from stirring the political pot."
Delhi has the leverage to restrain Hasina from making political statements on Indian soil, Paliwal argues, but may not want to exercise it.
Nor, in his view, is it in India's interest to see the Awami League permanently excluded from Bangladeshi politics.
"The political party still enjoys pockets of support across Bangladesh and is weaved into the social and political fabric of the country," he says. "So, yes, it is in India's interest, and also in Bangladesh's long-term interests, to rehabilitate the Awami League and take the path of political reconciliation."
That view is increasingly contested in Dhaka.
"There is a perception in Bangladesh that India wants to rehabilitate the Awami League. There are issues India has not resolved, including the extradition of Hasina. India has also not renewed the transit facilities that could benefit Bangladeshi garment exporters, while the Ganges water treaty, external is nearing expiry without much progress. But has India done enough to win back trust?" says Alam.
"For now, only tourist and medical visas have resumed. Everything else remains in limbo."
A Dhaka-based foreign-policy expert, who asked not to be named, says the two countries remain locked in "mutual frustration".
Hasina, he says, remains central to the impasse. "She remains the elephant in the room, but we also have to find a way to move beyond Hasina."
Paliwal argues that the least damaging outcome for India would be Hasina returning to face a fresh trial, with the Awami League rehabilitated under a different operational leadership.
"It will reintroduce a degree of balance in Bangladeshi politics, and will afford India space to protect its long-term interests and equities better," he says.
For now, 16 December is not yet a confirmed journey. But Hasina has already succeeded in making her return a question that neither Dhaka nor Delhi can ignore.
"December could be chaotic. Everyone in Dhaka is on edge," says the foreign-policy expert, warning of protests and confrontation as Hasina's proposed return date approaches - and the possibility that it could be postponed yet again.
"Hasina is unlikely to return, as she would face a death sentence. But her comments have clearly galvanized her supporters," says Pearl Pandya, Acled's South Asia analyst.
But the impasse is also complicating India's ties with Bangladesh. As Paliwal puts it, the "next window of serious negotiations will now open only after Hasina returns to Dhaka, or Dhaka relents under pressure and returns to the table".

bbc.com.title: My dad's watch stopped the moment he died - I found it in the ashes of Hong Kong tower fire
bbc.com.text:
My dad's watch stopped the moment he died - I found it in the ashes of Hong Kong tower fire
Mr So's parents, both in their 80s, were among the 168 people killed in last year's Hong Kong tower-block blaze - the deadliest the city had seen in decades.
Their building was the first of the Wang Fuk Court complex to catch fire, and their bodies were burned beyond recognition.
In this video Mr So, who is only using his surname, visits his parents' grave and shows what is left of his parents' possessions.
Video by Phoebe Kong and Yik Lam, BBC Chinese

bbc.com.title: US too focused on Middle East and not pushing Russia hard enough, Zelensky tells BBC
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, saying delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles are costing Ukrainian lives and complaining that the US is not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks.
In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president also said it was "strange" that Donald Trump had posted a photo of himself embracing Vladimir Putin as "my friend".
"Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.
"He's an aggressor, and a killer…He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, adding it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during World War Two.
Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the United States.
Trump's two envoys have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.
The latest round of peace talks, mediated in Abu Dhabi earlier this month, made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.
He said talks were expected to resume in December.
On Thursday, Donald Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".
But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions – on everything.
And Zelensky revealed that it was not clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced.
The Kremlin appears to be resisting.
Ukraine urgently needs the talks to move forward and bring five exhausting years of Russia's full-scale invasion to an end.
Russian strikes across the country have been growing more frequent and more deadly: the number of civilians being killed is at an all-time high.
So Zelensky called for "real helpful allies, who can push Russia" to achieve results and urged the US to live up to its reputation as a strong country with "power and respect".
"When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It's not right," he said.
The US argues that it is neutral: in the complex search for a peace deal between the two sides that can hold.
In the meantime, Kyiv is struggling to defend its skies.
The air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities.
Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.
Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.
But there is a "very, very big" deficit of interceptors to stop ballistic missiles and he said the Americans were delaying deliveries of its Patriot systems.
"It's a pity they made a focus on Middle East and they help them more… It's a pity. We have huge questions with this," Zelensky said.
"The deficit of these missiles - that is people's lives."
He also confirmed that the US satellite communications system, Starlink – and its military version, Starshield – were still being restricted in occupied areas of Ukraine.
Ukrainian drone units have described their problems to the BBC, as their interceptor drones can no longer catch up with Russian Shaheds. It means those weapons then fly deeper into Ukraine, unhindered.
So whose decision was that?
"Technically SpaceX, politically - I don't know, I really don't know," Zelensky replied. "It's like... ping pong. We are asking one side, they say it's the other."
Tough winter
Ukraine's own long-range strikes against Russian targets have increased in recent weeks, including oil refineries and ships carrying weapons or fuel.
On Thursday, Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said an attack that sank a Russian warship docked in eastern Libya this week risked spreading war to the Mediterranean, which was unacceptable.
Zelensky defended the move, calling the warship Merkury an "absolutely fair goal".
He accepted that such strikes were "very dangerous" but said Ukraine's forces "never attack" without co-ordinating with its partners.
He declined to be more specific.
But he acknowledged that Ukraine was bracing for a difficult and dangerous winter.
Recent attacks on Kyiv have targeted bridges over the vast river Dnipro, apparently trying to cut the city in two.
Some residents have already left town for the winter and businesses closed, as power cuts and strikes on logistics networks have pushed operating costs unmanageably high.
They have also plunged much of the city into darkness.
"[Russia] wants us to run away, of course," Zelensky said.
"People can go, but we will try to defend our capital in any way. We need our capital. Without a capital, you don't have a country."

bbc.com.title: Zelensky questions 'strange' Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview
bbc.com.text:
Zelensky questions 'strange' Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview
Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced his frustration with the United States and questioned Donald Trump's relationship with Vladimir Putin in an interview with the BBC.
In a picture posted to Truth Social on Saturday, where Trump and Putin embrace, the US president described his Russian counterpart as "my friend".
"Of course it's up to the President of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky told the BBC's Sarah Rainsford at his office in central Kyiv.
"He [Putin] is an aggressor, and a killer…He can't be a friend. Just cannot be."

bbc.com.title: Diesel tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes capsizes near Ibiza, killing one
bbc.com.text:
- Published
An oil tanker carrying up to 7,000 tonnes of diesel has capsized off the coast of Ibiza, leaving one crew member dead, authorities have said.
The Med Emre, a Malta-flagged vessel, was carrying 17 crew members who were all rescued. However seven were taken to hospital and one was later pronounced dead, Balearic Islands emergency services confirmed.
The six crew receiving treatment reportedly suffered minor injuries, such as hypothermia, Spanish media reports.
The possible environmental damage is being assessed by a plane and Spain's pollution control vessel, Clara Campoamor, which is owned by the country's national maritime rescue service.
"There is still little information available about a possible fuel spill," Balearic Islands' President Marga Prohens wrote on X.
Elena Delgado, maritime captain of Valencia, told news agency AFP that a small slick that had formed around the boat had "disappeared".
"The situation is stabilised," she said, adding that further inspections would be carried out on Friday morning.
Earlier, regional emergencies director Pablo Gárriz said the tanker had not completely sunk, as had originally been reported. The vessel remains partially submerged.
The Med Emre capsized 25 nautical miles (46 km; 29 miles) from Ibiza's coastline and 57 nautical miles from Valencia. It is unclear what caused the sinking.
The chemical tanker was en route from Algeciras, in southern Spain, to Barcelona in the north-east.
Rescuers in Valencia received a distress call around 22:30 local time (21:30 GMT) on Wednesday, according to Spanish media. Minutes later, the vessel reported a leak and the crew said it was leaning at a 90-degree angle.
The injured crew members have been taken to hospitals in Valencia and Can Misses Hospital in Ibiza, President Prohens said.
Ibiza's marine environment was added to the Unesco World Heritage List in 1999. In particular, it is home to dense prairies of Posidonia oceanic seagrass, which is found only in the Mediterranean basin and plays a vital role in supporting local marine biodiversity.
In 2002, Spain experienced one of its worst environmental disasters when the Prestige oil tanker ran into trouble off Galicia's coastline. It spilled more than 60,000 tonnes of heavy fuel oil into the sea.

bbc.com.title: Two Italians killed in strike in Kuwait, as Iran denies responsibility
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Two Italian nationals have died following a strike on a facility in Kuwait which both countries have blamed on Iran.
The pair were technicians working for German arms manufacturing company Rheinmetall, Italy's foreign ministry said.
Iran has denied responsibility for the attack, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi saying the incident looked "suspicious" and that Tehran would work with Kuwait and Italy to "determine the cause".
Kuwait's defence ministry said earlier that four people - the two Italians, a Kuwaiti national and Pakistani national - had been injured from falling shrapnel after a number of drones from Iran were detected and intercepted.
It comes just over a week after Kuwait said it had repelled overnight Iranian drone attacks on an airbase which hosts US forces - the first strikes in more than two months on the country.
Recent exchanges of fire between the US and Iran, and a deadlock in negotiations, have raised fears of a major escalation in the war.
The conflict began when US and Israel attacked Iran in late February, with Iran retaliating by launching missiles and drones at Israel and Gulf Arab states hosting US military assets and personnel.
On Thursday, Araghchi said he had expressed condolences over the deaths in calls with his Italian and Kuwaiti counterparts and that the incident looked like a "precooked recipe for war", without expanding further.
Earlier, the country's armed forces spokesperson Abolfazl Shekarchi said "no military or offensive operations have been conducted" by Iran.
Kuwait's Army said the latest attack was on a "vital site in the country" and was the result of "heinous Iranian aggression", while confirming the deaths of the two Italian nationals.
Italy's foreign minister was quoted by Italian media as saying that investigations showed that the drone used in the attack was manufactured in Iran and that Iranian proxies were known to carry out attacks in the region.
"The Rheinmetall Group is in deep mourning," the German firm said in a statement confirming the deaths of two of its staff members.
"Two highly valued employees lost their lives while carrying out their professional duties, as they were providing technical support for air defence systems," it added.
"Protecting people in the country was a matter of profound importance to them.
"Company management and the workforce are devastated that our colleagues have now lost their lives."
Italian media outlets have named the two individuals. One of the men was reported to be 36, while the other was 65 and nearing retirement.
The men had been performing maintenance on systems used by the Kuwait Armed Forces, according to Italian press agency Ansa citing Italy's foreign ministry.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wrote on X: "On my own behalf and on behalf of the government, I express my deepest sympathy and offer my heartfelt condolences to the victims' families.
"My thoughts are with all those affected by the attack and their families."
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen wrote on social media: "We must step up pressure on Iran to end these unacceptable attacks against its neighbours and our partners in the Gulf.
"Today's events are a further reminder that security in the Gulf is a security issue for us all."

bbc.com.title: Watch: Roofs torn off and streets under water as severe weather hits US
bbc.com.text:
Watch: Roofs torn off and streets under water as severe weather hits US
Powerful storms are battering both US coasts as the Thanksgiving holiday weekend gets under way.
Hundreds of flights have been cancelled and hundreds of thousands are without power, in states including Virginia, North Carolina and New Jersey.
Strong winds have blown roofs off houses and floodwater has submerged streets.

bbc.com.title: Nine injured, three critically, after Bangkok oil refinery explosion
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Nine people have been injured after an explosion at an oil refinery in Bangkok, authorities have said.
Three of them are in critical condition, according to news agency AFP, which said the local hospital had revised its earlier assessment of four.
A fire broke out after the blast at the Phra Khanong facility run by energy giant Bangchak Corporation in the east of Thailand's capital at around 14:45 (07:45 GMT).
The company said the fire was brought under control and put out within 30 minutes, adding that the cause of the incident was being investigated.
Black smoke could be seen across Bangkok's skyline after the blast, as local officials told residents to leave the area.
An alert sent to mobile phones by Bangkok authorities confirmed that the fire was under control, but urged people to avoid the area.
Eyewitnesses shared video clips on social media of flames and smoke rising above the refinery.
On a visit to the scene, Thailand's energy minister Akanat Promphan said it appeared the impact of the explosion was limited because the fire started in a distillation tower about 100m (330ft) from where oil was being stored.
He said the incident was concerning as the refinery was in a residential area and the government was suspending production until it could be confident that operations would resume without any issues.
Bangchak Corporation said air quality monitoring in the immediate area around the refinery was within normal ranges.
It confirmed that production at the site, which can process up to 120,000 barrels of oil a day had been shut down. The company has a second refinery in Chonburi province, about 50 miles (80km) from Bangkok, handling a daily capacity of about 180,000 barrels.
An explosion occurred at the Bangkok refinery in July 2012, sparking a fire but no reported injuries.

bbc.com.title: New UK-EU treaty has 10-year termination clause
bbc.com.text:
- Published
The government and the EU have published the texts of two treaties agreed last week as part of a post-Brexit reset.
The treaties were published on Thursday afternoon, alongside legislation designed to enact the bulk of the deal.
The deal covering food exports has a 10-year termination clause that would mean if one party ended the agreement, they would have to pay "reasonable and proportionate costs" to rebuild border checks infrastructure, which will be significantly scaled back as part of the new deal.
Opposition leader Kemi Badenoch has said she would scrap the deal while Reform UK's Nigel Farage has suggested he would refuse to pay.
The Brexit reset deal has already sparked debate about its benefits, its costs, and a wider discussion on the future of the UK-EU relationship.
The deal covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.
Two of the three legal texts were released on Thursday, covering the food trade and emissions trading scheme deals, alongside the government's cost-cutting bill to enact the deal.
A new assessment of the impact of the deal on different sectors and regions of the country was also released.
Under the deal, food exporters will be significant beneficiaries from the scrapping of considerable red tape and checks, and dismantling of border facilities. An internal analysis forecasts a 16% boost the export of major agricultural commodities.
The industry and government hope the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers, but there may be no clear visible impact at the checkout.
Privately, industry insiders told the BBC earlier this week that there are too many moving parts in the world economy, in particular the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.
Regarding the fine detail in the text of one of the treaties relating to the 10-year termination clause, European affairs minister Hamish Falconer said: "The Cutting Costs Bill allows us to implement two major trade agreements."
"It allows us to eliminate paperwork for our food and drink traders, protect billions of pounds worth of British exports from carbon taxes, and make doing business with our largest trading partner cheaper and easier."
A plan to link British and European emissions trading schemes will see more coverage across the UK's aviation and maritime industries.
The treaty text also contains finer detail of how the UK will observe, shape but not vote on relevant EU rules. The UK will be invited to attend European Commission meetings and expert groups as an observer, as well as taking part in emergency food security planning.
However, the UK will not be given voting rights.
Plans to use secondary legislation, including granting direct so-called "Henry VIII powers" to ministers to align UK and EU laws, are detailed in the legislation.
Such powers will enable ministers to make changes to bills with less Parliamentary scrutiny.
Outlining the agreement with the EU to MPs earlier this week, the prime minister said new agreements with the EU are "pragmatic" and "not a prelude to anything".
Andy Burnham also said it would be "unthinkable" for the UK to rejoin the bloc without a referendum.
Several former prime ministers have urged him not to reopen the Brexit debate. Burnham said they are "stuck in the past" and later claimed there would be "no banging on about Europe" from Labour.
Badenoch said Burnham has "oversold" the deal and was "trying to take Britain back to 2015".

bbc.com.title: Gérard Depardieu to stand trial for alleged rape of actress in 2018, court rules
bbc.com.text:
- Published
French film actor Gérard Depardieu is to stand trial for the alleged rape of actress Charlotte Arnould, a Paris appeals court has confirmed.
Arnould, who was 22 at the time, had reported the alleged rape several days after going to his house in Paris to rehearse a play.
