She has waived her right to anonymity and her lawyer said Thursday's ruling was a "first" and the forthcoming trial would be historic.
Depardieu, 77, had contested his indictment on two counts of rape. In a letter published in Le Figaro in 2023, Depardieu strongly denied Arnould's allegations, saying "there was never any coercion or violence between us".
Depardieu was for decades a leading figure in French and international cinema for roles in Green Card, The Man in the Iron Mask and the Asterix films. He was awarded France's Légion d'honneur in 1996.
But in recent years a series of allegations have been made against him over his conduct on film sets and elsewhere in the wake of France's #MeToo movement, known as balance ton porc (call out your pig).
Last year, he was given an 18-month suspended jail term after he was found guilty of sexually assaulting two women on a film set in Paris in May. He was also placed on the sex offenders register and ordered to pay compensation.
He dropped his appeal against the ruling last week and offered "sincere apologies" for his behaviour on the set of director Jean Becker's 2021 film Les Volets Verts (The Green Shutters).
Depardieu had been a friend of Charlotte Arnould's father and on 7 August 2018 she had gone to his home, where much of what happened was captured on the actor's own CCTV.
Arnould's case was initially dismissed for insufficient evidence, but after she filed a civil complaint, a judicial investigation was opened in the summer of 2020.
Speaking outside the Paris appeal court on Thursday, her lawyer Carine Durrieu Diebolt said the ruling was a victory for her client for whom it was "genuinely a relief".
The appeal court said that while Depardieu should stand trial for what took place on that day, he would not be tried for a further alleged rape at a hotel six days later.
Depardieu's lawyer David-Olivier Kaminski told reporters that court had partly ruled in his favour: "As soon as we get the ruling, we will look into the possibility of appealing to the Court of Cassation."
Meanwhile, Depardieu is under a separate investigation alongside French author Michel Houellebecq for "allegations of a sexual nature".
French authorities confirmed their inquiry last week, following reports of an alleged "gang rape" on the set of the film Thalasso in 2018.
If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, details of help and support in the UK are available at BBC Action Line.

bbc.com.title: Pregnant US inmate escapes in prison vehicle after medical appointment
bbc.com.text:
- Published
A pregnant inmate has escaped from custody in the US state of New Mexico, after taking control of a police vehicle while returning to prison from a prenatal appointment, the state's corrections department has said.
Rebecca Taylor, 26, took control of the Dodge Journey and drove away when the team transporting her and another inmate stopped to pick up food in Albuquerque, local media reported.
The New Mexico Corrections Department said that the vehicle and her prison jumpsuit were later recovered, but Taylor remains on the run.
She had been imprisoned for multiple theft and burglary charges, the department said in a Facebook statement.
Local media reported that another inmate, also travelling back from a prenatal appointment, was able to get out of the car as Taylor took control on Wednesday morning.
The corrections department has said that a multi-agency search for Taylor is under way. The BBC has approached it for an update.
The Albuquerque Journal reported that Taylor is currently in her second trimester of pregnancy. For this reason, she was not restrained during transportation, department spokesperson Brittany Roembach said.
"It is the understanding right now that one officer was with the vehicle but not inside of the vehicle when this occurred," she was quoted as saying.
All prisons in New Mexico went into lockdown following Taylor's escape, but it was lifted at 06:00 on Thursday.
However the prison where she was being held, the Western New Mexico Corrections Facility, will remain on "modified movement", and no visitors are currently allowed.
The public has been told not to approach Rebecca Taylor if they see her, and call police straight away.

bbc.com.title: Tributes for Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor after his death aged 65
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Simon Le Bon, Sir Rod Stewart and Gary Kemp are among the pop stars who have paid tribute to Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor following his death at the age of 65.
Taylor co-wrote some of the group's biggest hits including Save A Prayer, Rio and Girls On Film.
Le Bon and his bandmates paid tribute, saying "he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music", while Sir Rod remembered his "dear pal" and Spandau Ballet's Kemp called him "a great player who set the tone for the 80s".
Taylor's wife Tracey called him "the rock of our family", adding: "We will miss him every single day." He died after "a long and courageous battle with prostate cancer", Duran Duran said in a statement on Wednesday.
He died "peacefully at home, surrounded by his family, on Monday 23rd November", a statement said.
Paying tribute, his Duran Duran bandmates said: "From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music.
"His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed."
They said their thoughts were with his wife, children and grandson.
Le Bon said there was a "a massive Andy Taylor shaped hole in my heart".
"Andy never took the easy musical route. His overdrive overdrove us into being the only funk/rock/punk band in the New Romantic movement, with songs that still survive, decades later."
Sir Rod, who wrote five songs with Taylor for the 1988 album Out of Order, recalled them making "some good music together" and having "some outrageous fun".
Kemp said Taylor "influenced many of us along the way with his sparse staccato style", adding: "He brought shameless rock to the mix."
In a band tribute, Spandau Ballet called him "a hugely talented musician and an important part of the British music scene".
US guitarist Nile Rodgers, the co-founder of Chic, recalled "countless great days and nights" with his "dear friend".
Belinda Carlisle said she was "blessed" to have worked with Taylor, who played the guitar solo and was in the video for her song Mad About You.
Former Led Zeppelin frontman Robert Plant called Taylor "a tough fighter", while Then Jerico's Mark Shaw remembered him as "one of the greatest musicians and songwriters I've ever heard and had the privilege to work with".
Taylor's wife Tracey, a hairstylist he met during the early days of Duran Duran, and whom he married in 1982, said: "For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first for Taylor, adding: "Nothing made him happier than having us all together."
She said he faced the last few years "with so much courage and determination" and said they were "grateful" for the "kindness and support shown to him by fans throughout his illness", saying it brought him "immense comfort and strength".
The son of a fisherman, Taylor taught himself guitar, bass, and drums and began playing professionally at age 13.
He played with several bands around the UK before answering a music paper advertisement for a "live-wire guitarist", which led to his audition for Duran Duran in Birmingham in April 1980.
The group went on to achieve global fame through the New Romantic movement, which combined slick, melodic synth-pop with aspirational music videos and chiselled good looks.
Taylor's guitar lines - full of glassy, powerful riffs - were often a highlight of their songs, from the choppy opening of Girls on Film to the sleazy scuzz of Hungry Like The Wolf.
Duran Duran were one of the biggest pop acts of the 1980s, and its five members became global hearththrobs.
Their indelible hooks and airbrushed music videos found a natural home on the newly launched MTV, giving their career a huge boost in the US.
They became so popular in the US that the press labeled them the leaders of a "second British invasion" of the charts - alongside groups like Spandau Ballet, Human League and Eurythmics.
During a hiatus in 1984, Andy and John Taylor enlisted Robert Palmer for their successful but short-lived side project the Power Station.
The following year, the guitarist decided to quit Duran Duran after a miserable experience performing at Live Aid.
"We'd reached rock bottom and we had absolutely nothing to say to each other," he wrote in his autobiography, Wild Boy.
"We drove to the venue through streets packed with excited rock fans, but inside the bus the atmosphere was as if we were on a way to a funeral."
He went on to play on Palmer's Addicted To Love, and released a solo album, Thunder, in 1987.
After a period writing and producing albums for other artists, he rejoined Duran Duran in 2000, lasting for just one album (2004's Astronaut) before parting ways again.
In 2022, when the band were inducted to the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, Taylor was notably absent from the ceremony, despite public plans for a reunion.
When the group took the stage, Le Bon read a letter from the guitarist, in which he revealed his diagnosis with stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer.
Nonetheless, he contributed to the following year's Halloween-themed album Danse Macabre, marking his final collaboration with the band.
The following BBC programmes will pay tribute to Taylor:
- Duran Duran at the BBC, on BBC Four on Friday 27 November at 21:30 GMT
- Sounds of the 80s, on Radio 2 on Saturday 28 November at at 18:00 GMT

bbc.com.title: Egyptian authorities arrest motorist over tanker crash that killed 31
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Egyptian authorities have arrested a man accused of causing a tanker crash and massive fire that killed 31 people on a busy Cairo highway.
The public prosecutor's office said the motorist had confessed to driving at 110km/h (68mph) along a section of ring road, to the north of the old city centre, and clipping the tanker with the side of his car as he changed lanes.
Sources close to the investigation were earlier quoted by state media as saying a high-voltage cable had fallen in front of the fuel truck, causing the driver to lose control.
Twenty-one others were injured in the crash in the Warraq neighbourhood on Wednesday evening, with hospitals treating patients for burns and smoke inhalation.
The public prosecutor's office said on Thursday that "upon questioning the suspect and confronting him with the findings of the investigation... he confessed to committing the act".
"He added that, while moving between traffic lanes and overtaking vehicles, the left side of his car collided with the right rear side of the tanker. This caused him to lose control of the steering wheel and his car veered to the far right of the road."
At the same time, one of the fuel tanker's tyres burst, causing it to veer into the highway's central reservation, hit the concrete barrier and overturn, spilling fuel and igniting a fire, the prosecutor's office said.
Egyptian authorities have not named the suspect accused of causing the fatal crash, but they said he had been travelling with his father at the time.
The raised motorway - a major artery for traffic around the Egyptian capital - was reopened by emergency services hours after the crash occurred, with the burnt-out wrecks of cars shifted to the side by bulldozers and diggers.
A cabinet minister said on Thursday that 10 million Egyptian pounds (£139,000; $182,000) had been donated to the families of the victims, while the nation's sports minister said all state-run celebratory activities would be cancelled in the aftermath of the crash.
Egypt has suffered several deadly fires in recent years. Road collisions are also common, attributed to poor maintenance and violations of traffic laws, and leading to thousands of road deaths a year.

bbc.com.title: Hope for millions as cheaper HIV prevention jab reaches Africa
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Uganda is set to receive its first supplies of a cheaper version of a ground-breaking injection to prevent HIV, raising hopes of expanding access to the drug across Africa, where the burden of the disease remains highest.
The first global shipment of the generic drug, known as lenacapavir, arrived in Zambia on Wednesday, with deliveries to Uganda expected in the coming days, the Global Fund has said.
The drug, administered as an injection twice a year, is nearly 100% effective at preventing HIV infection and is expected to cost just $40 (£30) per person annually.
Zimbabwe is due to receive supplies early next year, with several other countries expected to follow.
The arrival of the generic drug comes just a year after the original version, developed by US pharmaceutical giant Gilead Sciences, became available in sub-Saharan Africa.
The original version cost about about $28,000 annually in the US, putting it beyond the reach of many of those in developing countries.
Lenacapavir works by targeting the protective protein shell of HIV, disrupting the virus's ability to multiply and establish an infection in the body.
In a landmark clinical trial involving more than 5,000 adolescent girls and young women in Uganda and South Africa in 2024, none of those who received the injection contracted HIV.
Health experts say the injection offers a major advantage over existing HIV prevention pills, known as pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), which must be taken every day and can carry social stigma.
The World Health Organization (WHO) recommended the drug for HIV prevention in July 2025.
The Global Fund described the arrival of the drug in Africa as a "major breakthrough" in the fight against HIV, saying cheaper supplies would help reach millions more people at risk of infection.
"These deliveries mark an unprecedented acceleration and expansion in access to a highly effective, quality-assured generic HIV prevention medicine in low- and middle-income settings," the group said in a statement on Wednesday.
More than 189,000 people across 10 countries have already received their first injection of lenacapavir, according to the Global Fund.
The organisation expects 24 countries to have received supplies by the end of this year and, working with the US government, plans to reach at least three million people by the end of 2028.
It is eventually expected to be available in 120 low- and middle-income countries.
Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for nearly two-thirds of people living with HIV globally, with adolescent girls and young women disproportionately affected.
South Africa has the world's largest HIV-positive population, with nearly eight million people living with the virus. It is among the countries expected to receive the cheaper injection.
Some 41 million people worldwide were living with HIV last year, while 570,000 died from HIV-related illnesses, according to the WHO.
The rollout comes amid concerns that sweeping cuts to US foreign aid under President Donald Trump's administration could undermine decades of progress in tackling HIV in Africa, where many countries rely heavily on international funding for prevention and treatment.
The UN aims to end Aids as a public health threat by 2030.

bbc.com.title: Myanmar refuses to comply with parts of ICJ genocide ruling
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Myanmar will not comply with "inappropriate" parts of the genocide ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ), its leader Min Aung Hlaing has said in his first public comments since the court decision.
The ICJ's landmark ruling last week found Myanmar guilty of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority in a 2017 military crackdown that killed thousands and forced more than 700,000 to flee.
Myanmar denied committing genocide, saying its forces had responded to attacks by armed groups. It is the first state to have been found in violation of the 1948 Genocide Convention.
Min Aung Hlaing said "the term 'genocide' had seriously affected the country's reputation", state media report.
"Myanmar would take actions appropriate for a responsible country but would not comply with requirements it considered inappropriate," the country's coup leader-turned-president said at a meeting on Wednesday, according to state media.
The statement did not specify which parts of the ruling the country objects to.
The genocide case, brought by The Gambia in 2019, centred around so-called "clearance operations" initiated in 2017 in Rakhine State, where many of the Rohingya Muslim minority resided.
The ICJ determined that about 10,000 Rohingya were violently killed during the operation, while more than 700,000 are thought to have fled to Bangladesh by foot or by sea. The court found that approximately 815,000 had been targeted in some way.
The verdict was reached by a majority of nine votes to six among a panel of judges from around the world.
The ICJ also found in favour by majority that Myanmar had violated several other parts of the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The ruling is final and cannot be appealed.
The ICJ ordered Myanmar to pay proportionate reparations, but said an exact figure should be determined at a later date.
The court also ordered Myanmar to stop ongoing violations and immediately investigate those suspected of breaking the Convention.
But the ICJ does not have the power to enforce these demands. Instead it has to rely on the UN Security Council and political pressure to make its rulings stick.
While the ruling was largely symbolic, it was welcomed by Rohingya communities and human rights groups who have long called attention to the suffering faced by the Rohingya.
More than a dozen countries have acknowledged the ICJ ruling, and the UK has announced sanctions on several senior Myanmar military leaders.
Myanmar has been devastated by civil war since Min Aung Hlaing led a military coup to oust civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi in 2021. The move turned Myanmar into an international pariah, and its military regime has faced sweeping international sanctions.
Since then, Min Aung Hlaing has been trying to reintegrate Myanmar into the international community, but it remains largely shut out of key diplomatic arenas.

bbc.com.title: Hamas political official and wife among eight Palestinians killed in Israeli strikes on Gaza
bbc.com.text:
- Published
A Hamas political official and his wife were among eight Palestinians killed in three Israeli air strikes across the Gaza Strip on Thursday.
Local sources told the BBC a residential apartment in Deir al-Balah was targeted at dawn, killing Khaled Abu Nada - the deputy education minister - and his wife, Abeer Mohammed Ismail Abu Nada.
A Hamas Civil Defence spokesman said that rescue teams and medical personnel had transferred eight bodies to Al-Aqsa Hospital in central Gaza and Al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City.
In a joint statement, Israel's prime minister and defence minister said the operation was "part of a series of targeted killings" against Hamas officials.
Thursday's strikes also reportedly killed three Palestinians on al-Nafaq Street, east of Gaza City. Their identities have not yet been established, eyewitnesses said.
In a separate strike on Shati refugee camp, west of Gaza City, three Palestinians working for Hamas's security services were killed. They were identified as Yasser al-Lahham, Iyad Ahmed and Ibrahim al-Mashal.
In a post X, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu confirmed the death of Khaled Abu Nada and said about 80 Hamas officials have been killed in the last month.
"No one in Hamas's leadership will succeed in evading us," he said, adding that the military would "continue to pursue our enemies and protect the security of Israeli civilians".
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it had carried out a strike on a "senior" Hamas operative, and would provide further details later.
The attacks came a day after Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, 47, the head of Hamas's internal security service in northern Gaza, his wife and their two teenage daughters were killed in Israeli air strike on their apartment in Shati refugee camp in Gaza City.
On Tuesday, the overall commander of Hamas's internal security service was among 10 Palestinians reportedly killed in Israeli strikes.
Violence has continued in Gaza since Israel and Hamas agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire in October last year. Israeli strikes take place almost daily in areas under Hamas's control, which are home to 2.1 million people, most of them displaced.
At least 1,705 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza during the same period.
The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,772 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

bbc.com.title: Politics and peek-a-boo in Australian parliament as senator brings baby to work
bbc.com.text:
Politics and peek-a-boo in Australian parliament as senator brings baby to work
Australian Senator Fatima Payman brought her baby daughter, Aaliyah, to a parliamentary vote on holding social media platforms accountable for online harms.
While the lawmaker was speaking, baby Aaliyah captured the attention of Senator Lidia Thorpe and enjoyed a game of peek-a-boo.
Payman made history when she became the first hijab-wearing woman elected to Australia's Parliament in 2022, and the first sitting senator from Western Australia to give birth while in office, in 2026.

bbc.com.title: Musk's plan to send a million SpaceX data satellites into space approved
bbc.com.text:
- Published
US regulators have given SpaceX the go-ahead to launch a million satellites into Earth's orbit to help build data centres in space - the first approval of its kind.
The company, which is owned by Elon Musk, wants to use sunlight to power satellites that will process data for AI and send the results back to Earth.
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said on Wednesday that the project, known as Starmind, would "support America's booming super intelligence economy".
However, rival firm Amazon has criticised it as a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan", while astronomers in the US said the move would "significantly undermine" the public's ability to study and observe the night sky.
There is increasing opposition to data centres on earth, including in the US where experts say they were a factor in the Republicans big losses in the midterm elections.
SpaceX believes the "orbital data centres" are the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing power that is beyond "terrestrial capabilities".
FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement that the project "opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth".
"This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home," Carr said.
Responding to the announcement, Musk wrote on X: "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."
Under the FCC licence, deployment of the satellites must begin no later than November 2033. SpaceX will be required to have deployed 10% by November 2035, rising to 50% by November 2038.
The company has already said it wants to launch its first Starmind satellite next year.
It is unclear whether a million satellites will indeed be launched or whether SpaceX has sought approval for a higher number than it will use.
Like SpaceX's current Starlink network, which provides high-speed internet via more than 10,000 satellites, Starmind's satellites will operate in low-Earth orbit at altitudes ranging between 500-2,000km (310-1,242 miles).
Starmind's satellites will communicate with Starlink's and then relay the data to Earth.
Speaking to the Today programme, on BBC Radio 4, Prof Sir Martin Sweeting, founder and executive chairman of Surrey Satellite Technology Ltd, said while the idea of data centres in space seemed "technically feasible", whether it "makes sense at scale yet" still needed to be analysed.
Being able to get the data from the network of satellites, he added, would depend on being able to use laser links from the ground to them.
"That has not yet been perfected to the level at which it would be able to support the huge amounts of data that are likely to be transferred backwards and forwards," he said.
Meanwhile, the American Astronomical Society (AAS) said it was "disheartened and dismayed" by the decision.
It said the proposed constellation would "significantly undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities" as well as "the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky".
It noted that the constellation "involves larger (and therefore brighter) and more numerous objects", meaning the satellites would "be visible as extremely bright objects for longer periods in the night sky".
Jan Hasselman, a senior attorney at the non-profit group Earthjustice, said in a statement: "Drastically expanding satellites in space has a direct impact on people's everyday lives as well as the future of our planet."
The orbiting data centre concept is also being explored by other firms - including Google and Blue Origin - and is being pitched as a greener alternative to traditional centres, which require enormous amounts of power to run and water for cooling.
The ever-expanding use of AI computing has seen a massive increase in the amount of data that needs to be stored and processed around the world.
New facilities continue to be built but it is becoming difficult to find places to put them. Data centres are large and sprawling, use enormous amounts of power and water for cooling, and increasingly local people don't want them built nearby.
An expert previously told the BBC that launching hardware into orbit remains expensive and that the infrastructure to protect, cool and power them can be complex - while a growing quantity of space debris puts the physical hardware at risk.
Separately, another cautioned that the growing number of low-orbit craft increases the possibility of crashes between objects - which could damage machines or send materials falling back to earth.
Starlink has been accused of creating congestion in space, something Musk denies. He has also rejected claims his satellites have been taking up too much room and crowding out competitors.

bbc.com.title: Watch: Alaskan flying team airdrops Thanksgiving turkeys to remote communities
bbc.com.text:
Alaskan flying team airdrops Thanksgiving turkeys to remote communities
For the last few years, "turkey bombers" Esther Keim and Heidi Hastings have taken to the skies to airdrop Thanksgiving turkeys to residents in off-grid communities in south-central Alaska.
Hastings pilots the plane while her best friend Keim drops the turkeys out the plane window, delivering to families who may not otherwise get one of the birds, since they are cut off by snow and ice.

bbc.com.title: Guinea orders residents to clean up the capital months after deadly rubbish dump collapse
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Guinea has ordered residents to do a mass clean-up of the capital, Conakry, months after a rubbish landfill collapsed, killing dozens of people.
Prime Minister Amadou Oury Bah on Wednesday announced a deadline of 31 December to clear rubbish in the city and its suburbs, which has seen an increase in illegal dumping in recent months.
In August heavy rains caused a landslide at the capital's main waste dump, with the rubbish collapsing onto homes killing 31 people and injuring others.
The site in the city's Dar es Salaam area was subsequently closed permanently, which has led to piles of rubbish accumulating outside homes and on the streets.
At a public forum on sanitation, Sanitation Minister Aboubacar Camara said Conakry was generating about 3,000 tonnes of waste every day.
He said much of the garbage was ending up in the streets because of weaknesses in the collection system.
The prime minister called on local authorities to become more involved in organising waste collection, saying this could become a way to create jobs.
"The state will do its part, but the municipalities must also organise themselves to ensure waste collection and provide jobs for young people," the prime minister said.
"Conakry must be completely clean by the end of December," he added, relaying a directive from the country's president, Mamady Doumbouya.
He cited measures the government was taking to improve waste collection and recycling, including a national sanitation fund that would guarantee financing for the sector.
Camara said talks had been finalised with a waste collection operator, with a plan for equipment to move waste from transit and sorting centres to a new disposal site in Baretodé, outside the capital.
The August tragedy at the Dar es Salaam landfill was not the first - 10 people were killed at the same site in 2017.
The government had ordered people living close to the site to move, but many residents chose to stay.
According to the prime minister, the government now plans to transform the closed waste site into an urban park.

bbc.com.title: Thirteen dead as mine disaster highlights illegal hunt for gold
bbc.com.text:
- Published
It's been three days since Rani last saw her father as he left for work on Monday. Early on Tuesday, she received news that he was trapped underground.
Rais, 50, had been working as an illegal gold miner in Bogor, Indonesia's West Java province. On Monday night, he and at least 25 other miners were digging in an open-pit mine about 100m (328ft) deep, when torrential rain caused a nearby river to overflow and flood the two shafts.
Authorities on Thursday confirmed that 13 people had died and their bodies were recovered from the site. At least 13 more are thought to still be missing.
Search-and-rescue operations are ongoing, with personnel using ropes to access the depths of the dark, narrow and slippery mine shafts, which are continually being flooded from below.
Above ground, ambulances and medical personnel are ready and waiting to transport victims.
"We are coordinating with all search and rescue personnel involved in the operation to monitor water conditions and assess access to the mine shaft," Desiana Kartika Bahari, head of the Jakarta Search and Rescue Office, said in a statement on Wednesday.
"The depth of the shaft, narrow access and limited lighting are key considerations in determining the search strategy so that personnel can operate safely."
Small-scale gold mining is banned in Indonesia, but remains widespread in rural parts of the mineral-rich archipelago.
Multiple studies show that over the past ten years the illegal industry has rapidly flourished, often in correlation with rising gold prices. In early 2026, those prices reached an all-time high – spurring a gold rush that prompted mine operators across the country to expand their operations.
This included state-owned mining company Aneka Tambang (Antam), which owns the business permit for the area in which this week's flooded mine is located. Antam have said the mine was not theirs and was operating without their authorisation.
On Wednesday, while rescue operations there were underway, West Java Regional Police separately announced that they had uncovered 24 cases of illegal mining across the province between October and November alone.
But Bisman Bakhtiar, Executive Director of the Center for Energy and Mining Law Studies, told the BBC earlier this year that the actual number of illegal mines in Indonesia is higher than the government's figures.
"[The government figures are] what's been recorded. That means there must be more than that," he said, noting that law enforcement operations have had little impact on the sector.
"It's still very massive and very big because this has been going on for a very long time."
Others allege that the illegal industry is underpinned by corruption.
Laode M Syarif, former deputy chairman of the Corruption Eradication Committee, said that unofficial mining is difficult to eradicate because every illegal mine has "backing", usually from "police and military or high-ranking officials in local and provincial governments".
"As long as these backers are not dealt with firmly, illegal mining will continue," he said.
In many cases, though, the allure of these mines is simple: they offer an economic lifeline to people with few other viable prospects.
Despite the value of gold having dipped in recent months, countless illegal miners throughout Indonesia are still eagerly digging for paydirt.
But the lack of regulation and poor construction in the pits also means accidents are relatively common – whether from landslides, floods, or exposure to hazardous gases, all of which have claimed lives in recent years.
Earlier this year, in the same area as this week's flooded mine, 11 illegal gold miners reportedly died after a carbon monoxide leak inside a shaft.
Elsewhere, in West Sumatra, nine people were killed at an illegal gold mine in May after heavy rain triggered the collapse of a 30-metre cliff, burying 12 miners in total.
There are numerous reports of other such incidents across the Indonesian archipelago. But the illegal nature of the small-scale gold mining sector obfuscates the true number of casualties.
Even this week, when asked how many miners were in the pits in Bogor when they flooded, M Adam Hamdani, head of emergency and logistics at the Bogor Regency Regional Disaster Management Agency, said the total casualty figure "is still unclear".
"Some say 20 people, others say 29 people," Hamdani told Indonesian news outlet Detik. "The problem is that no one reported it and no one wants to report it."
The Indonesian Ombudsman on Thursday urged law enforcement officials to conduct a thorough investigation of the incident and to address the larger systemic issue behind it.
"This should be a momentum for all parties to resolve the [illegal gold mining] problem comprehensively, not just taking action after the incident or closing the holes discovered," said Abdul Ghoffar, a member of the Indonesian Ombudsman.
"We need to uncover the entire [illegal gold mining] chain," he continued. "We must not allow only the miners in the field to be seen and prosecuted, while those who control the activities, provide capital and facilities, store, and market the mined products remain untouched.
"Law enforcement must target the actors and networks that keep this illegal activity going."
As rescue operations continue and more bodies are recovered, the picture is becoming less murky. But even if there are survivors among those who remain missing, time may be running out.
More than three days since the shafts flooded, the relatives of the anonymous men in the mines are desperately waiting to hear whether their loved ones survived.
As she waits for news of her father, Rani says: "I hope he's found soon."

bbc.com.title: DR Congo demands answers over Ugandan general's threats
bbc.com.text:
- Published
The Democratic Republic of Congo has summoned Uganda's top diplomat in Kinshasa over social media posts by Uganda's military chief, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is also the president's son.
In a series of X posts, Gen Kainerugaba appeared to support a rebel takeover of Walikale, a mineral-rich territory in eastern DR Congo. He insisted that Uganda's military involvement was purely driven by security concerns.
The DR Congo's foreign ministry summoned Uganda's envoy to explain the remarks, describing them as "particularly serious" and damaging to diplomatic relations.
The Ugandan government has yet to respond.
The diplomatic row comes despite close military ties between the neighbours.
Their forces have been conducting joint operations against the Islamic State-linked Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) in eastern DR Congo since 2021.
Uganda has also recently been involved in efforts to mediate between the Congolese government and an armed group led by former warlord Thomas Lubanga in Ituri province.
In his posts, Gen Kainerugaba accused the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR), an armed group operating in eastern DR Congo, of targeting members of the Bahima ethnic community.
The Bahema are a traditionally cattle-herding community mainly based in DR Congo's north-eastern Ituri province.
They have historical and cultural ties to the Bahima people of neighbouring Uganda.
He also threatened a rebel takeover of Walikale, in North Kivu province, while defending Uganda's military presence in DR Congo.
Walikale is rich in mineral resources , including some of the country's largest tin deposits and several major gold mines.
Gen Kainerugaba's X account, which had nearly 1.4 million followers, has since become inaccessible.
It is unclear whether he deactivated it, as he has done in the past, or whether the platform had suspended it.
During the same week he declared: "My tweets in Uganda are directives that must be obeyed."
The posts followed reports that a DR Congo military aircraft had allegedly been shot down by rebels, with foreign mercenaries reportedly among those on board.
Gen Kainerugaba criticised the reported presence of foreign mercenaries in DR Congo.
"These remarks, which are particularly serious, have caused a major media incident and undermine the necessary restraint that must prevail in relations between sovereign states," the DR Congo foreign ministry said in a statement on Wednesday.
"The Congolese government expects the Republic of Uganda to clarify its official position and take the necessary measures to prevent such transgressions from recurring in the future".
The ministry added that DR Congo remained committed to regional peace and stability but would defend its dignity and institutions against "any form of provocation or interference".
It is not the first time Gen Kainerugaba's social media posts have strained relations between the two countries.
In February last year, he threatened to seize the eastern DR Congo city of Bunia, claiming that members of the Bahima ethnic community were being attacked.
In 2024, DR Congo also summoned Uganda's diplomatic representative after the general made threats against foreign mercenaries operating in eastern DR Congo.
The 52-year-old general, widely seen as a potential successor to his father Yoweri Museveni, has become known for his provocative social media posts.
In 2022, he sparked a diplomatic row with neighbouring Kenya after threatening to invade the country and capture its capital, Nairobi, prompting his father to apologise forn the remarks.

aljazeera.com.title: India’s Pant plays for New Zealand side under false name ‘Stan Stan’
aljazeera.com.text:
India’s star wicketkeeper-batsman Rishabh Pant used an unlikely forum to keep his eye sharp before the second New Zealand Test – a social Last Man Stands match in Christchurch.
The 29-year-old, who plays for Lucknow Super Giants in the Indian Premier League, is one of the six most prolific hitters in Test history, hitting 108 across his 53 matches to sit second all time.
Six of those came in Wellington last week, where his 128 from 153 balls helped India set a record in New Zealand, 720-9 in the drawn match.
After a chance encounter in central Christchurch, Pant played Wednesday for the Open House Swingers in a Last Man Stands match against The Chosen Ones at Hagley Park – not to be confused with neighbouring Hagley Oval, where Pant will wear Indian whites this week.
Listed on the scorecard as Stan Stan, Pant blasted 54 from 21 balls to maintain his glittering form in New Zealand.
“I saw Rishabh going around on an electric bike,” Open House Swingers player Mohammad Safi told the New Zealand Herald.
“So I went and stopped him, and we start talking and taking a few photos and stuff, and I asked him, do you want to play cricket for us?
“He was like, OK, I’ll come and play for you guys. Then he came and padded up, went batting, and smashed a few sixes.”
Indian bowling coach Morne Morkel said he “nearly fell off my chair last night when I saw that”.
New Zealand captain Tom Latham said Pant’s midweek performance was “brilliant”.
“He’s obviously a real character of the game is Rishabh, so it’s great for him to give his experience back to the LMS teams.”
Safi told the New Zealand Herald the opposition did not recognise Pant while he wore his striking blue tracksuit.
Safi also said Pant used his cousin’s bat during the match.
“He was asking me to basically give him a single and stuff. Obviously, I was smashing longer sixes than him, and then he was like, give me a turn, let me show you how to hit it,” Safi said.
The Open House Swingers won the match by 16 runs, a feat Pant could not achieve in Wellington, as the Test ended in a draw.
India’s second Test against New Zealand begins Friday at Hagley Oval.

aljazeera.com.title: Spain’s 2026 election explained in maps and charts
aljazeera.com.text:
Spain will hold a snap election on November 29 that could bring the far right into government for the first time since the end of Francisco Franco’s dictatorship in 1975.
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez called the early vote last month after parliament rejected his government’s housing relief measures, which came during mass protests over rents and house prices.
Polls suggest the centre-right People’s Party (PP) will win most seats but will need the far-right Vox party to reach the 176 seats required for a majority in the 350-seat Congress of Deputies. Voters will also elect 208 members of the Senate.
About 38.7 million people aged 18 and above are eligible to vote, according to Spain’s National Statistics Institute (INE).
When will polls open?
Polling stations across Spain will be open on November 29 at 9am local time (08:00 GMT) and close at 8pm (19:00 GMT).
How does voting work?
Spain is a parliamentary monarchy. King Felipe VI is head of state, while the government is led by a prime minister who answers to the Cortes Generales, a parliament made up of two houses: the Congress of Deputies and the Senate.
The 350 members of the lower house, the Congress of Deputies, are elected in 52 constituencies by proportional representation. Rather than choosing individual candidates, voters pick a party, and each party puts forward a ranked list of candidates in every constituency.
Every province is guaranteed at least two seats and the autonomous cities of Ceuta and Melilla in North Africa get one each. The rest are distributed by population, which is why Madrid and Barcelona elect far more deputies than smaller provinces.
Within each constituency, seats are divided according to each party’s share of the vote and go to the candidates at the top of each list. A party needs at least 3 percent of the vote in a constituency to qualify for any seats there.
A party needs 176 of the 350 seats for a majority. If no party reaches that number, parties must form coalitions or strike deals to govern. After consulting party leaders, the king proposes a candidate for prime minister, who must then win an investiture vote in Congress.
Most members of the upper house, the Senate, are elected directly, with voters choosing individual candidates by name. In most provinces, each voter can back up to three candidates and the four with the most votes are elected. The remaining senators are appointed by Spain’s regional parliaments.
When will the results be announced?
Provisional results from the Interior Ministry will start coming in straight away, with the overall picture clear before midnight on Sunday.
In 2023, about 99 percent of votes had been counted by 11:45pm.
Spain’s current coalition government
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez leads a minority coalition government made up of the Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE) and the left-wing Sumar alliance. The 22-member cabinet comprises Sanchez, three deputy prime ministers and 18 other ministers.
The three deputy prime ministers each oversee a major policy area: Carlos Cuerpo oversees the economy, Yolanda Diaz labour and the social economy and Sara Aagesen the ecological transition. Cuerpo is also acting transport minister after Oscar Puente resigned after last month’s train crash that killed 69 people.
Thirteen cabinet members belong to the PSOE and five to Sumar, while four are independents appointed by the PSOE.
Which are the main parties on the ballot?
- Socialist Party (PSOE), centre-left – Incumbent Pedro Sanchez is running again after more than eight years in office, which makes him Spain’s second-longest-serving prime minister since 1978, after Felipe Gonzalez. His final two years in power were overshadowed by corruption investigations involving his wife, his brother and former close allies.
- People’s Party (PP), centre-right – Alberto Nunez Feijoo, who has led the PP since 2022, is the party’s candidate. The PP won the most seats in the 2023 election but could not gather enough support to form a government.
- Vox, far right – Led by Santiago Abascal, who co-founded the party in 2014 after leaving the PP, Vox has become Spain’s third-largest party. It campaigns for tougher immigration rules, lower taxes and a hard line against Catalan and Basque separatism.
- Broad Front (Frente Amplio), left – Headed by Ada Colau, the former mayor of Barcelona, it is a new alliance that replaces Sumar, the left-wing grouping that has governed alongside Sanchez since 2023. Podemos, a former partner of Sumar, is running separately.
- Regional parties – Could again decide who governs. EH Bildu (Basque Country), the BNG (Galicia), the Basque Nationalist Party (PNV) and the left-wing Catalan pro-independence ERC have largely backed Sanchez. The centre-right Catalan pro-independence party Junts supported his 2023 investiture but has since repeatedly voted against his government.
What are the main issues?
According to a YouGov poll published on October 30 , the main issues according to the Spanish public are:
- Housing – Spain is short of 750,000 homes, according to the Bank of Spain, which warns that the gap could surpass one million by 2028. The average rent has reached 1,176 euros ($1,318) a month, almost exactly a young person’s average monthly salary of 1,191 euros ($1,334), according to the Spanish Youth Council. Anger over housing costs has fuelled nationwide protests.
- Immigration – Sanchez has been one of Europe’s leading advocates of migration and this year offered undocumented migrants a path to legal status, drawing almost 1.2 million applications. Vox, on the other hand, has pledged to deport all undocumented migrants, while the PP has promised tighter border controls in its manifesto.
- Corruption – Sanchez is facing up to nine judicial investigations involving his party, government and family. His former transport minister Jose Luis Abalos was sentenced to 24 years in prison for corruption in June. Opposition parties have put corruption at the centre of their campaigns and accuse Sanchez’s government of being mired in scandal.
- Healthcare – Long waiting lists are a growing concern across Spain. Doctors have postponed a national strike over working-hours reforms until after the election, but regional walkouts continue.
- State of the economy – Spain’s economy has grown faster than the eurozone average, but inflation near 5 percent and soaring housing costs mean many Spaniards are not feeling the benefits.

aljazeera.com.title: Israel uses south Lebanon Christian villages to try to divide and conquer
aljazeera.com.text:
Beirut, Lebanon – On Lebanon’s Independence Day on Sunday, Israel’s Arabic-language military spokesperson Ella Waweya posted a video on X in a classroom in Dibil, a Christian village in south Lebanon.
In the video, she wished Lebanese a happy national day, praised the singer Fairuz, and blamed the Lebanese armed group Hezbollah, which is fighting an ongoing war against Israel, for the hardships faced by the people in southern Lebanon.
The video drew widespread condemnation from Lebanese officials, including from Dibil’s municipality, who told local media that the visit took place around a month before the video was posted.
The council said the visit took place “without prior coordination with the school administration”. The Israeli military said an investigation was reviewing the incident and it is not clear whether Waweya had official approval to post the video.
Unlike neighbouring Shia Muslim villages, Christian villages in southern Lebanon have generally been allowed to stay on their lands during Israel’s war on Lebanon. But they still live under Israeli occupation.
“We’re in a giant prison,” Ayoub Khreish, the president of Ain Ebl municipality, told Al Jazeera from his village on Lebanon’s southern border. “We can only move around in these [neighbouring] villages. Anytime we want to go to Beirut, we need to get permission.”
This system goes through a so-called “mechanism”, whereby a request is submitted to the Lebanese Army, which passes it to the UN and then onto the Israelis for approval.
Now living under the Israeli military’s authority, these Christian villages are being used as part of an Israeli strategy to foment divides among the Lebanese population, experts told Al Jazeera.
Villages under the control of Israel
Israel launched a massive assault on Lebanon in October 2023, shortly after genocide in Gaza began, with approximately 9,000 people killed since then, according to Lebanon’s Ministry of Public Health.
Southern Lebanon, where Hezbollah has a presence, has been the area worst affected by the violence, with thousands of Israeli air raids and repeated Israeli raids in villages.
Israel’s war on Lebanon has left Christians in southern villages in a precarious position. Much of the south has been made uninhabitable by Israeli attacks and demolitions. While Shia Muslims have taken the overwhelming brunt of the violence, Christians have been killed in attacks and been displaced, too.
In early November, the mayors of five Christian villages appealed to the Council of Catholic Patriarchs and Bishops of Lebanon, asking for help so residents can remain on their land and displaced people can return.
“Help us make staying on our land a choice of life based on security, dignity, work and hope, rather than an anxious wait in uncertainty,” they wrote at the time.
Khreish, municipal president of Ain Ebl, said a little more than half of the town’s population fled since the start of the war. Daily convoys bring in food and other necessities, but the local economy has ground to a halt.
He initially hoped for a political solution to the crisis, but a June framework agreement between Israel and Lebanon that looked to have Israeli troops withdraw from the south and Hezbollah disarm has not progressed as originally hoped. Talks between the two sides have been stalled since August.
“We thought peace and a political solution would be closer than this,” he said. “But the opposite seems to be true; it’s far off.”
As the occupation drags on, Lebanese in these villages feel they are forced to deal with the political reality in front of them. Khreish said Israeli soldiers enter the village regularly and interact with locals.
“We’re no longer afraid of them,” Khreish said. “We’re under their authority, the authority of the Israeli military.”
Political weaponisation
Experts say this particular treatment of Christians in Lebanon is part of a wider strategy to fragment and divide the local population.
“It’s part of a longstanding strategy on behalf of Israel towards the minorities of the region to divide and conquer,” Munira Khayyat, author of Landscape of War: Ecologies of Resistance and Survival in South Lebanon, told Al Jazeera. “You see this happening, of course, in Palestine, and in Lebanon, they’ve always done this. They always had this strategy of separating the Christians from their social, ethnic, national and historical environment to reinvent them as foot soldiers for the Zionist cause.”
In July, Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who may soon be out of office, claimed that Lebanon’s Christians were asking Israel for protection from its Muslim neighbours.
“Christian villages in Lebanon, some of them have actually asked to be annexed to Israel, because we protect them against Hezbollah, Hezbollah fanatics who want to kill them, and we do the same things with Christians everywhere,” Netanyahu told Fox News.
Netanyahu’s claims were rejected by Lebanese officials, including Hanna al-Amil, president of the Rmeish Municipality, the largest Christian-majority border village.
A statement was signed by 15 villages in southern Lebanon that called the claim “completely fabricated” and “unrelated to reality”.
Michael Young, a Lebanese political analyst and writer at the Beirut-based Carnegie Center, said Israel aimed to show the outside world, and the US in particular, that it protects Christians and other minorities after its actions in Gaza turned public opinion heavily against it. In Gaza, Israel had bombed Christian churches, where many Palestinians sought refuge from the Israeli genocide.
“People like [US political commentator] Tucker Carlson are playing this up, so from a public relations perspective, they want to show they are friendly to all minorities; Druze, Christians and so on,” Young said.
Fractured states
Experts said that the Israeli efforts to cater to minorities in the region are more than an external public relations campaign.
“There is another much more sinister reason,” Young said. “The Israelis have a policy in the region of fragmentation.”
Young pointed to a paper (PDF) published in October by Tamir Hayman, a former chief of the Israeli military’s Intelligence Directorate and the current executive director of the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), an Israeli think tank.
In the paper, Hayman outlines what he discerns as Israel’s new, unwritten national security concepts. One key concept is the Israeli national security view that “Arab states are not genuine nation-states, but collections of tribes and ethnic groups lacking a shared history and a foundational national vision.”
“Consequently, undermining their stability is viewed as a natural process, one that Israel can manage more effectively than it can contend with strong nation-states, and one that it should even encourage,” Hayman continues.
In south Lebanon, locals of all denominations have expressed frustration or anger towards Hezbollah over the last few years.
“There is anger against Hezbollah, no doubt about it. But people criticising Hezbollah are not automatically with Israel,” said Young.
Many Lebanese Christians have been shocked by the destruction wrought on Shia villages around them and find it “inconceivable they can live without their Shia neighbours”.
Back in Ain Ebl, Khreish said the war and occupation had left them feeling stuck and that any effort to travel outside their area brings “constant anxiety”.
“We just hope for peace and that there won’t be war on us. What has this war brought us?” he said.
Like many others from south Lebanon, these Christian-predominant towns and villages feel they are stuck in limbo, waiting to see what comes next.
“We don’t think of the future. We live day by day. We don’t have eyes on the future because we don’t know what will happen,” Khreish said.

aljazeera.com.title: New Zealand’s Opportunity Party poised to become election kingmaker
aljazeera.com.text:
New Zealand’s Opportunity Party poised to become election kingmaker
New Zealand’s parliament is deadlocked between left and right parties, says the election commission after counting all the votes from the November 7 ballot. The tie puts the next government’s future in the hands of the newly-elected Opportunity Party.

aljazeera.com.title: Estonia closing land borders with Russia to keep out spies
aljazeera.com.text:
Estonia closing land borders with Russia to keep out spies
Estonia is set to close its land border crossings to Russia by December 1. Families living on either side of the border are preparing for a long separation. Estonia’s government says that the closures are necessary to prevent Russian intelligence agents from carrying out attacks.

aljazeera.com.title: Thanksgiving storms leave nearly a million without power across the US
aljazeera.com.text:
Strong winds and heavy storms have knocked out power for nearly a million US homes and businesses and resulted in the rare postponement of Macy’s annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York City.
As Americans marked the annual holiday on Thursday, heavy storms disrupted travel across the country, with more than 2,000 flights to or from US destinations delayed and more than 400 cancelled, according to the flight tracking service FlightAware.
More than 900,000 homes and businesses were without electricity on Thursday evening, with the majority in East Coast states, according to the outage tracking website poweroutage.us. New Jersey and parts of New York were placed under a state of emergency.
The US National Weather Service issued wind advisories for northern Georgia, the majority of the mid-Atlantic and southern New England.
Two people were rescued from their cars in New York City due to flooding, according to Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
“There is no destination worth your safety,” Mamdani said. Similar rescues were reported in other coastal communities.
In Maryland, nearly two million water customers in Montgomery and Prince George’s counties were asked to conserve water because of intermittent power disruptions related to heavy rain. The storms also prompted several brief tornado warnings, including for a rare twister southeast of Seattle, Washington.
The Midwestern region witnessed heavy snowfall on Thursday, with some areas of Missouri recording up to 35cm of snow.
Meanwhile, waves driven by high tides caused flooding along the Pacific coast. The conditions were expected to continue into Friday, according to the National Weather Service.
Record tides along the California coast forced evacuations in areas from Humboldt County in the far north to southern Ventura County near Los Angeles.

aljazeera.com.title: At least 13 Niger soldiers killed in Sanam armed attack
aljazeera.com.text:
At least 13 members of Niger’s National Guard have been killed and 20 wounded in an attack on their compound in Sanam, in the west of the country, the Defence Ministry has said.
In a statement read on state television, the ministry said the attack on Thursday was carried out by “numerous heavily armed assailants”, referring to the incident as a “terrorist attack”.
The ministry gave a provisional toll and said soldiers killed several attackers and destroyed their logistical infrastructure. Operations to track down the attackers are ongoing, it added.
The assault took place at about 5am local time (04:00 GMT), local and security sources told the Nigerien outlet ActuNiger.
Sanam is in the Tillaberi region, near the Mali border, where armed groups regularly attack security forces.
It was not clear who was behind the attack.
The attack comes two days after the ministry said 11 soldiers were killed in an attack attributed to Boko Haram in the Diffa region, in the southeast.
Violence across the border
In neighbouring Nigeria, suspected members of an armed group killed at least 30 people in villages in the central state of Niger on Tuesday.
They described it as retaliation for the killing of many Fulani herders days earlier.
In Nigeria’s northeast, President Bola Tinubu promised on Wednesday to restore peace to a region hit by a rebellion led by Boko Haram and the ISIL (ISIS) affiliate in West Africa Province, as he campaigns for re-election.

aljazeera.com.title: Trump downplays Russia, China support for Iran during talks with US troops
aljazeera.com.text:
United States President Donald Trump has claimed Iran possesses missiles capable of reaching Europe and downplayed Russia and China’s support for Tehran while speaking to US military personnel by phone for the Thanksgiving holiday.
Taking questions from reporters at his Mar-a-Lago residence in Florida on Thursday, Trump said without “peace in the Middle East”, Iran could launch nuclear attacks against Israel and other countries in the region.
“We don’t need Middle East oil. But what we do need is we need peace in the Middle East,” Trump said, as OPEC ministers are scheduled to meet on Sunday to weigh 2027 oil production targets.
The US president and First Lady Melania Trump called US service members deployed across the region to praise their role in the war on Iran, including personnel at the al-Dhafra airbase in the United Arab Emirates and the Prince Sultan airbase in Saudi Arabia.
“Each of you is playing an essential role to protect not only our country today but future generations of Americans by ensuring that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon,” he said.
When asked if the US would renew strikes on Iran, the president said: “If we do something, we will definitely hit Pickaxe Mountain.” Trump also told reporters he spoke with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in recent days.
The US is still offering Iran an opening to negotiate, according to Trump, who said: “We’re trying to be nice. We’re giving them every chance to make a deal and save a lot of lives, but I’m not sure if they are gonna take advantage of that.”
He downplayed the importance of intelligence-sharing by Russia and China with Iran, amid reports that the two countries helped Tehran target US bases.
“My meeting with President Xi was an incredible meeting. I think that they’re very little involved with Iran. They could get involved, but involvement to me would mean shooting, not giving them little information,” Trump said during the short news conference.
“We do the same thing, by the way. And you know, when they say that they may be spying on us, well, we spy on them too,” he added.
Trump’s statements come as Iran steps up attacks on US military targets across the region. On Saturday, Bahrain reported an Iranian attack on a civilian industrial facility while Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed it targeted US air defence radars in the country.
Kuwait said on Thursday that an Iranian drone attack on a “vital site” killed two Italian workers and injured four others. Tehran has denied involvement in the attack.
Trump told deployed service members, “You’re going to continue that deployment, and we have victory at hand,” referring to the war on Iran.
“It’s [victory] going to be whenever I want it to be, to be honest,” he added.

aljazeera.com.title: Asian stock markets rise after earlier tech rout
aljazeera.com.text:
Asian stocks have opened higher as technology firms enjoy a period of calm following ructions at the start of the week.
Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 on Friday added 0.7 percent to 57,919.30 in morning trading. Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 rose 0.4 percent to 8,800.50. South Korea’s Kospi surged 2.2 percent to 4,812.65.
Hong Kong’s Hang Seng edged up 0.4 percent to 22,310.11.
Stocks in Indonesia, Singapore and the Philippines also rose, while New Zealand’s bourse edged down as Prime Minister Christopher Luxon’s right-wing coalition lost its parliamentary majority, plunging the country into political uncertainty with a centrist party set to play a decisive role in forming the next government.
Buying of stocks tied to artificial intelligence (AI) has been pushing benchmarks higher, despite some profit-taking that has kept those gains in check.
In Japan, Tokyo Electron and Advantest Corp stocks dropped in morning trading but quickly recovered their losses, underlining the continuing appeal of stocks in the semiconductor and AI sectors.
With Wall Street closed for the Thanksgiving holiday on Thursday, traders had no new business-driving catalysts heading into the weekend, though they remain on edge over concerns about the AI boom.
They were also keeping an eye on possible retaliation against US President Donald Trump’s proposed tariffs of up to 20 percent on some of the United States’ biggest trading partners, including China, the European Union, India, Japan and South Korea.
Also in view is the Federal Reserve’s next interest rate decision next month, with speculation swirling that it could opt for a hefty 50-basis-point increase instead of the usual 25 points.
Oil prices extended Thursday’s gains of more than 1 percent amid fresh concerns over an escalation of hostilities in the Middle East after Iran-aligned Houthis struck a Saudi refinery, temporarily halting some operations. That came after an attack on another hub in the Gulf earlier in the week.
In company news, Japan Tobacco rallied more than 4 percent following a report that it was considering joining up with US giant Altria for a takeover of Britain’s Imperial Brands. Imperial jumped 13 percent in London on Thursday.
Japan Tobacco is dealing with an $8.9bn hit after the Russian government seized all seven of its local subsidiaries, as relations with Tokyo worsen following the arrest of a Japanese journalist on spying allegations.

aljazeera.com.title: Spain and Morocco under-17 stars target World Cup 2030
aljazeera.com.text:
Spain and Morocco under-17 stars target World Cup 2030
Spain and Morocco are two of the co-hosts of the next Men’s World Cup in 2030. Both nations faced off at the under-17 World Cup in Qatar, and Al Jazeera’s Sohail Malik asked players whether they believe playing top level international football is in their future.

aljazeera.com.title: Zelenskyy warns of major Russian attack as Trump urges Putin to ‘pull back’
aljazeera.com.text:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Ukraine has information that Russia is preparing a new mass strike on the country in the coming days.
“Unfortunately, we have information about a new mass strike being prepared by the Russians,” he said in his nightly video address on Thursday. “In the coming days, please pay attention to the alarms of missile threats.”
It was the second such warning from Zelenskyy this week. He also had a message for Moscow: “We will rebuild what is ours and retaliate against every Russian strike.”
Trump urges Putin to pull back
US President Donald Trump said he had pressed Russian President Vladimir Putin to ease Russia’s military actions in Europe.
In a post on Truth Social, Trump said he spent “a lot of time” in talks with Putin in China on the issue of Putin pulling back “all Military aggression against territories throughout Europe”.
“Thousands of people are being killed each and every month, A COMPLETE BLOODBATH,” Trump wrote. He said he hoped that would allow a deal between Russia and Ukraine to be “made quickly”, which he called “a strong possibility”.
Trump said he updated NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte on the talks during a meeting at his Mar-a-Lago club in Florida on Wednesday night.
Latest attacks
Russia struck Kyiv with ballistic missiles overnight, wounding seven people and hitting a shopping centre and two other buildings, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
Moscow said it hit drone-related sites in the city. Russian forces have attacked Kyiv and other cities almost continuously since September.
Ukraine said its drones hit an oil refinery in Russia’s southern Krasnodar region, oil reservoirs at a Transneft facility in Bashkortostan and the Marinovka military airfield in the Volgograd region.
Ukraine has also widened its attacks at sea. On Monday, Zelenskyy said Ukraine used seven naval drones to hit the Russian corvette Merkury and the cargo ship Angara off Libya. Libyan officials told the Associated Press news agency that the Merkury was heavily damaged but not sunk.
At about the same time, a suspected Ukrainian drone struck the Russia-bound cargo ship Sparta II in the Baltic Sea, near Finland. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov called the attacks a “very dangerous trend“.
At least four Russian vessels have been targeted this month.
Europe’s funding for Ukraine
European Union leaders are struggling at a summit in Brussels to agree on a new 45 billion euro ($49bn) loan to help Ukraine meet its economic and military needs next year. It would come on top of a 90 billion euro ($99bn) loan, agreed nearly a year ago, that covers most of Ukraine’s government needs for 2026 and 2027.
Early on Friday in Brussels, European Council President Antonio Costa said that 24 member states supported the new loan, as talks on the bloc’s next seven-year budget stretched on.
The loan is tangled up with the EU’s budget for 2028 to 2034, which includes about $110bn for Ukraine over seven years. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has threatened to hold up the budget unless all member states make a “collective commitment” to Ukraine.
North Korea ‘pauses’ arms deliveries
Ukraine’s military intelligence agency (GUR) said on Thursday that North Korea has temporarily halted some military cooperation with Russia after diplomatic tensions between the allies.
It said this includes deliveries of KN-23 ballistic missiles and artillery shells, and Russian military flights over North Korean territory.
GUR said North Korea’s Foreign Minister Choe Son-hui announced the pause last month in response to a Russian deputy foreign minister’s assertion that Moscow would help ease tensions between Seoul and Pyongyang.
GUR also said Pyongyang is holding off on a Russian request to raise North Korea’s military presence in Russia from about 8,500 to 50,000 troops.
It added that North Korean units remain in Russia’s Kursk region and that a North Korean missile unit has been in the Voronezh region since mid-summer, from where Russia strikes Ukraine.
South Korean and Western intelligence agencies have said Pyongyang sent more than 10,000 soldiers to Russia’s Kursk region in 2024, along with artillery shells, missiles and long-range rocket systems.
Strikes continue
On November 20, Russia fired more than 400 drones and 110 missiles at Ukraine, killing eight people, Zelenskyy said.
It was one of the largest attacks of the war and followed Putin’s vow to retaliate for Ukrainian strikes on the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to Crimea.

aljazeera.com.title: Trump says the US has ‘close to 50%’ of world’s oil
aljazeera.com.text:
Trump says the US has ‘close to 50%’ of world’s oil
On a call to soldiers deployed to the Gulf, US President Donald Trump claimed that the US does not ‘need Middle East oil’ and that they were maintaining their presence there to protect ‘Israel and other countries’.

aljazeera.com.title: Clashes halt match as Turkiye football fans raise Palestinian flags
aljazeera.com.text:
Clashes halt match as Turkiye football fans raise Palestinian flags
Clashes broke out between Georgian police and Turkish club Besiktas supporters during a UEFA match. Besiktas was playing against Israel’s Hapoel Be’er Sheva. Play was halted for 30 minutes when scuffles began after fans raised Palestinian flags and chanted anti-Israel slogans.

aljazeera.com.title: Global news agency AFP reports cyberattack, shuts down content platform
aljazeera.com.text:
Agence France-Presse (AFP) has been hit by a cyberattack, requiring the AFP Forum content platform to be taken offline.
The France-based international news agency’s management said on Thursday that it is currently investigating the circumstances of the cyberattack, including who was behind it.
“AFP was hit by a cyber attack overnight, starting at 1:30 am (Paris time) [00:30 GMT]. The target was AFP Forum, one of the platforms our clients use to browse and download our content,” an internal email from AFP management said.
“As soon as the intrusion was detected, our teams moved immediately to contain the intrusion and took AFP Forum offline as a precautionary measure. AFP Forum remains unavailable until further notice.”
AFP is reportedly offering backup solutions to the agency’s subscribers while the portal is offline.
France’s cybersecurity chief, Vincent Strubel, warned on Thursday that the country faces an unprecedented level of cybersecurity threats and called for collective efforts to strengthen defences against attacks.
“We are facing a level of threat that is unprecedented, with an intensity we have never experienced before,” Strubel said in an interview with France Inter radio.
The incident is the latest in a slew of cybersecurity disruptions across European countries. FIFA, which is based in Zurich, Switzerland, confirmed to Al Jazeera on Thursday that it had been the victim of a cyberattack that gave unauthorised access to personal and business information.
In October, several French supermarkets were hit by an “unprecedented” cyberattack that raised the temperature of fridges and freezers to as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122F).
Temperature spikes were also recorded in stores in 10 other European countries in early November, including the United Kingdom, Germany, Belgium and Sweden.
France accused Tehran of being behind the October attack and summoned Iran’s ambassador to Paris to “lodge a very strong protest”.
Iran called Paris’s accusations “baseless” and condemned the “hackneyed policy of levelling accusations against the Islamic republic”.

aljazeera.com.title: Inside Ukraine’s power crisis amid its war with Russia
aljazeera.com.text:
Inside Ukraine’s power crisis amid its war with Russia
Electricity and water shortages have become part of daily life in Ukraine’s capital, with businesses using generators when the power goes out. Al Jazeera’s Audrey Macalpine shows how residents are adapting.

aljazeera.com.title: America’s Thanksgiving holiday seen through different eyes
aljazeera.com.text:
America’s Thanksgiving holiday seen through different eyes
As millions of Americans celebrate Thanksgiving, Indigenous people gathered in Plymouth, Massachusetts, for the ‘National Day of Mourning’ – an annual protest by Native communities against centuries of colonisation, land dispossession and violence.

aljazeera.com.title: Argentina bars Central Bank from printing money to fund government spending
aljazeera.com.text:
Argentina’s legislature has pushed forward a series of bills that would implement changes sought by President Javier Milei, including barring the Central Bank from printing extra money for government expenses.
On Thursday, the Argentinian Chamber of Deputies gave final approval to a bill imposing restrictions on the Central Bank, defining its “primary and fundamental mission” as maintaining the value of the country’s currency.
Under past administrations, the Central Bank has printed additional funds to help cover government expenses, contributing to the country’s once sky-high inflation, which reached more than 200 percent in 2023.
Milei, a libertarian economist, swept into office that year on a promise to tame runaway inflation and slash government spending.
Under his leadership, inflation has declined, though poverty has surged. Economists also believe Argentina may be drifting into a recession, with economic activity diminished in recent months.
Still, Milei’s office celebrated the Senate’s passage of the Central Bank bill with a presidential statement.
“This marks the end of nearly two decades of political manipulation at the Central Bank,” the statement said.
The bank, founded in 1935, had experienced “91 years of plunder, expropriation, impunity, and institutional decay” up to this point, it added.
The vote in the Chamber of Deputies was 141 to zero, with 99 abstentions.
The Senate previously passed the bill, though it removed language Milei had pressed for, which would have required a two-thirds vote in both chambers of Congress to remove Central Bank governors.
Bill seeks to suspend primary elections
Also on Thursday, Argentina’s Senate advanced a bill to reform the country’s elections by suspending its primaries.
Unlike the Central Bank reform, that bill was not final. It still needs to pass the Chamber of Deputies.
The bill, however, comes less than a year before Argentina is slated to hold its next presidential election. Milei is expected to seek re-election in the October 24 vote.
Critics see the suspension of primaries as a means for Milei to avoid early pushback in his campaign.
A dismal primary result, they say, could weaken his momentum ahead of the general election and cause unfavourable economic fluctuations. Milei has long faced public discontent over his programme of economic austerity.
Thursday’s bill would also reduce public financing for political parties and eliminate a mandatory presidential debate ahead of general elections.
Senators approved the legislation by a vote of 43 to 29. While members of Milei’s La Libertad Avanza party touted the bill as a means of simplifying Argentina’s elections, opponents warned it could erode democratic norms.
“Milei now wants to change the rules of democracy to improve his chances of reelection by cheating,” Buenos Aires province Governor Axel Kicillof, a potential challenger to Milei, said in a social media post.

aljazeera.com.title: Iran war live: Iran’s Araghchi calls deadly Kuwait attack ‘suspicious’
aljazeera.com.text:
Iran war live: Iran’s Araghchi calls deadly Kuwait attack ‘suspicious’
US President Donald Trump says Washington has “victory at hand” in its war on Iran and is giving Tehran a chance to negotiate a deal to prevent further loss of life.
- Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says the deadly incident in Kuwait is “suspicious” and looks like a “pre-cooked recipe for war”, as Kuwaiti authorities report that two Italians died from falling debris during efforts to intercept incoming Iranian drones at a “vital site”.
- US President Donald Trump says Washington has “victory at hand” in its war on Iran and is giving Tehran a chance to negotiate a deal to prevent further loss of life.

aljazeera.com.title: Georgian police clash with Turkiye’s Besiktas fans over Palestinian flag
aljazeera.com.text:
Georgian police have clashed with fans of Turkiye’s Besiktas after they unfurled a Palestinian flag during a Europa League game against Israel’s Hapoel Beer-Sheva.
The clashes resulted in a suspension of about 30 minutes during the 26th minute of the game held in Batumi, Georgia, but it resumed after the interruption on Thursday. Besiktas eventually won 2-1.
Turkish media outlets reported that Georgian police entered the stands and used pepper spray against fans of the Istanbul giant, prompting Danish referee Morten Krogh to stop the game with the score 0-0.
The game was relocated by UEFA to Batumi after Turkish authorities said Istanbul could not host it for safety and security reasons. Unlike two previous Hapoel away games, spectators were allowed in the stadium.
Besiktas accused Georgian police of using “disproportionate” force against supporters before and during the game.
“We strongly condemn the security forces for their use of disproportionate force against our fans,” the Turkish club said in a statement. “We also extend our best wishes for a speedy recovery to all our fans affected by these incidents.”
The Turkish Football Federation also strongly condemned the treatment of Besiktas supporters, saying they were subjected to unacceptable behaviour and discrimination in a statement on X. The federation said it would press for an investigation into the incident.
