Jones has pleaded not guilty to 19 indecent assault and two sexual touching charges brought by five men who allege the offences took place between 2003 and 2020.
On Friday afternoon, after a break for the crown to read the defence submissions, Bashir presented two medical reports and a restaurant receipt, along with a corresponding bank statement.
After half an hour of objections to the documents by the crown, Bashir said: “Your honour, that closes the defence.”
No witnesses were called on Friday although some defence witnesses were called by the crown during the four-month trial.
The prosecutor Georgina Wright objected to the restaurant documents on the basis they carried no weight “whatsoever” – but judge Glenn Walsh admitted them.
Bashir argued the documents were relevant to the “credibility and reliability” of complainant C, who alleged he was assaulted by Jones at an end of year lunch at a north shore restaurant.
The alleged victim, a former driver for Jones, earlier told the court that Jones had instructed him to sit next to him and then spent the entire lunch with his left hand under the table either on his leg or on his penis over his pants.
The defence has argued the end of year lunch took place at a different north shore restaurant and presented a receipt for that establishment for $1,247.
Jason Morrison, a former 2GB colleague of Jones, earlier told the court he recalled a different name of the restaurant to complainant C and other witnesses.
“This has been a big trial,” Walsh said. “There are something like 290 or so exhibits and about 5,000-odd pages worth of transcripts.”
The judge gave the parties four days to prepare closing submissions, which are scheduled to begin on Thursday.
The judge-only trial has sat for 70 days at Sydney’s Downing Centre local court and the defendant has been present for all the evidence. Jones has sat in the front row next to his solicitor Bryan Wrench.
The youngest complainant, known as complainant A, alleged that Jones touched him on the bottom when he stayed overnight at Jones’s Fitzroy Falls farm when he was 17.
The trial has heard from a prominent athlete, known as complainant M, who told the court Jones would welcome him with a hug and a kiss on the cheek and use flattering terms like “champion” and “beautiful man”.
M told the court the defendant kissed him and pressed his genitalia against his thigh causing him to shout out “OK mate” and flee Jones’s harbourside apartment. He alleged that on another occasion Jones kissed him on the side of his mouth at an awards night.
Jones has denied all wrongdoing and said the allegations were either baseless or distorted the truth.
Bashir has said the alleged victims were egged on to complain by media rivals, and that their reliability and credibility were questionable.
Media rivals, Bashir alleged in her opening statements, included shock jock Ray Hadley and Sydney Morning Herald columnist Peter FitzSimons.

theguardian.com.title: Race hate exploded in this Spanish town last year. Now its residents are bracing for more
theguardian.com.text:
Sitting on a park bench, taking in the sunny day, Naima reflected on all that had seemingly changed since she moved to Spain three decades earlier.
Back then, the Moroccan national had felt warmly welcomed by Spaniards. “I had never, at any point in my life, felt like there was racism,” she said. “But now things are changing. And the blame lies with rightwing politics.”
Over the years, she has steadily watched as a growing crop of politicians sought to win votes by demonising migrants, minorities and Muslims. The impact reverberated deeply in places such as Torre-Pacheco, whose fertile fields and constant demand for farmhands has long attracted workers from around the world.
“They peddle racism, and lots of people end up suffering,” said Naima, 53. “Here everyone knows me, but others speak of being treated differently, looked at in a certain way, or having gestures made at them.”
On Sunday, Spain is set to gain a glimpse of how deeply engrained these divisions have become as voters cast their ballots in a snap general election.
Most polls suggest the government of the Socialist leader, Pedro Sánchez, will be replaced by a rightwing coalition led by the conservative People’s party (PP) and supported by the far-right, anti-immigration Vox party. If so, it will be the first time that a far-right party has governed Spain since the return to democracy after the death of General Franco.
The possibility has left many in Torre-Pacheco, where migrants make up at least 30% of the 42,000 residents, worried about what comes next, according to cafe owner Allal Abourayane. “A lot of people are afraid of Vox,” he said. “They’re worried about what the party will mean for their children’s futures.”
In the lead-up to Sunday’s vote, the far-right party has pointedly targeted people from north African countries, announcing plans that include revising the nationalisation of more than 300,000 people of Moroccan origin and limiting the number of pupils from “other cultures or with insufficient command of Spanish” in classrooms.
Other Vox initiatives have more broadly targeted all migrants, such as a promise to impose a tax on remittances similar to the one launched last year in the US by Donald Trump’s administration. Last year, a party official briefly floated the idea of deporting up to 8 million people of foreign origin, including the children of immigrants, before the party backtracked. In September, another official reportedly told the country’s major corporations of plans to lower the cost of housing by expelling 1.5 million migrants.
The PP has responded by hardening its discourse, with promises to bar the burqa and niqab in public spaces and expand the process of residency renewal to include Spanish language tests and constitutional knowledge questions. This sparked wider questions as to what this could mean for some British or American pensioners and digital nomads living in Spain.
On the tree-lined streets of Torre-Pacheco, many were swift to point to the risks of this discourse. They speak from first-hand experience: the Murcian town made headlines last year when extremists from across Spain arrived, intent on exacting revenge after reports of an assault on an elderly man.
The pensioner had told local media he believed his attacker was of north African origin. This sent racist messaging on social media rocketing by 1,500%, according to tracking by the central government.
In Torre-Pacheco, locals watched in shock as the hatred leapt off social media platforms and on to their streets. As baton-wielding groups roamed the town for two nights, determined to “hunt” down people with foreign origins, the mayor called on migrants to stay indoors. Some refused, leading to clashes between the extremists and small groups of residents, at times carrying Moroccan flags.
At least 10 people were arrested, including three young men of north African background who were linked to the attack on the elderly man. Six Spaniards and a Moroccan national were also detained on accusations including assault, public disorder and hate crimes.
More than 16 months later, many are still coming to grips with those events. “The hatred came from the outside,” said Antonio León, a politician with the Independent party and mayor of the city from 2015 to 2023. “We’ve always lived together peacefully. People here didn’t take part in what happened, they understand the social and cultural diversity we have in this town.”
Even so, Torre-Pacheco had now become synonymous with extreme hate, he said. “The name Torre-Pacheco has been tainted. Everywhere I go in Spain, I say I’m from here, and they associate me with what happened.”
The Socialist-led central government was unequivocal in linking the events to the discourse of the far right. Its representative in Murcia, Mariola Guevara, said at the time: “We are normalising and giving space in institutions to radicalised, xenophobic, racist political organisations that constantly incite hatred and associate any kind of crime with immigration.”
As the blame game played out, those who had been targeted were left with lingering scars, said Abourayane. “Something has shifted here,” he said. “There are people who are still fearful or who don’t feel as comfortable here as they used to.”
It was a hint of how things could play out if Vox ends up securing a role in Spain’s central government, said Ousama Alalo, a political scientist from Torre-Pacheco.
The region of Murcia, whose economy is deeply reliant on migrant labour to sustain its global exports of fruit and vegetables, burst into the spotlight in the 2019 general elections after Vox emerged as the most popular party there. It soon became a prominent force in the region, transforming Murcia into what analysts have described as a “laboratory” for anti-migrant policies.
“The People’s party doesn’t have the necessary majorities to govern, so they look to Vox,” said Alalo. “So then what happens? Migrants become an easy bargaining chip.”
The result was a series of measures that have targeted Muslims and migrants in Murcia, from a ban on religious gatherings in sports centres that mainly affected Muslims in Jumilla to the scrapping of an extracurricular scheme that had allowed 350 children to learn Arabic and about Moroccan culture.
“They’ve been trying and testing things again and again – everything works here in Murcia,” said Alalo, who is among a group that has sought to counter these initiatives with the launch of the Platform for the Rights of the Muslim Community in Murcia. “To them we’re an easy target, we’re vulnerable and don’t have political power.”
The discrimination coming from the top levels of the regional government has added to the challenges for a population that was already deeply marginalised, Alalo added. “Right now we’re in the neighbourhood of San Antonio, where about 60% of the population hails from abroad and the average income is €10,600,” he said – less than half the average salary in the region.
“Many of them live in deteriorating houses, there’s a lot of school absenteeism and young people who can’t see a future for themselves, all while they’re being discriminated against.”
The result had left some migrants feeling as though they are waging battle on multiple fronts, according to Nabil Moreno, the president of the Al Manar Islamic Community in Torre-Pacheco.
Many were grappling with issues common across Spain, such as the soaring cost of housing, but with the added burden of being demonised by rightwing forces who seize on every conflict and every issue involving them, he said. “We’ve been in this city for 30 to 40 years, we have families, we contribute to the economy. Many of us have helped to grow the economy of this town. But of course, nobody talks about this.”
The view was echoed by Naima, who said the far right would probably do little to curb migration once in power. “We work in their homes, we work in their fields, we work in everything, they’re never going to throw us out,” she said.
Instead, she felt racism was being used to rally people behind a platform that would ultimately prove disastrous to many in Spain. “If the rightwing forces win the election, the middle class will be screwed. Retirees, schoolchildren – people will see their rights rolled back,” she said. “They’re not only going after foreigners. Hopefully people won’t be taken in by all of this.”

theguardian.com.title: Former RAAF pilot convicted of murder after staging wife’s death as lawnmower accident
theguardian.com.text:
Former air force pilot Robert John Crawford has been found guilty of the murder of his wife after a jury accepted her death was staged as a fatal lawnmower accident.
Gasps and sobs could be heard in Brisbane supreme court on Friday after the jury returned a guilty verdict after deliberating since 10am on Tuesday.
Robert Crawford did not visually react to the verdict.
Frances Crawford’s body was found by paramedics at the bottom of a retaining wall near an overturned ride-on lawnmower at 4am.
Her husband was attempting to resuscitate her.
Robert Crawford was accused of murdering Frances Crawford by strangulation at the couple’s property, west of Brisbane, in the early hours of 30 July 2024, or late on 29 July.
Over three-and-a-half weeks, jurors heard evidence that included police forensic analysis of Frances Crawford’s injuries, texts between the couple and a UK forensic physician called by the defence.
They also visited the Crawfords’ hilltop home, surrounded by bushland in the Lockyer Valley.
Robert Crawford was described as a “love rat” who was motivated to kill his wife because he stood to lose financially in a divorce settlement brought on by his serial infidelity.
The former pilot faced the loss of his beloved $2m home and his early retirement plans if his wife followed through with divorce plans, jurors were told.
“He knew he stood to lose out,” crown prosecutor Chris Cook said.
“That’s why he was telling his lovers all about it.”
Referred to as a “master manipulator”, Robert Crawford embarked on a plan to make his wife’s death appear like a tragic accident, the jury was told.
“It was Mr Crawford who caused Mrs Crawford’s body to be at the bottom of the retaining wall of the property,” Cook said.
“It was Mr Crawford who also moved the lawnmower over the retaining wall.”
Robert Crawford’s defence had attacked the case against him as full of gaps filled in with speculation and wrongful suspicion.
“It is one of the weakest circumstantial cases you will ever see in a criminal court,” Robert Crawford’s barrister Saul Holt KC said.
The defence said he had engaged in multiple infidelities and lied about them but was trying to repair his marriage before his wife suffered an accident.
Robert Crawford had been busy with work calls and had let his wife move the lawnmower away from automated lawn sprinklers, Holt said.
But the prosecution said Frances Crawford would not have gone outside in her pyjamas in zero-degree weather to move an almost 250kg lawnmower that her children had never seen her use.
Robert Crawford, who was on bail throughout the trial, awaits sentencing.

theguardian.com.title: Heatwaves, floods, fires and rain: weekend of weather extremes expected across Australia
theguardian.com.text:
Major fires are among a multitude of weather extremes forecast across Australia on Friday and into the weekend, which also includes severe storms, heavy rain, floods and heatwaves.
Firefighters contending with an out-of-control bushfire on Flinders Island expected conditions to deteriorate further on Friday, as authorities confirmed at least eight buildings had been destroyed or significantly damaged.
The northern deputy regional chief of the Tasmania fire service, Steve Richardson, said: “It’s going to be fairly hot and dry.
“There won’t be much moisture in the air. It will be fairly dry, but the wind could be 20 to 30kmh that may have gusting strengths up to 50 to 60kmh.”
TasAlert has issued bushfire advice warnings for several areas in the island’s north.
People in the Leeka, Mount Tanner, Killiecrankie and Mt Killiecrankie recreation areas have been warned to take shelter after it became too late to leave, while residents of Mt Boyes, Carnacs Flat and surrounds were advised not to return, and those in Palana to monitor for changing conditions. An evacuation centre is open at the Furneaux Arts and Entertainment Centre.
Richardson said it was “unfortunate” that some residents had chosen to remain in Killiecrankie “against all the advice”.
“They’re gambling with their own lives,” he said. “We can’t guarantee that we can get firefighters in to help protect them or protect their property.”
While rain was heading towards Tasmania late on Friday, the Bureau of Meteorology’s Sarah Scully said the heaviest falls would probably miss Flinders Island, but the rainband fed by tropical moisture was an evolving situation.
“It’s a bit of a watch this space,” she said.
Scully said heavy falls were expected in northern Tasmania.
Severe weather warnings have been issued, with the potential for six-hourly rainfall totals of 40 to 70mm and the risk of flash flooding early on Saturday morning.
The rain would increase from the north on Friday evening, and extend statewide overnight.
River and creek rises were likely, and flood watches have been issued for the north-west and central coastal rivers, Forth, Mersey, Meander, North Esk, Tamar, Ringarooma and north coastal rivers.
The weather was expected to take “a big turn later today”, which may come as a surprise to “a lot of Tasmanians who would have woken up to a really dry and sunny morning”, Scully said.
Intense rain in Victoria for polling day
On Friday afternoon, rain was already beginning to fall across Victoria, where a severe weather warning has been issued for heavy rainfall and damaging winds, stretching from the south-west to the north-east. The atmosphere was “laden with moisture” that was ready to come down, Scully said.
Six hourly rainfall totals of 55 to 70mm were likely, with isolated falls up to 110mm possible, and damaging winds with gusts up to 100km/h expected to develop in the north-east on Saturday morning.
On Friday morning, some parts of the Mallee and Wimmera had already received a month’s worth of rain in about an hour, Scully said.
Yaapeet, a town of about 75 people in western Victoria, received 63mm in six hours, including about 36mm in just one hour.
“To give you an idea how heavy that is, when you look at other nearby locations through that region the monthly rainfall is expected to be less than 30mm,” Scully said.
Flash flooding could occur across the central ranges and Otways, with flood watches in place across the north-west, central and north-east catchments, including for the Yarra and Bunyip rivers.
Victorians voting on Saturday could expect conditions to ease from mid-to-late morning, although there was still the potential for showers and storms, Scully said.
To the east, storms with the potential for heavy rain, damaging winds and large hail, could affect areas stretching from southern Queensland to northern and central NSW, including Canberra and Sydney, on Saturday.
By Sunday, the rain band and thunderstorms would begin to shift into north-east New South Wales and south-east Queensland, including parts of Brisbane.
Heatwaves in the north and west
Prolonged heatwave conditions across northern Australia were expected to intensify to severe to extreme levels across northern Western Australia, with temperatures reaching into the mid-40s in the Kimberley.
Perth could see lower intensity heatwave conditions developing over the weekend, and temperatures reaching into the high 30s.
Global heating, driven mainly by the burning of fossil fuels, has increased the frequency and severity of extreme weather events, including heatwaves and bushfires.

theguardian.com.title: New Zealand election: final results show ruling coalition needs minor party to govern
theguardian.com.text:
The final results of New Zealand’s general election show the incumbent rightwing coalition will need the support of a centrist newcomer party to form a government, and to avoid sending the country back to the polls.
Preliminary results on 7 November handed the National party and its two coalition partners, the populist New Zealand First and libertarian Act parties, a slim two-seat majority, making the election too close to call until final votes were tallied.
On Friday, the electoral commission released the results from nearly 485,000 “special votes” – those cast from overseas or outside a voter’s electorate. National dropped two seats to 40, Labour stayed on 36 seats, the Greens picked up one seat to 17, Act had 13, New Zealand First 12, Opportunity seven and Te Pati Māori five.
The National-led bloc currently has 65 seats. In the 130-seat parliament, 66 seats are needed for a majority.
The revised results mean the National-led coalition has the only realistic path to power – if it can negotiate a deal with Opportunity. If it cannot, New Zealand will probably need to hold another election.
Three electorate seats changed hands after the special votes. Labour won Wairarapa off National with just 81 votes, and took Hamilton East from National with 173 votes. The Greens won Wellington Bays from Labour with 1,610 votes.
If National applies for a recount and wins back just one of those seats, it could return to power with a slim majority and without needing Opportunity. Applications for a recount must be made by 3 December, and results could take another five days.
Special votes in previous elections have favoured the left, and typically have cost the right one or two seats. Until Friday, a question mark hung over whether National would be able to govern comfortably alongside its coalition partners, or whether it would be forced to cut a deal with the Opportunity party – a newcomer centrist party that incumbent prime minister Christopher Luxon had previously ruled out working with.
After the election, Luxon softened his stance on his initial rule-out, saying he intended to find common ground with the Opportunity party.
On Friday afternoon, Luxon said National will now begin formal negotiations with New Zealand First, Act and Opportunity, but he cautioned discussions would be “challenging” and could take some time.
“Getting it right matters far more than getting it done quickly,” Luxon said. “Kiwis won’t thank us for rushing to an agreement that falls apart, or for sending them back to the polls.”
Lara Greaves, a political scientist at Victoria University of Wellington, said the prospect of New Zealand heading back to the polls was unprecedented, because negotiations between the four parties will be so complex.
“It’s not a 0% chance, it’s the highest chance we’ve ever had of it being another election,” she said.
Opportunity, led by Auckland businesswoman Qiulae Wong, has long said it will negotiate first with the party that secures the highest number of seats.
After the final results were announced, Wong confirmed she would speak with Luxon and that her party’s bottom-lines – which include climate and environment policies and capping political donations – were non-negotiable.
The party would focus on bringing New Zealanders a stable government, Wong told media, and she did not rule out heading back to the polls.
“Clearly stability is important. But setting that more hopeful and aspirational vision, where we can come together as much as possible as New Zealanders and move forward, I think is the priority,” she said.
Having Opportunity in parliament was a “pivotal moment” for the country, Wong said.
“I have every expectation that we will get in there and we will deliver, regardless of what shape the government takes.”
Previously, Wong has said its vision for a low-emissions future, and an inclusive New Zealand, will drive its final decision. Its five bottom-line issues include action on New Zealand’s supermarket duopoly, capping political donations, a 10-year cross-party plan for health, ending bottom trawling in the fishing industry and strengthening New Zealand’s climate commitments.
Negotiations with Opportunity could hit a snag with National’s coalition partner New Zealand First. On Friday, Wong confirmed she would not strike a deal if New Zealand First’s leader, the veteran politician Winston Peters, serves as foreign affairs minister – a position he has held on three occasions.
“We think that his behaviour over successive governments is not the kind of behavior that we expect of someone in that position,” she said.
In other points of tension, New Zealand First and Act have diametrically opposed climate policies, and Act are also unlikely to back Opportunity’s drive for political donation reforms.
Greaves said the Opportunity party will have to make difficult decisions over what it is prepared to gain, or lose. “For minor parties, it’s really hard to go into coalition, or be seen as being too close to a major party or propping up a government, and then turn around later and sell their brand ... as separate from that [major] party.”
Labour leader Chris Hipkins said he was proud the party had gained the highest share of the party vote, but was disappointed it could not deliver a change of government.
It is the second election Hipkins has lost, raising questions over his political future. Hipkins said a decision over his leadership would be made after a government had been formed.
New Zealand could be facing weeks of negotiations in what could become its first ever four-party coalition. In 2023, negotiations took five weeks. With Christmas just four weeks away, New Zealand may need to wait until 2027 to know the shape of its next government.

theguardian.com.title: Threat from China looms large over Taiwan’s local elections
theguardian.com.text:
Taiwanese voters go to the polls on Saturday in closely watched local elections that will shape the fortunes of the ruling Democratic Progressive party (DPP) as it navigates an increasingly precarious set of relationships on the global stage.
Saturday’s vote will choose mayors, council members and other local leaders across 22 districts. Unlike the presidential elections, in which foreign policy is often a key issue, the local elections, held every four years, are largely focused on bread-and-butter issues such as housing affordability and wealth distribution.
Nevertheless, China looms large over the vote, which takes place against the background of intense military pressure from Beijing. China claims Taiwan as part of its territory despite never having ruled the self-governing island. Taiwanese officials have raised the alarm over thousands of incidents of suspected misinformation or election interference, and certain candidates have been subjected to harassment from the Chinese authorities. There have also been reports of hundreds of China-linked AI-generated videos spreading disinformation about Taiwanese politicians disliked by Beijing.
Beijing calls the allegations of election interference “completely fabricated”. Zhu Fenglian, a spokesperson for China’s Taiwan affairs office, said the allegations “stir up anti-China sentiment to win votes”.
Wei-Ting Yen, a political scientist at Academia Sinica, Taiwan’s national research academy, said: “Even though local elections are not about China, the outcome of local elections will have huge implications for cross-strait relations.”
Most races are a tight competition between a candidate from the ruling DPP and the main opposition party, the Kuomintang (KMT). The KMT promotes closer ties with Beijing, and its chair, Cheng Li-wun, travelled to China this year to meet Xi Jinping, China’s leader. Xi has vowed to unify China with Taiwan, and has not ruled out using military action to achieve that aim.
Yen said if the KMT loses some of its traditional strongholds, Beijing “may need to reconsider what is the most effective strategy for influencing Taiwanese people”.
One of the most contentious votes is the race for Taipei mayor, an office that has been held by the KMT for three decades. The DPP has selected as its challenger Puma Shen, a national legislator whom Beijing declared a “diehard separatist” in 2024. It is the first time a candidate under sanctions by Beijing has run to be mayor of Taiwan’s capital city. In the neighbouring New Tapei City race, the DPP’s Su Chiao-hui is also proving to be a ferocious challenger to the incumbent KMT.
Shen said in a recent interview that even if he didn’t win, the capital’s mayoral race was “a slap to China” because it proved that “democracy works here in Taiwan”.
Huang Bo-kai, a 23-year-old law student, said his top concern was cross-strait relations and how US-China relations were evolving. “The world’s three major powers are increasingly willing to flex their muscles: the US attacking Iran, Russia attacking Ukraine. I think Taiwan could very well be the next target [of China],” he told the Guardian.
Taiwan’s president, the DPP’s Lai Ching-te, is detested by Beijing and has taken a bolshier stance on cross-strait relations than his predecessor, Tsai Ing-wen, who was admired for her ability to drum up support in Washington while walking a delicate tightrope to avoid angering China.
Lai has pushed for greater spending on weapons to deter military aggression from China. The government has proposed a record 18% increase in defence spending for next year, including for drones and missiles, taking it above 1tn Taiwan dollars (£23bn) for the first time.
But many Taiwanese voters would rather that money was spent on more immediate economic issues. Lev Nachman, a political scientist at National Taiwan University, said the national leaders of the DPP and KMT had been notably absent from the mayoral races, reflecting the extent to which campaigns were focused on local issues.
Going into the campaigns for the 2028 presidential elections, Lai would “try to take advantage of the momentum that [Shen] and Su have built for the DPP,” Nachman said, noting that support for those candidates would not necessarily translate into support for Lai.
Tony Yeh, a Taipei man in his 70s, said: “To put it simply, the authorities should do more to boost the economy and buy fewer weapons.”
Taiwan’s economy has boomed this year, largely thanks to the pivotal role that its semiconductor industry plays in the global artificial intelligence rally. The economy grew by more than 14% in the first nine months of the year, the fastest rate in 50 years. But nearly 70% of workers earned less than the average monthly wage of 49,152 Taiwan dollars (£1,137) in the same period.
Yeh said: “Most traditional industries are having a really tough time.”
William Yang, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, said: “The issues that really are going to determine their votes are livelihood issues including the stagnant wage, the astronomically high housing price, the affordability issue, and how the government can better make sure Taiwan’s incredible economic boom fuelled by the global AI growth is going to be distributed more evenly.”
Other voters have more niche concerns. Walking her dog in a park, Kuo Wei-tong, a nail salon worker, said policies affecting pets were among her top concerns.
“People are having fewer children and getting more cats and dogs,” she said. “I think that’s something worth giving serious consideration to as well.”

theguardian.com.title: Qantas and Air New Zealand planes too close at Sydney airport as ‘mental models’ of crews to be investigated
theguardian.com.text:
The Australian Transport Safety Bureau is investigating flight crews’ “mental models” after a Qantas plane aborted its landing at Sydney airport on Wednesday after noticing another aircraft crossing the runway while on its descent.
The ATSB said Qantas flight 426 from Melbourne was due to land just before 10.15am on Wednesday, with the Boeing 737 jet told to expect a late landing clearance due to aircraft crossing the runway.
As the Qantas plane continued to approach the airport, and before it received a clearance to land, the crew reported seeing an Air New Zealand plane crossing the runway.
The Qantas crew decided to conduct a go-around, aborting the landing before trying again.
The ATSB said it would investigate what it called an “aircraft separation issue”. The agency will gather evidence, including interviewing flight crew, looking at flight data and monitoring air traffic control audio and any available CCTV into the incident.
“In particular, the investigation will seek to ascertain what information was provided to the crews of both aircraft, and what mental models those crews held,” the agency said in a statement.
“The ATSB notes that, during the occurrence, important safety defences were in place and operated, such as the flight crew’s go-around decision.”
A preliminary report should be complete in about eight weeks, the ATSB said.
Qantas did not immediately reply to a request for comment.
“Our pilots were following air traffic control instructions and elected to conduct a go-around as the other aircraft was crossing the runway,” the airline told the Sydney Morning Herald.
Sydney airport has seen a series of near-miss incidents this year, including when a Jetstar plane narrowly avoided a collision with a Qatar Airways plane on the tarmac in August.
In another incident, a Virgin plane was forced to abort takeoff when a Qantas plane began to cross the runway in front of it.
Angus Mitchell, the ATSB chief commissioner, released preliminary investigation reports in September that found staffing levels at Sydney airport had “emerged as a recurring area of inquiry”, with a review finding runway incursions and near misses at 20% above national averages there.
“This should be viewed in the context of Sydney airport being the most complex in the country,” Mitchell said at the time.
The ATSB stressed it “has yet to determine whether staff resourcing factors directly contributed to any occurrence, or whether they were simply underlying conditions that were recognised and being effectively managed by Airservices, Australia’s air traffic services provider”.
The ATSB added Friday its examination of the recent incident would seek to look at safety defences in place “and to establish or rule out any underlying safety issues and contributing factors common across the other occurrences at Sydney airport currently under investigation”.

theguardian.com.title: Water firms to identify 250,000 vulnerable households in England eligible for discounts
theguardian.com.text:
Water companies will use government data to identify as many as 250,000 vulnerable households in England eligible for discounts, after criticism that not enough people are aware of the £428 support for their annual bills.
The Department for Work and Pensions will provide information to identify and contact a quarter of a million households who are missing out on support to which they are entitled under the WaterSure scheme.
The scheme is open to people on benefits who need to use a lot of water either for medical reasons or because their household has three or more children under 19.
The government said that 300,000 customers are signed up to WaterSure, but fewer than half of eligible households claim it because either they are unaware or they may have difficulty proving they qualify.
The Labour government has sought to portray itself as tough on the water industry. However, Andy Burnham has yet to outline his plan for the sector, despite saying he would bring in “more public control” of companies.
Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, said it was “common sense” to share information about eligible households with companies.
“Hundreds of thousands of the most vulnerable people aren’t getting help with their water bills because they don’t know how to access it,” she said. “That’s not right. By sharing data across government and water companies, we’re fixing that problem – meaning getting that help will be far easier for those who need it.”
The changes received the backing of Martin Lewis, founder of the MoneySavingExpert advice website.
He said: “Too many people miss out on help they desperately need and are entitled to. Water companies shoulder some blame for confusing applications and underpublicising support. Yet it is important the government joins the dots too. If one part of the state knows someone needs help, another shouldn’t leave them in the dark. Help is only effective if it actually reaches those who need it.”
Eagle also announced that the Consumer Council for Water, which helps households with complaints, will be given new powers to investigate water companies’ customer service and work with regulators to rectify problems. It will be named the Water Watchdog.
A spokesperson for Water UK, a lobby group for the industry, said: “Water companies have long called for government to automatically provide us with the information needed to give people heavily discounted water bills. As a result, hundreds of thousands more people will now benefit from WaterSure.”

theguardian.com.title: Nearly half of ethnic minority people in UK have faced racism at work in last year, survey finds
theguardian.com.text:
Nearly half of people from minority ethnic backgrounds have experienced racism at work and the majority have no confidence that HR would take their concerns seriously, a survey has found.
It also found that 75% of people from the UK’s five largest minority ethnic communities had experienced racism or unfair treatment linked to their race, ethnicity or religion in the previous year, and three-quarters of those who had experienced racism said it had affected their mental health to some degree.
Susan Solomon, a senior research manager and lead author of the Centre for Mental Health’s report, said: “When three-quarters of people who have experienced racism report an impact on their mental health, it is clear that racism is not just an equality issue. It is a public mental health issue.”
The findings of the survey of 2,506 adults come amid reports that racial equality is worsening and discrimination is becoming more common in the UK.
Jabeer Butt, the chief executive of the Race Equality Foundation, said the research demonstrated “how widespread racism remains in everyday life and the cumulative toll it takes on the mental health of Black, Asian and minoritised ethnic people”.
In the workplace, 45% of ethnic minority workers said they had experienced racism at work in the past year, most often passed off as “banter”, while 56% had no confidence that HR would take them seriously.
The research also revealed that 42% of ethnic minority people who had faced racism linked it to anti-immigrant protests and demonstrations, 57% saw negative posts about immigrants or minorities on social media every week, and 46% heard politicians blaming immigrants for the UK’s problems just as often.
Butt said the results showed that “racism does not occur in a vacuum”. He said: “Hostile anti-immigration rhetoric, amplified in politics and across social media, can legitimise racist attitudes and behaviour, echoing our findings following the racist riots of 2024.
“The response cannot be to ask people to become more resilient or simply to report individual incidents. Political leaders, employers, public institutions and social media platforms must challenge the narratives that fuel racism and take effective action to prevent it.”
The research highlighted a gap between experiencing racism and seeking support and help. Of the respondents who had experienced racism or unfair treatment, half said they felt they had to be constantly “on guard” and ready for racist encounters, while only 5% of people who experienced racism sought professional mental health support.
Solomon said: “Our findings show that the harm does not come only from overt acts of discrimination but from the constant effort of anticipating, managing and responding to racism in everyday life. People described living in a state of vigilance, weighing decisions about where they go, how they behave and whether it is safe to speak up.”
She added: “The research also shows that the mental health impact of racism is not limited to personal experiences of discrimination. It is compounded by exposure to anti-immigration and discriminatory rhetoric in political speeches, newspaper coverage and social media. If we are serious about protecting mental health, action must be taken to prevent the harm caused by racism before it reaches crisis point.”

theguardian.com.title: Chance of snow forecast for northern England and Scotland in next few days
theguardian.com.text:
Parts of England could see snow in the coming days as cold and unsettled weather continues into the weekend, forecasters have said.
Heavy rain sweeping eastwards on Friday could turn to snow over higher ground in northern England and Scotland.
The Met Office has issued a yellow ice warning for parts of northern England and the Midlands from 4am to 2pm on Friday.
Freezing rain could leave roads and pavements icy, particularly on higher routes across the Pennines, with up to 3cm of snow also possible, the warning states.
Forecasters also said there is a small chance of road closures, public transport disruption and injuries from slips and falls.
The Met Office meteorologist Honor Criswick said: “The cold is here to stay over the coming days.
“Not only this but it’s set to be rather unsettled at times, with heavy outbreaks of rain, possibly even some hill snow.”
Criswick added: “Also, a chance we could see some freezing rain towards high ground in northern England.
“This can lead to some slippery surfaces, so do take care if you’re out and about early first thing on Friday.”
Temperatures could plummet to -10C in parts of Scotland on Friday night, while widespread frost is also expected across Northern Ireland.
Heavy rain and hill snow are possible in northern England and Scotland on Saturday, with temperatures largely in single figures, although parts of the south-west could reach unseasonable highs of 14C.
The Met Office said that Saturday is expected to be wet and breezy for most of the UK with a brighter showery interlude on Sunday before more rain bands sweep through on Monday.

theguardian.com.title: Strobe Talbott, Time magazine reporter and deputy US secretary of state, dies aged 80
theguardian.com.text:
Strobe Talbott, a former Time magazine reporter who later served as deputy secretary of state under Bill Clinton and then headed the Brookings Institution, died Thursday. He was 80.
His son, Devin Talbott, confirmed he died peacefully after a long illness in his East Hampton, New York, home.
The elder Talbott was educated at Yale and Oxford, where he bunked with Clinton. While at the British university, after interning for Time in Moscow, the magazine asked Talbott to help translate the leaked memoirs of Nikita Khrushchev, the former first secretary of the Communist party of the Soviet Union.
Talbott did, and it landed him a job at the magazine.
After 21 years at Time, where he focused on Soviet-American relations and held positions including Washington bureau chief and a foreign-affairs columnist, he joined the Clinton administration.
Talbott joined the US state department in 1994, swiftly becoming deputy secretary of state. In that role, he was the architect of the administration’s approach to Russia and other formerly Soviet countries and conducted negotiations between the US and India after the latter’s nuclear tests in 1998.
He served as the president of the Brookings Institution, one of the US’s most prominent thinktanks, from 2002 to 2017. In that time, he also chaired the US state department’s foreign affairs policy board.
Talbott authored over a dozen books. His last book was titled Our Founders’ Warning: The Age of Reason Meets the Age of Trump, which was published in 2020.
He was born in Dayton, Ohio, in 1946, and is survived by two sons, Devin and Adrian; stepdaughter Rebecca Ascher-Walsh; siblings Kirk, Marjo and Page Talbott; and eight grandchildren, according to the New York Times.
His first wife, Brooke Shearer, died in 2009, and he later married author Barbara Lazear Ascher.

theguardian.com.title: Israeli strikes kill 16 schoolchildren so far this month, Gaza ministry says
theguardian.com.text:
Israeli strikes have killed at least 16 schoolchildren in Gaza since the start of November, as young people across the territory face intensifying bombardment and a struggle to find food, clean water and shelter.
On Wednesday, Gaza’s ministry of education said: “Palestinian students had been targeted for the third time in less than 24 hours, in an escalation reflecting the continued Israeli violations against children in the Gaza Strip. The number of schoolchildren killed since the beginning of November has now risen to 16.”
The statement follows the death of two sisters, Yusra, 15, and Jana Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, 13, in the early hours of Wednesday in an airstrike targeting a residential apartment in western Gaza City.
Yusra was a pupil at Kafr Qasim school, while her sister Jana attended al-Manar private school.
The ministry added: “The girls’ father, Mohammed Majed Abu Al-Ouf, and their mother, Noura Ezzat Abu Al-Ouf, were also killed in the strike which injured several other Palestinians.” The father was a director of internal security services for Hamas in northern Gaza.
Earlier this year, an independent UN inquiry found that Israel continued to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children in Gaza.
On 6 November, Mohammed Nidal Barbakh, 15, was shot by Israeli forces in the Bir 19 area of al-Mawasi, Khan Younis, and later died from his injuries.
He was in the 10th grade at the Muscat school and dreamed of becoming a professional football player.
“That day, after lunch, Mohammed went to the sports academy at 1.30pm to take part in training,” his father, Dr Nidal Mohammed Barbakh, said. “An Israeli tank had advanced and positioned itself on a nearby hill before firing two rounds towards the pitch. One of them ricocheted after hitting a metal object, striking Mohammed in the back and exiting through his neck.
“He was talented and an excellent student. He was killed at the age of 15, on a sports pitch in al-Mawasi, an area where people had been told to go because it was considered safe. I do not absolve the Israeli army of responsibility for what happened. It kills every ambition within us and buries our children’s dreams before they have a chance to come true.”
On 13 November, Israeli artillery shelling killed three people in Deir al-Balah, central Gaza, including a father and his 12-year-old son, Ahmed Abu Daher, as well as a woman.
Ahmed dreamed of becoming an Arabic language teacher, like his grandfather Saleh, said his mother, Walaa Abu Daher.
“That day, my husband was heading to a condolence gathering in the al-Qastal area, east of Deir al-Balah,” Daher said. “Ahmed asked his father if he could accompany him. While they were at the gathering, they were targeted by Israeli artillery fire.
“Ahmed ran to ask the people attending the gathering for help. He then rushed back towards his father when a second shell was fired. Shrapnel struck Ahmed in his legs, abdomen and head. I cannot describe how deeply their loss has affected me. I feel as though my life stopped that day.”
Thousands of school-age children and hundreds of education workers have been killed in Israel’s war in Gaza, while tens of thousands of children have been unable to attend school regularly.
On Thursday, Israeli attacks killed at least nine Palestinians across Gaza, including Khaled Abu Nada, the undersecretary of Gaza’s ministry of education, and his wife, according to health officials, as attacks continued despite the ceasefire in the territory.
A few days ago, the ministry of education said Israel’s attacks against students, civilian leaders and teachers were “part of a systematic assault on the Palestinian education system”.
According to Unicef, 98% of school buildings in Gaza have sustained damage, with more than 93% requiring major rehabilitation or full reconstruction, while approximately 81% were directly hit.
Young Palestinians in Gaza face a fourth winter in overcrowded tents and makeshift shelters, with limited access to basic services as the humanitarian and public health crisis deepens.
Children and young people are among those most vulnerable to meningitis, for which Gaza’s health ministry issued an epidemic alert on Tuesday after a sharp rise in infections, with more than 270 new cases reported in October.
Health organisations attribute the rise in infections to the destruction of infrastructure, overcrowded shelters and the contamination of drinking water with sewage – a crisis made worse by winter flooding and restrictions on humanitarian aid.
At least 74,746 Palestinians have been killed in Israel’s war in Gaza over the last three years, according to the territory’s health ministry. More than 20,000 children have been reported killed by Israeli strikes.
The Israel Defense Forces said there was not enough information to comment on the incidents involving Ahmed and Mohammed.
It said that on the day Ahmed died it was carrying out operations that resulted in the killing of “10 terrorists” and “prior to the strikes, measures were taken to mitigate harm to civilians”.

theguardian.com.title: Net migration to UK falls to lowest level since 1997 excluding pandemic
theguardian.com.text:
Net migration across the UK has fallen to its lowest level since 1997 with the exclusion of the years of the Covid pandemic.
Figures released by the Office for National Statistics and the Home Office show that the difference between people arriving and leaving the UK was 77,000 in the year ‌to ‌June ‌2026.
The ONS figures cover the year ending June 2026, down from an estimated 171,000 in 2025 and a peak of 944,000 in 2023. Annual net migration to the UK in 1997 was 48,000.
UK net migration is also for the first time in the “tens of thousands” since that target was set but never fulfilled by David Cameron’s government in 2010. An estimated 738,000 people immigrated to the UK in the year to June while 661,000 emigrated, according to the data published on Thursday.
The 62% fall over the past 12 months – from 204,000 in the year ending June 2025 – results from lower immigration. Net migration has fallen more than 90% since the peak of 944,000 in the year ending March 2023.
Immigration fell by 17% over the year to June 2026, driven by fewer non-EU citizens being granted permission to work, study, bring family members to the UK or apply for asylum.
Keir Starmer’s policies last year made care workers and some mid-skilled jobs ineligible for work visas, suspended family reunion for refugees and toughened restrictions for universities sponsoring international students.
Emigration remained relatively high but fell by 4% (-28,000) compared with the year ending June 2025.
Most people leaving the UK to live in another country were non-citizens who previously migrated for work or study, including those who moved to the UK as part of the “Boriswave” from 2021 onwards when immigration was unusually high.
Reacting to the figures, the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said Labour’s policies should be credited for the drop. It will be seen as a boost to Andy Burnham’s plans to keep hold of “red wall” seats in any future general election.
“The Conservatives lost control of our borders. Year upon year, they promised they would bring net migration down to the tens of thousands. Instead, they let it reach close to a million a year, overseeing four decades worth of migration in their last four years alone.
“This government has restored control. Where they failed, we have delivered for the British people,” she said.
Burnham said of the figures: “I think we are finally, as a country, getting into the position that the public has long wanted to see.”
Asked about the UK’s future relationship with the EU and whether freedom of movement should be up for discussion, he said the Channel crossings crisis “arose significantly in the post-Brexit years when we lost that ability to collaborate with our European partners, and we’ve had to work hard to catch up again … So, no, I don’t think you can say that Brexit did anything other than weaken control of immigration in this country.”
The drop has been driven by policies pushed through by Labour and Conservative governments.
Home Office visa data from January to June 2026 shows visa grants to international students fell by 38% (-39,200) and grants to skilled workers including those in the health and care sector and their dependants also dropped by 38% (-26,300) compared with the same period in 2025.
The end of social care visas has caused numbers to fall from 108,000 at their peak to just 1,400 last year.
Migration remains a key political issue, with Labour’s 2024 manifesto promising to reduce net migration, and aiming to “smash the gangs” involved in irregular migration and bringing asylum seekers across the Channel in small boats.
Burnham’s arrival in No 10 has signalled a shift in the way the government views legal migration. Some Labour insiders say that policy is now being driven by economic demands rather than a fear of the rise of Nigel Farage’s Reform UK, which has suffered a dip in the polls.
The Conservatives claimed their policies under Rishi Sunak’s administration were responsible for the drop, including restrictions on family members that could be brought over by care workers and changes stopping dependants moving to the UK with international students.
Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, said: “The fall in net migration is mainly a result of changes made by the previous Conservative government. We now need to go even further with a legally binding annual cap, set by parliament, at a far lower level.”
Ben Brindle, a senior researcher at the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford, said net migration could drop even further next year, and may have a “fiscal cost”.
“We are entering an unusual period where immigration has come down and may still have further to fall.
“Falling net migration is not automatically a problem for the UK economy, especially in the long run. Falling asylum migration is expected to benefit public finances. On the other hand, the number of migrants on skilled work visas has fallen even more over the past year, and that is expected to have a fiscal cost,” he said.
Sunder Katwala, the director of the British Future thinktank, said the figures “will come as a surprise to most of the public” who still tended to believe that immigration was rising. “It must now be time for the political and media debate to catch up and start a new phase of the debate about what happens next,” he said.
Other data published by the Home Office showed the number of asylum seekers living in hotels was at the lowest level since records began in 2022, but there was a 9% rise of those in “dispersal” accommodation – privately managed houses, flats or rooms in properties of multiple occupancy. There has been a drop in the number of new asylum applicants and Channel crossings are down 39% year on year, with 23,983 people having arrived in the UK in small boats in 2026.

theguardian.com.title: Trump alleges ‘fake’ economic figures released before US midterms but doesn’t provide evidence
theguardian.com.text:
Donald Trump has alleged without evidence that economic figures published by the US federal government before this month’s midterm elections were “fake” and demanded an investigation after voters roundly rejected his Republican party.
In a holiday message on social media tinged with bitterness, the US president wished a happy thanksgiving “to even those who issued fake Economic Numbers, just prior to the Election, and corrected them yesterday, three weeks late, showing that the GDP was actually 4.3%, versus 3.4%”.
While revisions to official economic figures are commonplace, Trump has tried time and again to challenge trust in economic data that does not support his claims that a historic boom is underway in the US.
The US Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), an agency within the US Department of Commerce, calculates gross domestic product, or GDP, numbers.
“Why wasn’t the correct number issued before the Election? I am asking for an immediate investigation of this situation,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform on Thursday. “This is not a small error, this is a massive, and purposeful, error”.
Trump has repeatedly claimed since taking office in January 2025 that an economic “golden age” is taking hold on his watch. Many Americans have been grappling with a higher cost of living, however – exacerbated by the economic fallout of his war on Iran – and backed Democrats in the midterms.
Trump continued his acerbic well-wishing for “a very Happy Thanksgiving to all of those people that have worked so hard to bring our Country to the Radical Far Left” as well as “those who want to redistribute Property, so that all of the hardworking people that have built up, over a lifetime, a certain Wealth, will now be forced to distribute it throughout the Country, even to those who refuse to work”.
And he revisited another ongoing beef with the news media over his controversial focus on White House renovations and decorations. “I want to commiserate with those reporters and citizens who don’t understand filth, dirt, lack of maintenance, and corruption, and are upset with me because I took time out of my very busy schedule to fix the 17 broken windows, numerous chipped and decaying columns, broken, dilapidated, and missing moldings, and lack of a proper plaster and paint job on the White House.”
The sarcastic intervention continued with a message of thanks to “the murderers, drug dealers, and criminals of all shapes, sizes, and colors” whom he claimed are “mostly gone now”.
“Happy Thanksgiving to them anyway, even though from faraway lands,” he concluded. “We miss you dearly, but you will never be back, and America will never allow what you have done to us to happen again!”
Democratic senator Chuck Schumer, vying to be majority leader in the chamber following his party’s victories in this month’s election took a more conventional approach, wishing “everyone in New York and across America a joyous and restful Thanksgiving holiday with your friends and family”.
Hakeem Jeffries, whom Democrats have nominated to be the first Black speaker in the House of Representatives, also played it straight. “Happy Thanksgiving to everyone in the community and throughout our great country! Grateful for the civil servants on the job who are working through the stormy weather to keep everyone safe,” he posted on X. “May God bless you all.”

theguardian.com.title: How much of the sharp fall in UK immigration is due to Labour’s policies?
theguardian.com.text:
David Cameron was the leader of the opposition when he made a comment on overall migration that was used to interrogate every Tory leader for the next 14 years.
Asked in January 2010 on the BBC by the interviewer Andrew Marr to address comments made by the archbishop of Canterbury calling for the population to remain under 70 million, Cameron said net immigration levels of 200,000 a year were “too much”.
“We would like to see net immigration in the tens of thousands rather than the hundreds of thousands,” he said.
It became a full-blown promise in Cameron’s Tory manifesto that year; and it was there again when he won the 2015 general election, alongside a promise to hold an EU referendum. And the promise was repeated by Theresa May in 2017 as she narrowly defeated the then Labour leader, Jeremy Corbyn.
Both Tory leaders struggled with the actual net migration numbers, which fluctuated between 195,000 and 303,000.
Boris Johnson was pressed on whether he would revive Cameron’s pledge, and his 2019 manifesto said “overall numbers will come down”. Rishi Sunak, five years later, said he would like to see the figures get to tens of thousands but his manifesto promised that “numbers would fall every year”.
It has led to some crowing by Labour – and frustration from the Tories – that numbers have finally dipped below six figures under the current government.
Migration analysts said the Tories struggled throughout the 2010s because the UK was a full member of the EU and had no way of controlling inward EU migration.
EU citizens made up a majority of immigration and net migration in the run-up to the 2016 EU referendum. Since 2022, however, EU net migration has been negative.
As the UK emerged from the Covid pandemic, Johnson opened the doors to non-EU migration and to Ukrainians and people from Hong Kong.
Madeleine Sumption, the director of the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford, said: “The previous government introduced some relatively liberal policies, including visa schemes for care workers, mid-skilled workers, Ukrainians and Hongkongers, and post-study work visas for international students.”
Several conditions that enabled Labour to achieve net migration of below 100,000 did not exist for most of the time that the Tories were in power, Sumption said.
First, the UK was part of the EU for most of the Tories’ time in office and so it had little control over inward EU migration.
Second, the Office for National Statistics still relied on an older methodology for estimating migration of British citizens under the Conservatives. The new method, introduced last year, has taken “tens of thousands off the net migration figure”, she said.
Third, high migration under the previous government – and particularly under Johnson – has left a temporary legacy of high numbers of non-EU citizens leaving the UK under Labour.
“Non-EU emigration is around 130,000 higher than it was for most of the 2010s, and that is only possible because so many non-EU citizens arrived a few years ago,” she said.
The Tories throughout the 2010s were also under pressure from business and their own party to ensure that they could expand the economy and offer tax cuts, a former cabinet minister said.
“Migration was an issue then but not top of the agenda as it has been for the last few years,” they said.
The Tories claimed credit for the fall on Thursday, after introducing immigration restrictions in the last parliament. But Labour insisted it had been the one to “restore control” at the borders after net migration came close to 1 million under the Tories.
Sumption said the net migration figure could fall further but may also be expected to rise again.
“The lower figures we see today are partly a result of government policy but partly the result of methodological changes and an increase in emigration that is expected to be temporary. The numbers could still have further to fall but there is no reason to assume they will remain below 100,000 ffor ever, even if policy remains the same,” she said.

theguardian.com.title: US Senate ‘permitting bill’ threatens clean water protections to speed up energy projects
theguardian.com.text:
An industry-backed “permitting bill” approved by the US Senate would gut key clean water protections with changes that would do little to speed up the development of major energy projects, advocates warn.
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (Baaja) passed the Senate 62-33 and is now being debated in the House. The Baaja is a “permitting reform” bill that aims to reduce the time it takes federal agencies to approve major energy and infrastructure projects, like power lines, fossil fuel pipelines, natural gas plants and datacenters.
But the legislation also includes provisions that would make it more difficult for states to put in place protections against water pollution, double the amount of time between automatic reviews of water pollution permits, and reduce transparency around the types and levels of water pollution.
More than 50 groups in communities impacted by Pfas “forever chemical” water pollution have come out against the bill, warning that they would suffer further if the legislation is approved because it would weaken some of the few mechanisms in US law that regulate the chemicals’ discharge. The law would “put us in more danger”, said Emily Donovan, co-founder of the Clean Cape Fear advocacy group in Wilmington, North Carolina, where drinking, surface, and ground water is polluted by discharge from a nearby Pfas factory.
“We already see how hard it is for the [Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)] to [regulate] Pfas,” Donovan said. “What frustrates us is we don’t need to make it harder.”
Baaja has drawn wide industry support, including among trade groups like the American Chemistry Council and American Petroleum Institute. It is opposed by virtually every major US environmental group because it would eliminate some foundational environmental protections.
The bill’s supporters say the cost is worth it because it will allow energy projects to be built faster, and hasten the transition to clean energy. Opponents say industry is using the need to transition to clean energy as cover to ram through a range of unnecessary changes to water laws that do nothing to improve energy permitting.
“BAAJA is a handout to the oil and gas industry, while doing very little to solve the permitting problems being used to justify those changes,” the Clean Water Action advocacy group, which is lobbying against the law, said in a statement. “Congress is trading away protections for states, tribes, wetlands and streams even though those protections are largely unrelated to the years-long delays at the center of the permitting debate.”
Among other changes, the bill would allow industry to sue to undo the EPA’s guidance for states on water pollution discharge. The EPA currently develops criteria that states use to limit discharge into waterways. The agency does this without issuing a formal rule, and the criteria cannot easily be challenged in court.
The Baaja would require a formal rule-making process, which would slow the clean water criteria issuance by several years, and open it to lawsuits. The criteria are used by states to develop limits on Pfas water pollution, and the change would shift more responsibility onto states that are largely under-resourced and unable to meet the challenge, Donovan said.
Another provision would change the EPA’s mandatory review of water pollution permits from five years to 10 years. The EPA uses this review mechanism to require polluters to track their Pfas and other water pollution.
Donovan pointed to the Pfas pollution in North Carolina to highlight how the provision would prolong the public’s exposure to dangerous chemicals. North Carolina regulators in 2019 put in place a health advisory limit of 140 parts per tn (ppt) for GenX, one of the main Pfas compounds polluting the state’s waterways. By 2022, the EPA established a health advisory of 10 ppt.
Advocates fear that the extended review period for pollution permits from five to ten years would create a scenario in which a company issued a water permit in 2020 may continue to pollute at higher levels for much longer.
“Imagine not being able to make a change for 10 years despite that the science is showing that a chemical is more toxic than originally thought – that’s what terrifies and frustrates us,” Donovan said. The transition to clean energy does not need to sacrifice clean water, she added.
“We can get clean energy without having to cause cancer,” Donovan said.

theguardian.com.title: Oxford museum displays seized belongings of Naga freedom fighter Gaidinliu for first time
theguardian.com.text:
In 1932, British forces in north-east India imprisoned a 17-year-old girl called Gaidinliu for leading an uprising against colonial rule. While pursuing the freedom fighter through hills and valleys in the homeland of the Naga people, colonial officers also seized some of her most treasured possessions.
They were sent to the University of Oxford’s Pitt Rivers Museum and kept in storage. Now, for the first time, the museum is exhibiting the collection of 27 items, including a basket of Gaidinliu’s notebooks believed to contain her prophetic visions as the leader of a Naga Indigenous religion, clothes, bracelets and amulets.
Also on display are protective ritual objects, taken by the British from Gaidinliu’s hiding places, which they believed she had used against them. These are a stick with a monkey skull used to ward off evil spirits, and small wooden clubs, traditionally used by Naga people to cast an omen on an enemy.
The exhibition, The Afterlives of Captured Objects, raises questions about the colonial extraction of artefacts from Indigenous communities, which were often originally catalogued using prejudiced and discriminatory language, according to the curator, Clare Harris, a professor of visual anthropology.
For example, Harris said Gaidinliu’s notebooks were derided as “meaningless scribbling” by the colonial anthropologist JP Mills, who collected them. But he also recorded that these writings “gave her immense prestige”, which suggests that they may have been seized as part of British efforts to suppress the religious and political movement that Gaidinliu led, called Heraka.
While most of the objects on display were taken by the British after Gaidinliu abandoned them while on the run, two items were more violently extracted. Textiles displayed on mannequins in the show were taken from a pair of male and female sacred clay figures from a Heraka temple in the village of Kambiron in 1931.
The textiles are shown along with a photograph taken by a British officer of another soldier kneeling with the sacred figures, which were destroyed along with the temple.
“By showing the photograph at the same time, you can make the equation visually about what was extracted by the British there,” said Harris. “The British destroy the temple and they destroy the figures, so they take away the potency of those things.”
The show follows a four-year project by researchers from India and the Universities of Edinburgh and Oxford to digitise the Gaidinliu collection and share it with Naga communities in Assam, Nagaland and Manipur. Their craftspeople have used the images to revive and revitalise traditional crafts such as basket weaving and textile making, with some of their creations included in the exhibition.
Arkotong Longkumer, a professor of anthropology and modern Asia at the school of divinity, University of Edinburgh, who co-led the project with Harris, said attempts were also being made to translate Gaidinliu’s notebooks in an effort to reconstruct a new Indigenous language for the Naga people.
He said: “There are some symbols which are recognisable within stories and myths. They may be untranslatable in a conventional sense but they are being used to try and construct a language system.”
The exhibition also aims to raise international recognition of Gaidinliu, who has long been revered as an important leader in the resistance movement that led to Indian independence. After her release from prison in 1947, she became head of a political movement advocating for recognition of a Naga homeland.
Alila Chang, one of Gaidinliu’s grandnieces, said her family felt a deep sense of pride about the exhibition. She said: “These objects are connected to our family’s history and the struggles and sacrifices of our people as well. We want the world to know her struggles and for what reason she fought.”
Chang, who has come to Oxford for the exhibition’s private view, also shared a more personal recollection of Gaidinliu as a “very affectionate grandmother”.
“I remember [her] giving us sweets,” she said, adding how Gaidinliu, who died in 1993, would pray for her and her sibling when they went to school in the morning.
“She will always be in our hearts, but I think she belongs to the world now.”

theguardian.com.title: Fifa confirms cyber-attack exposed ‘personal and business information’
theguardian.com.text:
Fifa confirmed that hackers gained access to a “limited set of personal and business information” in a cyber-attack, amid heightened concern over digital vulnerabilities of leading organizations and institutions.
The global soccer governing body said it “condemns in the strongest possible terms the unlawful acquisition and publication of information, particularly personal data”, in a statement to the Associated Press on Thursday. “Such actions constitute a serious and unacceptable violation of privacy and can have significant consequences for the individuals concerned.”
Last week, a group calling itself the Handsome Boy Hacking Club posted a screenshot on X of what it claimed were Fifa files. The post has since then been removed after the account was suspended from X.
The Fifa cyber-attack is the latest high-profile digital disruption to hit a major organization in recent weeks.
Microsoft experienced a widespread outage earlier this month that caused disruption to millions of users, organizations and businesses across the globe. The company said the outage was a “technical issue” not related to cyber-attacks or AI agents.
The following day, the US experienced an unprecedented nationwide disruption to air travel that prompted a “ground stop” order to be issued by the US Federal Aviation Administration, which cited “communication issues” impacting air traffic control centers.
Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, later said in a news conference that preliminary investigations into the stoppage did not indicate that it was tied to a “nefarious attack”.
Three days later, customers reported service outages and difficulty accessing their online accounts at several major US banks and the money transfer service Zelle after a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase caused ripple effects throughout the financial system.
Such disruptions have intensified fear and concerns about the advancement of artificial intelligence, and the potential risks, even though there is no direct evidence that AI directly sparked the issues.
ESPN reported that unnamed sources said the Fifa hack accounted for less than 0.1% of data held by the organization, an that the breach was not a result of systems or technology failure on Fifa’s part, with hackers said to have gained access by impersonating staff.
As of now, it has not been shared when the cyber-attack took place, or the precise nature of the hacked information.
“FIFA is working closely with the relevant authorities, including law enforcement,” the organization said its statement sent to the Associated Press.
The cyber-attack comes as Gianni Infantino, Fifa’s president, is under scrutiny for a proposal to sell chunks of the World Cup to private investors.
Infantino admitted the project “has created divisions of a nature that are no longer in the interest of the objective”, amid widespread anger globally.
The plan has caused tensions within football around the world, leading Uefa to threaten a boycott of future Fifa tournaments if it was not shelved.
Uefa and other confederations have stepped up their search for candidates to run against Infantino in next year’s Fifa election, in which he had been expected to comfortably win a fourth term.

theguardian.com.title: What would happen if Russia detonated a nuclear weapon in space?
theguardian.com.text:
German media outlets have reported, citing western intelligence agency assessments, that such a satellite could be launched within 60 days and would be operational shortly afterwards.
Here we look at the implications of a nuclear weapon being detonated in space.

theguardian.com.title: EU leaders wrestle over Ukraine aid as potential Le Pen victory sparks fear
theguardian.com.text:
EU leaders were bracing for a clash over long-term financial aid for Ukraine amid an effort to finalise high-stakes budget talks by the end of the year.
Arriving in Brussels on Thursday, the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, reiterated his view that all EU member states should support a €45bn (£38bn) loan for Ukraine for 2027. “When the European Union provides funding, it does so as the European Union – and that union consists of 27 member states, not 23 or 24,” he said.
Merz has previously threatened to veto the bloc’s next seven-year budget unless all countries sign up to the Ukraine loan, which would be a painful outcome for member states that are net recipients of EU funds.
Slovakia, Hungary and Czechia, net beneficiaries, want to opt out of the loan. Slovakia’s prime minister, Robert Fico, who has maintained close ties to the Kremlin, has accused Merz of blackmail.
Separately, Germany is seeking to insulate future EU funding for Ukraine from a Marine Le Pen victory in next year’s French presidential elections. The far-right National Rally leader, who is leading in opinion polls, has vowed to stop French financial aid for Ukraine. Berlin wants to ensure future decisions on funding Kyiv via the EU budget are made by a majority of EU member states, rather than unanimously. The current system requires consensus, enabling one country to veto a decision.
In a more hopeful sign for Kyiv, Bulgaria, which had been against the loan, said on Thursday it was ready to contribute as long as its share was not linked to weapons.
“Bulgaria is going to ‌take part in the loan of 20bn [for] non-military support for Ukraine,” the country’s prime minister, Rumen Radev, said as he arrived at the summit. “We have a huge historic diaspora of Bulgarians living in Ukraine. Our wish is to concentrate our support in that ‌area. We are going to contribute, but no money from Bulgaria for weapons.”
The European Commission last week proposed a €45bn EU loan for Ukraine to fill a funding hole caused by Russia’s relentless attacks. EU officials proposed €25bn for military spending and €20bn for Ukraine’s civilian needs, such as schools and hospitals.
Arriving at the summit, Czechia’s populist prime minister, Andrej Babiš, was in no mood for compromise. “Cohesion is really the goal of the European Union and [the] Czech Republic. We will fight for this money,” he said, referring to the EU’s cohesion funds, which are intended to help poorer regions catch up with richer ones.
Babiš said his country needed a highway to Austria and more hospitals. “Financing of Ukraine should be negotiated separately. And the most important is the life of our citizens,” he said, adding that the EU should “do everything” to support peace in Ukraine.
But Merz’s stance has won widespread support, especially among western European, Nordic and Baltic states. Sweden’s prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, said: “It’s not acceptable to simply kidnap the support for Ukraine by saying that we will accept the European Union support for Ukraine, but we will not pay for it ourselves. That is not a reasonable way of thinking.”
However, some governments that support Merz’s goal have reservations about his tactics, fearing the public threat to block cohesion funds could make it harder for recalcitrant governments to climb down.
The discussion on support for Ukraine has become entangled in negotiations over the EU’s next long-term budget, which will set the bloc’s spending priorities for 2028-2034.
EU leaders are discussing a €1.78tn proposal presented by the European Council president, António Costa, last Saturday, which represents a 10% reduction on the original €2tn plan from the European Commission.
EU officials want to finalise a budget deal by the end of the year before a sequence of big elections in 2027 complicates finding an agreement, with most concern over French presidential elections in the spring. As well as ceasing funding for Ukraine, Le Pen has vowed to slash France’s contributions to the EU budget.
The French president, Emmanuel Macron, who is battling to preserve EU farm subsidies for French farmers and a larger budget, has also indicated he could walk away from talks if there was no deal by the end of the year. “An agreement is not an end in itself, nor an objective in itself if it were based on unbalanced foundations,” an Élysée source said before the summit. If the elements are not right, “the president thinks it will not be possible for him to continue this discussion beyond December”, the source said.
The Irish taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said it was important to get a budget agreement before the end of the year as “the prospects of doing it in the first half of 2027 are very dim”.
Others have pushed back against allowing French elections to dominate the EU budget timetable, and have said making Le Pen the focus gives her ammunition to make a case that the EU is against her political movement. “We should be aware of a self-fulfilling prophecy,” said one senior EU diplomat. “Let’s not be paralysed by elections happening in six months.”
